sources.title: How John Rush builds and grows $5K/month online directories with keyword research, no-code and SEO
sources.originalTitle: Do this to build a $200,000 side hustle (The Online Directory Blueprint)
sources.summary: John Rush walks through his directory playbook live: validate ideas with Google Keyword Planner, buy a keyword-matching domain, launch a minimal no-code site in one evening, promote on Reddit and social, then add SEO. He also covers monetization (sponsors, affiliates, paid listings), selling directories, and using directories as a traffic channel for SaaS.

principles.text: Start every directory idea with keyword research: check search volume before building anything.
principles.quote: I basically spend hours in that tool every day just throwing all random ideas into that tool and seeing whether there is traffic or not

principles.text: Do the minimum to validate assumptions, then invest real human time only in what wins.
principles.quote: you have to be doing as little as possible to validate all the assumptions and then the assumption that wins going to take more of your time

principles.text: Launch no-code so you can iterate on marketing pages and experiments fast.
principles.quote: once you launch you have to do marketing and marketing goes around marketing Pages marketing experiments AB tests

principles.text: Run several small bets at once and double down on the best performer after 30 days; don't fall in love with one idea.
principles.quote: never fall in love with the idea for a directory but rather make maybe five bats and then in 30 days look at the one that does the best and then put more time into that

principles.text: After validation, data quality drives growth: experts who see great data share it with their audience.
principles.quote: if that expert who sees your direct sees that the value of the content is high the quality is high they really respect that and they they really want to share with their audience

principles.text: Directories are an easier SEO route than a branded SaaS, and can funnel traffic into your products.
principles.quote: it is much harder to win SEO traffic for a SAS tool than for a directory

sources.title: How John Rush runs 26 apps and $250K/month: presales, co-makers, cross-promo
sources.originalTitle: I Make $250K/Month From 20 Apps
sources.summary: John Rush explains his repeatable blueprint for launching 20+ products: start from your own pain, get a waitlist and presales, deliver manually, then build with a 50/50 co-maker. He covers marketing via SEO, daily social, directories and cross-promotion between apps, plus AI usage, margins and building in public.

principles.text: Validate before building: 100 waitlist signups, a 90% off presale, 5 sales, then deliver the solution manually before any code.
principles.quote: I launch uh a weight list and I see whether I am able to generate 100 signups. I email them all and I offer them 90% discount on a pre-sale before I build anything. And then if I get five sales, I build the first MVP.

principles.text: Iterate on a manual service first; it is far easier to change a routine than code.
principles.quote: it's easier to iterate when there is no product, when there's no code. It's much easier because I just have to change my own routine and my own service.

principles.text: Recruit a co-maker with a validated idea and split ownership 50/50.
principles.quote: if I pitch them the idea that has past the validation part I have pre-sales done and I have some users it's really easy to convince needs them to join and we share the ownership 50/50.

principles.text: Great marketing is a great product, but start average and use boring channels (SEO, daily social, directories) to get first users.
principles.quote: usually you start with an average product and you have to do the boring marketing methods to bring first users and then use those users to improve your product and make it great.

principles.text: Cross-promote and integrate your apps so users flow across the whole ecosystem; free tools feed premium ones.
principles.quote: I link tools with each other and the other thing that's more interesting is that I integrate tools with each other.

principles.text: Building in public builds a direct audience channel that lets you fix products before shipping, cutting failure from 90% to 10%.
principles.quote: Before building in public, my failure rate was really high. 90% of the things I've done failed. And when I start building in public, it flipped.

sources.title: How John Rush runs 24 AI products to $3M ARR: validate with Google, waitlists, and pre-sales
sources.originalTitle: He Makes $3M/Year From Tiny AI Tools (Here’s How You Can Too)
sources.outlet: Chris Koerner on The Koerner Office Podcast
sources.summary: John Rush explains how he builds small AI agents and tools as a solo bootstrapper. He covers finding ideas via Google autocomplete and keyword research, validating with waitlists, outreach and discounted pre-bookings, and his five growth channels: social, SEO, affiliates, distribution everywhere, and free tools.

principles.text: Build products that scratch your own itch; run them internally for a year or more before launching publicly.
principles.quote: Well, they all start as my internal agent and I run them for a long while so that I'm happy with them myself and also it's easier to run a project if you're the only customer

principles.text: Mine Google autocomplete and keyword tools for demand in small niches VCs ignore; they are good for million-dollar solo businesses.
principles.quote: it's not a billion dollar idea right but if you're regular person and you want to build a million dollar business that's on of the market right

principles.text: Try to kill your idea during validation; test with a simple waitlist, outreach, then discounted pre-bookings.
principles.quote: if you ask for a payment and you don't get at least 10% of your weight list to, you know, execute it, it means that it won't be easier after, right?

principles.text: Use landing page builders (Framer, Webflow, Unicorn) for landing pages, not vibe coding tools made for apps.
principles.quote: you have landing pages and you have your web app and for landing pages use landing page builder

principles.text: Start SEO on day one as both a traffic channel and a validation signal, since it compounds.
principles.quote: SEO traffic is a new source of validation because you know one thing that you have to also validate with a product is not just if people want it but also if you're able to drive traffic there

principles.text: Offer very generous affiliate commissions (up to 50%) and place your product everywhere, including for LLM training data.
principles.quote: You should be crazy generous. Like go 50%. Like if you don't have costs on your product, go for 50%.

sources.title: How John Rush builds SEO directories: keyword research first, no-code build, then monetize
sources.originalTitle: How to Build SEO Directories (Step-by-Step) With John Rush
sources.summary: John Rush walks through building SEO directory sites. Most of the outcome is decided by keyword research and the domain, with data curation second and technology a distant third. He validates keywords with Google Keyword Planner for traffic and Google search for competition, then builds fast with no-code, seeds listings by scraping, promotes, and monetizes.

principles.text: Directories are won on keyword research and domain; data quality is second, tech is a small slice.
principles.quote: the directories are 80% success lays in keyword research and domain that's 80% literally the other 15% is in the data duration like actual items so you have to have good items and 5% is in technology

principles.text: Start with good keywords; bad ones (low traffic, high competition) can never be won.
principles.quote: if you have good keywords to start with you have chance to win that traffic if you have bad keywords to start with the keywords with low traffic and high competition you will never win no matter what you try

principles.text: Validate demand with Keyword Planner and competition with a Google search.
principles.quote: I use Keyword Planner for the traffic research and I use Google search to understand whether the competition is high or not

sources.title: How John Rush runs a portfolio of bootstrapped startups with AI, a shared audience and co-makers
sources.originalTitle: AI IS MY CO-FOUNDER (this changes everything) | John Rush
sources.summary: John Rush explains how he validates many startup ideas by pitching them to a large audience he built on LinkedIn, X and Reddit, then building only the ones that draw engagement. Because the same audience uses multiple products, he treats lifetime value as the sum across his whole portfolio.

principles.text: Build a distribution channel first, pitch many ideas, and only build the ones that draw engagement.
principles.quote: I built this massive distribution channel on LinkedIn X and other and Reddit and then I pitch my ideas a lot of ideas and whenever I see one idea that gets a lot of comments and likes and questions from the users I take it forward

principles.text: A shared audience across many products multiplies lifetime value, since LTV sums across all products one person uses.
principles.quote: lifetime value now is a sum of all my products that are used by the same person in average. So if otherwise lifetime value of one product is $400 for example but if I have 10 products then it's $4,000.

sources.title: John Rush: directory ideas, micro-influencer buying, and selling validated startup drafts
sources.originalTitle: I can't believe he shared these $1M+/year startup ideas
sources.summary: John Rush explains why growth tools beat build tools, how to pick ideas by asking how you'd sell them, and why directories are underrated. He shares a keyword-gap method for validating directories and how he buys micro-influencer posts for $100-300.

principles.text: Building is easy; growth is the scarce skill, so build tools around growth and marketing.
principles.quote: it's easy to build stuff but it's not easy to grow like that's kind of like 99% of the makers can build stuff but only few can actually grow and sell and bring in customers

principles.text: Start ideas from how you'd sell them: watch what people ask for, then wrap the steps into a one-job micro tool.
principles.quote: I think the best way to come up with the idea is to start with how would you sell it so basically uh don't build stuff but just see what people are actually looking for

principles.text: Single-purpose tools are easy to remember and recommend in threads where people ask how to do X.
principles.quote: if tool just only does one thing then it's easy for the user to remember this tool and to recommend that tool comparing to the tools doing like a lot of things

principles.text: Validate directories with a technical test: find a high-traffic keyword with no directory on page one of Google, then build one.
principles.quote: find keyword with high traffic search for it if it doesn't have any directory on the first page of Google go and build it and you can do that for 10 ideas like it's cheap it's fast

principles.text: Copy working English directories into other languages and countries where none exist.
principles.quote: find the directory that's working really well in us uh and just find a country where there is no directory like that and it's easy to find you Just Google like the best thing about directories is that the whole research is in Google

principles.text: Buy micro-influencer posts, bargain down, and become a repeat buyer to get lower fixed prices.
principles.quote: usually they start with really high price so you would get like you know 700 or 800 at the start uh and you should just bargain that down to few hundred and and that usually works even if they say no

sources.title: John Rush on solo-founder AI agents, picking niches, and directories
sources.originalTitle: Insight Jam Podcast - John Rush
sources.summary: John Rush explains why he bootstrapped after a VC-backed decade and built agents that replace teams. He covers when an agent is good enough to ship, why founders should avoid popular ideas, how to validate via services, why directories are the easiest first product, and why startups take about 10 years.

principles.text: Solo founders and tiny talented teams will outcompete big funded startups.
principles.quote: we will move into the world where solo Founders or tiny teams with very focused and talented people will out compete these bigger startups and corporations

principles.text: Only launch an agent once it clearly saves users about 90% of their time.
principles.quote: before I go to the market with every tool I have every agent I have it has to be good enough that it the message is clear like it saves you 90% of the time

principles.text: Avoid competition: pick unsexy niches where you stay the only player, not just today but tomorrow.
principles.quote: your job as a Founder to make sure you avoid competition so to make sure that you are the only one doing what you do not just today but also tomorrow

principles.text: Start with a service in a niche, then turn the repeatable part into a product.
principles.quote: while you do the service you learn what could be turned into the product what part of the service could be turned into the product

principles.text: Directories are the easiest first product: quick to build and promoted through SEO.
principles.quote: it's the easiest tech product one can build it takes half an hour to to start and then it takes some time to collect the items and to you know write good descriptions

principles.text: Treat startups as a 10-year game; the first years are training camp, so pick fights you can win.
principles.quote: people should enter the game only if they accept the fact that the game will take 10 years and the first three to four years is almost like a training camp

sources.title: John Rush on why directories survive AI: quality data, Reddit, and LLM SEO
sources.originalTitle: An Unfiltered Talk with John Rush: Directories, AI SEO & Building To Win
sources.summary: John Rush explains why he went all-in on directories after years of being told they were dead, why crowding shifts the win to quality, and why LLM search will send more clicks to directories than blogs. He also lays out a simple LLM SEO playbook: Reddit, top Bing and Google rankings, and social mentions.

principles.text: When a space gets crowded, the one with the best quality and work wins and the rest lose.
principles.quote: when Place gets crowded uh the the one who does the best quality and the the best work kind of wins and the rest will lose

principles.text: Spend months thinking before building; collecting ideas over time makes the build itself fast.
principles.quote: I spent like month or years thinking and then people ask like how long how long does it take to succeed and I'm like well from the moment I started building and I built it it was pretty fast

principles.text: The main reason people sign up for a product is to be entertained, so keep the process simple, one step at a time, neither too hard nor too easy.
principles.quote: I think that the number one uh Reon people sign up for a product is to be entertained

principles.text: Gamify early progress for beginners: impressions show up before clicks, so showing them keeps people moving forward.
principles.quote: Impressions come before clicks but it's cool because they already see some some progress right with impression because if you only put analytics then it's only clicked clicks and clicks come way later

principles.text: LLMs raise the quality bar; directories with really good data win, because LLMs can't invest the effort a single focused directory can.
principles.quote: directories that are winning they're having really good data right and uh that means that you have to make better directories and and and then you're ahead because LMS will be always logging behind

principles.text: To rank in LLMs, be on Reddit, on top of Bing and Google, and mentioned on social media.
principles.quote: if you want to play the game really really well you have to be a on Reddit uh B on top of the bank C on top of the Google and be on top of social media

sources.title: How John Rush runs an 80% automated, 0-employee business with AI agents
sources.originalTitle: How I Run A 0-Employee Business With Ai Agents
sources.outlet: The Next Wave - AI and the Future of Technology
sources.summary: John Rush explains how he left VC-backed startups to run solo with AI agents. He prototypes ideas in Lovable and tests them with users, uses specialized agents for real work, and runs SEO content at volume, then improves only the winners. He also shares views on directories, SEO vs AIO, and agents as autopilot.

principles.text: Prototype ideas with AI instead of Figma: build many versions in a day and let users pick the winner.
principles.quote: I built like around 10 different prototypes using lovable within one day with different kind of ideas in place, the different designs, different UX, and then I bring that to my friends.

principles.text: Test prototypes silently: users try all of them without talking, and you see which one is understood.
principles.quote: I don't ask any questions. I just tell them, "Try that. Don't talk to me. Just try them all."

principles.text: Validate solo first; only bring in a co-maker once about 10 licenses sell.
principles.quote: when I manage to actually get attention and I sell at least 10 licenses for that, uh then it's a sign that it works. Then I go and find somebody who will build with me further.

principles.text: Use general agents for prototypes, then switch to specialized agents for real work, since they've fixed the corner cases.
principles.quote: the best way to use AI agents is to basically find specialized agents for every task and then you start by using general agent.

principles.text: Build agents that run on autopilot for busy founders; the user acts as a boss giving feedback, not a tool operator.
principles.quote: my main users are the busy founders like me who don't want to become more productive. I just want to do nothing and the whole thing happens

principles.text: Treat AI content like seed funding: generate 100 articles, then spend time improving the top 3 performers.
principles.quote: after the last day of the month I go to the analytics and I see which are the three articles that did the best and then I spend an hour to improve those three articles.

sources.title: How John Rush built a $3.5M ARR AI agent portfolio with no VC and tiny teams
sources.originalTitle: How I Built My $3.5M AI Empire Without VC Money (Stripe Screenshare)
sources.summary: John Rush explains his bootstrapped studio model: he builds the first MVP, pairs with a 50/50 co-maker, and holds every product forever as part of a cross-promoting ecosystem. SEO Bot reached about $120K MRR with two people. He also covers his growth split, pricing ladder and SEO backlink advice.

principles.text: Hold products forever; even non-earning tools work as marketing channels that feed the rest of the ecosystem.
principles.quote: they act as marketing channels for me. Like I have directories. I have like 25 or 35 directories right now. Like a lot of them and most of them make no revenue. But they drive traffic to all my other tools.

principles.text: Start pricing low with builders as first customers, then raise the price and move to teams once they love it.
principles.quote: I usually start with smaller check just that my first customers are the builders because I like to build product for builders first because they give me good feedback and they actually become part of my product team and once I get to a place where they love it then I increase the price

principles.text: Show how your own tools help you, and share the results publicly. It markets both products.
principles.quote: I show everybody how the tool is helping myself, right? So uh in case of SEO bot I use it for all my other products and then I share the results and that helps a lot

principles.text: Growth split: about 30% SEO, 30% cross-promo across products with one audience, 30% build-in-public social, 10% other.
principles.quote: So 30% SEO, 30% crossromo, and 30% is social media where I build in public and other people share uh that they use my product too.

principles.text: Talk directly to users at scale; fast fixes make them loyal and turn them into ambassadors.
principles.quote: I spend time to listen to the users and I have chats going on with a lot of the users. I don't think anyone on earth has more chats than me.

principles.text: To win a specific SERP, build exact-anchor backlinks to that exact URL and add many internal links.
principles.quote: the most typical serious work you can do on SEO is to take page by page and just try to win against competitors using backlinks to that exact page.

sources.title: John Rush: Go deep on one project, price at $49+, use AI SEO, and don't quit your job
sources.originalTitle: John Rush: Buying an $800k product, SEO, & why indie hackers should not quit their jobs | BBoJS #6
sources.summary: John Rush argues indie hackers should go deep on one project instead of launching many MVPs, and learn every founder skill over time. He covers lessons from buying an $800k product (Unicorn Platform), pricing so customers actually need the product, SEO as both traffic and copy, and not quitting your job.

principles.text: Don't spray MVPs hoping one sticks. Add a new founder skill with each project so your odds rise.
principles.quote: you have to increase your skill set over time. So in the first years you learn to build MVPs in the second year you learn to do SEO in the third year you learn to do cold sales in the fourth year you learn UX

principles.text: Go deep on one project. Once it's built, you're forced into marketing, content, SEO and sales.
principles.quote: if the project has been built, and there's no more code to write, then you have no choice but do marketing, content creation, SEO, sales, etc.

principles.text: Customers buy solved problems, not features. A $49 price filters for people who actually need the product.
principles.quote: if people don't pay you 49, it's not because it's too expensive, it's because you they don't need it. And if you make it cheaper, they make pay for it, but they still don't need it.

principles.text: A weak product can't be rescued by marketing. If it isn't doing well, the product is the problem.
principles.quote: If if my product is not doing well, it's because the product is bad, not because the marketing is bad.

principles.text: SEO gives traffic and also better copy, because search terms match how people describe the problem. Start with AI content, then edit it by hand.
principles.quote: the best thing you can do is AI plus human. So, whenever you use a tool that does things for you, go help that tool to do the work better.

principles.text: Don't quit your job early. Less time forces you to focus on what matters.
principles.quote: If you can't build your product with a mild traction by spending just two days a week on the product, even spending 5 days a week will not help you.

sources.title: How John Rush built 26 AI products in 3 years bootstrapped with a 50/50 co-maker model
sources.originalTitle: He Built 26 AI Products in 3 Years (No VCs, $3M ARR) | John Rush
sources.summary: John Rush explains his bootstrapped playbook: build an audience in public, sell before building, ship a tiny MVP with no-code tools, and split 50/50 with a technical co-maker. He also covers directories, AI agents, automating toward one-button tools, and staying productive by skipping unimportant work.

principles.text: Validate by sharing the idea publicly, then sell it manually to ~10 people before building anything.
principles.quote: I just don't even build the tool I do the job myself like I'm the tool and then I sell that to around 10 people to validate whether people are willing to pay for that or not.

principles.text: Keep teams tiny: split 50/50 with a co-maker who codes, and hire no one until ~50k MRR.
principles.quote: We hire no more people until we hit at least 50k MR and only then we probably hire some people.

principles.text: Build in public: marketing becomes a byproduct of your process, and you launch to an audience already waiting.
principles.quote: the marketing was a byproduct of you sharing your own process. So there's no extra special marketing you have to do on top of it.

principles.text: Focus on one social platform until about 4-5k followers, then expand to all platforms.
principles.quote: get somewhere to 4k or maybe 5k followers and then go everywhere like all 10 platforms stack LinkedIn everything else.

principles.text: Start with the audience, not the product: try to sell first, perfect the pitch, then build a simple MVP.
principles.quote: I start with the audience and then I go back and get to the product. You have to figure out whether you can build the audience for this because you will have to build the audience once you launch.

principles.text: Don't spend effort on unimportant things early; put almost all effort into the pitch, and use templates.
principles.quote: don't do anything that's not important yet. Just put 1% effort, get something out, don't care. Be embarrassed.

sources.title: Building AI agents people use: 10/90 speed, one-button UX, and building without expectations
sources.originalTitle: Building AI Tools People Actually Use with John Rush | Chipp Builder Series
sources.summary: John Rush explains his 10/90 approach (10% of action gives 90% of outcome), why AI agents beat copilots, and why he keeps agents to a single "turn on" button. He also covers how adoption needs viral show-don't-tell demos, why most launches die, and why founders should solve problems they see around them.

principles.text: Do every task quick and not perfect; the compound effect of 10/90 turns weeks or months into days.
principles.quote: basically I do everything quick and not perfect and if you you know sum that app The Compound Effect of that is huge you just do stuff in days not weeks or not months

principles.text: Build agents, not copilots: an agent works while you sleep and you wake up to finished work.
principles.quote: if you use it as an agent it works when you sleep so that's what I do

principles.text: Resist adding buttons to an agent; one 'turn on' button is the key, and users stop asking once they see the value.
principles.quote: the only button you need for the agent is turn on that's it you can have more buttons and it's really hard to resist urge

principles.text: People talk about AI far more than they use it; a viral demo showing exactly how to use it drives real adoption.
principles.quote: unless they see something viral that shows exactly how to use it so that's that that's the reality

principles.text: Expect nothing from launches since most die; enjoy the process and be very happy when one works.
principles.quote: people should not expect anything from from their launches like I try to enjoy the process

principles.text: Find ideas by looking around for problems that bother you, not by inventing them from inside; money as the motive is a way to fail.
principles.quote: never bring it from inside like look around and see the problems and then solve them

sources.title: How John Rush runs 24 products: niche-first, no-ask feedback, build in public, buying back time
sources.originalTitle: $2M a Year Running 24 Startups he Founded (feat John Rush from Unicorn Platform)
sources.outlet: Morning Maker Show with Sandra and Dan
sources.summary: John Rush explains how he left VC-backed startups for bootstrapping 24 products and grew on X from 72 followers. He covers niche-first strategy, never asking for feedback, turning his own problems into products, and buying back time with tools.

principles.text: Go as narrow as you can on niche. Broad markets are a lottery crowded with funded competitors. Widen later by removing filters.
principles.quote: I think the more Niche you go the better and you have to cut it from all the sides you can it has to be you know one problem one specific type of problem within that problem

principles.text: Never ask for feedback. Open a channel so users volunteer it, e.g. invite-only signup via DMs.
principles.quote: I never ask for feedback not a single time in my life like never and the thing I do instead is that I create a Channel between us so that you feel comfortable asking not asking but giving the feedback

principles.text: Feedback from free users, friends, or people you ask is unreliable. Trust unprompted feedback from people far from you.
principles.quote: feedback from free users is bad for you feedback from friends is bad for you and feedback from people who you ask for feedback is also bad

principles.text: Grow on X by copying what big accounts did early, then become yourself and post what your ideal followers would post.
principles.quote: I just look at people with a lot of followers I scrolled far back to their Old Post and there's filter on Twitter you can do that

principles.text: Your own problems are your best product ideas. Run tools internally first, and productize what costs you 10 hours a month.
principles.quote: my problem is my fuel and the way I come up with all the ideas if there was no problem my ideas would would be worthless because I would be just guessing what people need

principles.text: Buy back your time with paid tools rather than doing things by hand. Hours saved outweigh $100/month.
principles.quote: almost everything you do could be bought back if you pay something and you save time right

sources.title: John Rush on indie hacking: wrappers, niche boilerplates, and why bootstrappers win on speed
sources.originalTitle: Stripe acquires LemonSqueezy, SaaS boilerplates, indie hacking in Europe is hard
sources.summary: A conversation prompted by Stripe acquiring LemonSqueezy. John Rush argues indie makers can build wrappers on top of big platforms, win with niche boilerplates, and beat VC-backed teams by launching early and talking to users. He also covers why good products always find users and why Europe suits bootstrappers.

principles.text: Building a wrapper on top of a big platform is smart, not lazy. Users care about experience, not the layer underneath.
principles.quote: in fact it's a good thing everything is a rupper and the higher level it is the smarter you are

principles.text: Don't build a generic boilerplate against an incumbent. Pick a specific niche where you can win the audience.
principles.quote: don't do the generic one because there's one that's cool and everybody knows and you will not win that audience against mark But if you make something for specific Niche you might win

principles.text: Bootstrappers win by launching unfinished and talking to users early, while VC-backed teams build in a bunker.
principles.quote: if you're booster founder you launch as soon as you can if you're a good with Boost founder and it means you launch unfinished product but also it means that you talk to the user very early

principles.text: Paid growth no longer works well. Bots, weak retention and high cost make VC money less of an advantage.
principles.quote: paid growth sucks 10 years ago paid growth was amazing

principles.text: Great products find users. A weak landing page is a reliable signal of a weak product, because marketing and UX skill go together.
principles.quote: I never seen great product without users every time somebody says they have a great product and they have no users just because users are dumb

principles.text: The indie maker community is a free launchpad: early adopters give fast, critical feedback, then you grow beyond the bubble through SEO and social.
principles.quote: we sell to each other at the start we are very good users because we give good feedback and we are very critical

sources.title: How John Rush generates startup ideas: pain mining, keywords, clones and one-feature micro-SaaS
sources.originalTitle: How To Generate Startup Ideas. The Big Talk with John Rush.
sources.summary: John Rush walks through his methods for finding startup ideas: replying to public complaints with a solution, tweeting many ideas, cloning across markets, keyword research, automating your own job, and splitting out one feature of a big tool. He argues for starting with safe, simple ideas, being patient, and building for trends before they get big.

principles.text: Prefer B2B pain over B2C: businesses change habits to make more money, consumers rarely change habits.
principles.quote: with b2v it's easier because it's money if you use better tools you make more profits that's why people are more likely to change their habits

principles.text: Find a pain people complain about publicly, offer a solution on the spot, and validate with a waitlist before building.
principles.quote: single best way to find an idea is to see that people complain about something and then offer solution right there so that you validate whether the person who complaints thinks it's a good solution

principles.text: Pitch many ideas publicly; most flop unseen, and a hit with no followers proves the idea is good.
principles.quote: if you have chance to try 50 ideas just be by like one of them will be good you don't know which one and that's why you should try to pitch your idea to the market

principles.text: Start with safe ideas: clone a proven product into a new market, or change its price or audience. Skip the romantic world-changer story.
principles.quote: when you start you should remove the Romantic po of you being next to jobs changing the world at least for the first idea

principles.text: Take one feature of a big tool, build a micro-SaaS for only that, cheaper, with an obvious keyword name. It is validated, SEO-friendly and easy to recommend.
principles.quote: you take that feature and you build a tool a micros house with one feature all day you you don't add anything else only that one feature and then you drop the price

principles.text: Work on things of tomorrow: pick an area you know deeply, predict where it goes, and build before the wave is big.
principles.quote: you should always work on things of tomorrow okay so you should always try to predict because it takes time for you to gain experience

sources.title: How John Rush bootstrapped Mars X and acquired Unicorn Platform: acquisitions, AI and UX
sources.originalTitle: Million Dollar Exits Ep.10 with John Rush: On Bootstrapping, Acquisitions, and Market Trends
sources.summary: John Rush explains why he chose bootstrapping over VC for Mars X, how he scouted and acquired Unicorn Platform, and why the small-acquisition market will grow. He also covers building with AI early and where AI opportunities sit: UX in boring niches, not deep tech.

principles.text: Don't build a product the big platforms will ship as a feature; go to niches Google or Gmail will ignore, like bakeries.
principles.quote: do not build a product 4G for for the email right like yeah Gmail will come with that

principles.text: The biggest AI opportunity is UX on top of models, not deep tech, which needs too many resources.
principles.quote: I would just not recommend anyone to do anything deep tech there because that's just too complicated uh and you need resources but ux is easier

principles.text: Thin AI wrappers in unexpected niches can reach $5-10k MRR; ignore the 'wrapper' criticism.
principles.quote: some people could say it's a wrapper but who cares and then they're making like you know five or ten thousand dollars a month

principles.text: Distribution used to be easy because few people built startups; now builders and marketers are rarely the same person, which fuels acquisitions.
principles.quote: it's really hard to find people who are good at both distribution and building

principles.text: Before acquiring, research the target founder obsessively; he followed Alex for a year and a half to understand what he wanted and struggled with.
principles.quote: I followed Alex for one year so I follow him for even a year and a half he didn't even know that

principles.text: Declined VC to keep the community co-ownership vision; VC funding would have harmed the project.
principles.quote: I realized that if we have VC funded company uh we can't execute on the vision of uh sharing uh you know the whole project with everyone

sources.title: John Rush on bootstrapping vs VC: small tools, delighted users, open source, enjoy the journey
sources.originalTitle: From Bootstrapping to the VC World The Advantages of Bootstrapping
sources.summary: John Rush explains why he left 12 years of VC-backed startups for bootstrapping, where he now runs 24 projects. He argues bootstrappers win with small specialized tools, over-delivering to users, open source with royalty-style forks, and building for emerging trends rather than existing hype.

principles.text: Bootstrappers should over-deliver to early users rather than spend on growth; delighted users become the growth engine.
principles.quote: you have to do more for the user then they pay you a lot more because in youc back you it it's wrong to do that but here you have to do that

principles.text: Bet on small, targeted solutions for small problems; VC-backed products get generic because they must target huge markets.
principles.quote: I bet all my business on the idea that the world wants small solutions for small problems like very targeted small solutions for small problems

principles.text: Build for future trends, not existing hype or past trends; a small growing niche will carry you as it grows.
principles.quote: I always do the projects for the future Trends and I highly recommend people to only do that because if you do for the past trends then you're going to see decline eventually

principles.text: Build every product for yourself first, test it across your own projects, then launch it to others.
principles.quote: everything I build I build for myself first I see if it works for me because I have tons of projects so I try on all my projects once it works for all my projects I launch it for the rest

principles.text: Open sourcing code has little downside because code is no longer the hard part; distribution and UX are. It builds trust.
principles.quote: today you know writing the code is is not the difficult part the difficult part is everything else you know figuring out what to write how to distribute it how to um you know the ux

principles.text: Enjoy the journey rather than the outcome; you can't control outcomes and exits can leave you empty.
principles.quote: you should love the journey not the outcome

sources.title: How John Rush built 25 bootstrapped products by replacing startup jobs and obsessing over UX
sources.originalTitle: Product-Led Growth vs. VC Funding: Lessons from 25 Bootstrapped Startups with John Rush
sources.summary: John Rush contrasts VC-backed and bootstrapped life, and explains how he mapped 120 startup jobs into product ideas. He shares why UX beats features in B2B, how he competes in crowded niches, and why most of his tools are marketing assets.

principles.text: VC-backed founders optimize for the next round and exit; bootstrappers optimize for customers and profit.
principles.quote: when you're VC backed your KPIs are different and your brain is wired differently.

principles.text: Generate product ideas by mapping the jobs you'd hire people for and building tools to replace them, best ROI first.
principles.quote: I came up with 120 typical jobs done by people in my typical startup and I started just building one by one uh based on the best ROI

principles.text: Build products you use yourself; ideas outside your own needs failed, while self-used ones never did.
principles.quote: whenever I built something from this jobs to be replaced, it never failed because I was the user myself right away.

principles.text: Don't fear crowded markets; tailor to a niche so you don't directly compete with the giants.
principles.quote: people should not be afraid to build something that looks like all the other products as long as they don't compete with all the other products.

principles.text: Reuse a shared stack of micro apps so new products are mostly built and improvements propagate to all products.
principles.quote: whenever I build a new product, I actually reuse a lot of the things from the other products through this micro ops.

principles.text: Most B2B tools ignore UX; an obvious, easy product shocks users and makes them share it.
principles.quote: almost all businessto business tools ignore UX. They only focus on features.

sources.title: How John Rush runs 20+ bootstrapped startups with AI agents, no employees, no VC
sources.originalTitle: Running 20+ Startups With AI (No Employees, No VC)
sources.summary: John Rush explains his problem-first, solo-founder model: solve your own problem, pitch ideas on Twitter before building, automate everything repetitive with AI agents, and keep each product small enough to run without a team. He also covers high-effort content and brutal self-criticism as growth habits.

principles.text: Build to solve your own problem first, not to make money; it's hard to fail when you and your friends are the first users.
principles.quote: I just see a problem in my own work and I want to solve the problem and then I solve the problem for myself first and for my friends

principles.text: Pitch ideas publicly before building them: it's free validation, free help and free distribution.
principles.quote: I can actually pitch my ideas before I build them. It means that I don't even have to raise money like this way. I pitch the idea that's free.

principles.text: Improve what users already like instead of piling on features; more features can complicate a product people chose for its simplicity.
principles.quote: I rather improve stuff I have because I believe that users want this stuff to be great rather than to stuff to have a lot of features

principles.text: Automate everything repetitive so the founder only does ideas, strategy and creative work.
principles.quote: I think we will automate everything so much that the only thing that will be left to do for founders is to invent ideas.

principles.text: Cap each product below $1M MRR so the portfolio stays runnable solo without a team or stress.
principles.quote: They have to be all below 1 million um MR and then as long as they are each below 1 million MR then I can still run it without stress

principles.text: High-effort content wins; do the work for your audience for free so they'd have paid for it.
principles.quote: high effort content will win no matter what because people feel that like it it's a when you read something and you see somebody spend time doing that it means they save your time

sources.title: How John Rush launches 100+ products: traffic-first directories, Twitter validation, movie-style launches
sources.originalTitle: Hackathon Speech by John Rush from MarsX
sources.summary: John Rush explains how he picks and ships projects fast: scratch his own itch for SaaS tools, reverse-engineer keyword traffic for directories, and validate with a single tweet. He prioritizes by launching unfinished and letting users "scream", and markets with a movie-style teaser and launch blast.

principles.text: Launch unfinished, far earlier than feels comfortable; early users tell you the few things to fix, so priorities sort themselves.
principles.quote: I just launch stuff very early uh earlier than normal people do like way before you're embarrassed even way before it work it works to be honest

principles.text: Work reactively on what is urgent; products with users 'scream' at you, so you never need to-do lists, and keep 20-30% time for spontaneous projects.
principles.quote: I only work on urgent things uh it means that I just look at all the things I can do and I see like what I have to do today that I if I do tomorrow it's too late right

principles.text: Build SaaS tools to fix your own problems; if something is great for you, many others will like it too.
principles.quote: it turns out that if something is great for me it's also great for a lot of the people not all but there's huge number of people who are also happy with things I'm happy with

principles.text: For directories, reverse-engineer from keywords: find high-traffic keywords with no product, then build a fast information site before the window closes.
principles.quote: I go for the traffic I find the Anta potential in the traffic there's a lot of it it's like there are like a lot of key keywords uh with high traffic and no product so the traffic goes to blogs and I just build that product

principles.text: Validate ideas with traffic data plus one tweet; if your audience doesn't react within about 30 minutes, shelve it.
principles.quote: the only thing I do to validate ideas is to see traffic and see a reaction on Twitter

principles.text: Market like a movie: tease and build anticipation, then spend most of the effort in a blast around launch.
principles.quote: they burn 80% of all marketing money just in two weeks with a blast right that's what I do as well so pretty much my marketing strategy is 100% the same as the movie with strategy

sources.title: Extreme startup building with AI: distribution first, specialized agents, zero-cost co-makers
sources.originalTitle: Extreme startup building with AI w/ John Rush
sources.summary: John Rush explains why he replaced hired departments with AI agents, his three-step agent build process (Zapier, agent builder, hardcode), and why he automated distribution first. He also covers specialized vs general agents, co-maker deals, idea validation, and why great products still beat distribution alone.

principles.text: Be your own perfect customer: build tools for yourself, prove they work on you, and only then launch publicly.
principles.quote: I am kind of my own user. So I built all the tools for myself and I use the agents for myself and I show how it works for me and only when it works I launch to the uh public.

principles.text: Automate distribution first. Building can be slow, but SEO and social need months of compounding effort that can't be rushed later.
principles.quote: the thing that can't wait is distribution because it's not like you will build your tool bring to the market and suddenly it will sell itself right.

principles.text: Build agents in three steps: prototype in Zapier as the broker, move to an agent builder, then hardcode it in regular code.
principles.quote: So then usually I take what I built in Zapier and I connect that into uh this no code AI tool builder thing that I I put them together and users can use it.

principles.text: Specialized agents beat general ones: you know what to expect, so you can hardcode error catching and tight integrations. Niche keeps getting narrower.
principles.quote: the market will reward the agent that does only one thing really, really well.

principles.text: Team up with developers who lack distribution skills on 50/50 revenue share. No salaries, no upfront cost, no investors.
principles.quote: we own it 50/50 and uh there's no salary so we share the revenue or we share the profits right. So basically there's no upfront cost for me.

principles.text: Two ways to win: huge distribution, or a product so good users recommend it. Distribution alone isn't enough; great products still win.
principles.quote: too many people think that distribution alone is enough and is a solution for all problems but I think the great products are still winning.

sources.title: Build out of your own pain: John Rush on niche tools, unbundling and building in public
sources.originalTitle: Tech-Driven Growth and AI Progress - Sustainable Business Strategies - interview with John Rush
sources.outlet: Osom to Know - a WordPress podcast
sources.summary: John explains why ideas must come from your own pain (his VC-backed ideas failed for 11 years; own-pain products stopped failing), why B2B beats B2C for solo makers, and why niche single-purpose tools win. He also covers good vs bad bundling, platform diversification, and building in public.

principles.text: Only build products out of your own pain; build, use and iterate for yourself, then launch.
principles.quote: I build it for myself always and then I use it for myself and I iterate with myself until I'm happy once I'm happy I launch for the rest and it just works every single time

principles.text: You can only judge your own pain and motivation; asking others if they'd use your app gives useless answers.
principles.quote: you can only evaluate your own motivation and pain you can't evaluate someone else and if you ask someone like know people say go to people and ask it doesn't work

principles.text: B2B pain is fragmented with little competition, which suits solo makers; B2C is crowded and winner-take-all.
principles.quote: in B2B World there is more fragmentation of pain because there are more jobs and they're like hundreds of thousands of jobs in the world and every job has you know hundreds of pains

principles.text: Niche down to a single-use tool: hardcoded details and zero-config onboarding that newcomers can use intuitively.
principles.quote: once your tool is niched down and it knows that it's going to be used to build directories then you can start making a lot of details within it

principles.text: Bundle around one user's job to be done, not a huge suite where only 5% applies to each user.
principles.quote: the good bundling where you pick one user and you satisfy all the users needs everything and then it's all in one

principles.text: Build in public by sharing how-tos and learnings, not wins, which breed jealousy or distrust.
principles.quote: don't try to share wins just share ways of you know gearing somewhere and how you did that and all the actions you've done and educate people on things you do

sources.title: How John Rush scored 1M SEO clicks: a practical checklist from domains to AI search
sources.originalTitle: Everything I’ve done to score 1 million clicks from SEO
sources.summary: John Rush shares his SEO playbook after 1B impressions and 1M clicks. It covers domain naming, tech basics, indexing, a weekly analytics review, low-hanging fruit in positions 8-20, human-quality blogging, backlinks via AI-cited pages, social SEO, and treating AI search as the same game.

principles.text: Push pages ranking in positions 8-20 first; they are closer to page 1 than any new article.
principles.quote: Those are closer to page 1 than any new article

principles.text: Review GSC weekly: fix high-impression, low-click queries by putting the query in H1 and meta title; update decayed pages.
principles.quote: Queries with impressions but few clicks (take the queries pointing to these pages and embed them into h1 and meta title)

principles.text: Update old pages that already get traffic before writing new ones; Google likes regular real updates.
principles.quote: Update them before writing a new one (google kinda loves to see pages being regularly updated)

principles.text: Use AI to scale blog drafts, then manually upgrade the ones gaining traction into human-quality articles with original proof.
principles.quote: Manually turn the promising ones from AI-generated into high-quality human-made articles

principles.text: Get backlinks by asking AI "best tool for X", then paying or link-swapping with authors of the cited pages.
principles.quote: Ask them to include my URL in exchange for money or a backlink from you

principles.text: Repurpose each blog post to X, LinkedIn and Reddit with a link back; social gets indexed instantly and carries weight.
principles.quote: social media backlinks in my experience have really high weight for google

sources.title: The Death of Marketing: AI agents as customers and what indie founders should do
sources.originalTitle: The Death of Marketing (And What Replaces It)
sources.summary: John argues AI agents will make most buying decisions, so human-oriented marketing (SEO, ads, funnels) fades. Four channels survive: government lists, genuinely best product, human identity purchases, and paid AI placements. Bootstrapped founders should focus on the best product in a niche and a personal-brand audience.

principles.text: Your customer is increasingly an AI agent with a task and a budget, not a loyal human, so marketing playbooks built for humans are decaying.
principles.quote: Your customer is now an AI agent with a task, a budget, and zero brand loyalty.

principles.text: In the long run AI agents will run real evaluations, so the genuinely best product for a use case wins; gaming reviews is short-term.
principles.quote: The endgame: the best product wins. Every time. For every specific use case.

principles.text: Short term, be listed everywhere (launchpads, directories, listicles, ratings) since AI recommends based on those today.
principles.quote: Short-term game: be listed everywhere you can, on all launchpads, directories, listicles, ratings...

principles.text: Bootstrapped founders should be the best at one specific niche job; go long-tail to reduce competition.
principles.quote: The single best strategy here is to go after long-tail niche markets, just so that you reduce the competition and aim at being the best or one of the best among a few.

principles.text: Personal brand is the strongest remaining moat: people buy founders (the T-shirt effect), which AI cannot replicate.
principles.quote: Personal brand is the strongest moat that’s left. The founder with 100K followers who share their journey will outsell the faceless SaaS with a bigger feature set. Every time.

principles.text: Paid AI placements will be pay-to-play and price out bootstrappers, so skip them and the government-list channel.
principles.quote: This will be massive. It will also be pay-to-play. The companies spending millions on Google Ads today will redirect those budgets to AI placement. If you’re bootstrapped, you’re priced out of this channel too.

sources.title: The traditional SaaS is over: agents collapse tools, so sell results, data and trust
sources.originalTitle: The traditional SaaS is over → I think this is what comes next
sources.summary: John argues that AI agents connected via MCP replace SaaS UIs, killing UX moats, brand loyalty and switching costs and pushing tool prices toward zero. The remaining moats are data network effects and regulated trust. The new opportunities are the agent layer, one-time-paid code repos and outcome-based pricing.

principles.text: UX is no longer a moat: an agent in front of your product ignores your landing page, onboarding and feature naming.
principles.quote: the AI agent sitting in front of all of them doesn’t care about your landing page, your onboarding flow, your clever feature naming, or your freemium funnel.

principles.text: Most users touch about 5% of any SaaS, so a custom dashboard of just the needed 5% from each tool can replace them.
principles.quote: I only use 5% of any given tool. The rest was just noise to me. So I just picked the 5% from each and put it all into one dashboard.

principles.text: Brand loyalty and switching costs vanish when agents choose providers on price and whether it works.
principles.quote: I just care that the thing works and costs the least.

principles.text: Data network effects are a moat agents can't commoditize: products that get better as more people use them.
principles.quote: If your product genuinely gets better because more people use it... that’s the one thing agents can’t commoditize.

principles.text: Sell the result, not the tool: pricing flips from paying for access to paying for outcomes, and you can charge more.
principles.quote: The pricing model flips from “pay for access” to “pay for outcomes.”

principles.text: Sell full code repos for a one-time payment so buyers customize with Claude Code instead of starting from zero.
principles.quote: I’d happily pay someone $199 to purchase the code that I’ll then throw into Claude Code and ask to customize it for my needs

sources.title: I'm from 2058: John Rush's fictional AI dystopia and what it says about outsourcing decisions
sources.originalTitle: I'm from 2058. The AI Didn't Destroy Us. It Did Something Worse.
sources.summary: A long speculative fiction essay in which John Rush narrates a 2022-2054 AI timeline, from ChatGPT to a "brain hosting" economy. It has little actionable business advice. The durable ideas are about incentive-driven races, handing decisions to AI, and AI leverage for small teams.

principles.text: Competitive pressure pushes everyone to ship faster, even when they know the risks.
principles.quote: Every company said the same thing: "We'd love to slow down, but we can't be the only ones who do."

principles.text: Handing small decisions to AI compounds: each one makes the next easier to give away.
principles.quote: we were outsourcing the act of being a person. One decision at a time. And every decision we gave away made the next one easier to give away.

principles.text: Adding an AI layer to an existing product can lift revenue fast.
principles.quote: I added an API call to GPT-4 on top of our website builder. It could generate page layouts and copy automatically. Users loved it. Revenue tripled.

principles.text: AI agents let a tiny team do the work of a large engineering team.
principles.quote: Three Claude Code agents on a $200/month plan were doing the work of sixteen senior engineers. Better. Faster. No lunch breaks. No sprint meetings.

principles.text: Software is the first domain AI automates because code is text.
principles.quote: Software fell first because code is text and text is what language models eat.

principles.text: Algorithms optimized for engagement amplify rage, because attention is what they are rewarded for.
principles.quote: The AI systems controlling social media feeds had one job: maximize engagement. Engagement meant attention. Attention meant influence. Influence meant power.

sources.title: Bootstrapped founder report: revenue drop, burnout, and shipping a portfolio of AI products
sources.originalTitle: revenue dropped, comaker had a burnout, socialbot beta is live
sources.summary: John Rush shares a raw update across his SaaS portfolio: a 20% revenue drop, a comaker burnout, and many shipped features. Useful lessons: cut low-value pricing tiers, build experimentation into products, bundle agents in a store, and recruit beta testers publicly.

principles.text: Remove the cheapest plan to filter out difficult users who drain support.
principles.quote: Removed the $19 plan to cut out “difficult users” who drain my support agents

principles.text: Build automated experimentation into the product: the agent generates campaigns, copy and media to find what converts.
principles.quote: shipped A/B testing engine inside **[tinyadz.com](https://tinyadz.com/)** (the agent keeps coming up with different campaigns/copy/media to find what converts best

principles.text: Recruit beta testers by asking for a public comment, then DM them.
principles.quote: beta launched socialbot for my product accounts on social media, I need 10 beta testers now, reply with a comment and I’ll DM u

principles.text: Make your product ecosystem easy to adopt: one-click install of all your agents from an in-platform store.
principles.quote: launched an “Agent Store” inside unicorn platform. It’s so cool. You can install all my agents with just one click inside there.

principles.text: Share the bad alongside the good in founder reports; the rawness engages readers.
principles.quote: My bootstrapped founder report(good & bad):

principles.text: Move the business to lower-tax jurisdictions to keep more of what you earn.
principles.quote: started moving my biz from US to Dubai (to save on taxes)

sources.title: 20 startup mistakes John Rush regrets after building 30 startups in 20 years
sources.originalTitle: 99 mistakes I regret making:
sources.summary: John Rush lists 20 regrets from 30 startups (VC-backed and bootstrapped). Core themes: stay lean and founder-led, validate before building, start paid in B2B, use boilerplates, and invest early in SEO, content and social media instead of chasing investors, partners and conferences.

principles.text: Don't chase VCs. Make users happy and investors will find you once you have traction.
principles.quote: So, don't chase VCs, just make users happy and VCs are gonna find you.

principles.text: Founders should do all the work until traction; employees take no risk, so no innovation.
principles.quote: Only founders have enough incentives to take risks. SO the founders should do all the work until they gain traction.

principles.text: Avoid teams of specialized developers; one fullstack dev beats a team until about $30k MRR.
principles.quote: Today I have 1 fullstack dev doing 5x more progress on a project than a team of 12 back then. Avoid "teams" at all cost until at least $30kmrr.

principles.text: In B2B, start with paid (30-day no-questions refund). Free tiers attract the wrong crowd and bad feedback.
principles.quote: Free projects attract totally wrong crowd with irrelevant feedback and drive your project away from where it should head.

principles.text: Use boilerplates instead of coding auth, admin and CRUD from scratch; speed went up 10x.
principles.quote: The moment I started using boilerplates, the speed went up 10x.

principles.text: Start SEO, blogging and social media early. An hour a day on blogging is enough, and he regrets starting X late.
principles.quote: I thought blogging is a full time job, but it's actually possible to spend an hour a day on it and still do a good job.

sources.title: How John Rush got to 500k users: 23 marketing channels, what worked and what failed
sources.originalTitle: I did it 🥹 500k users! I'll share every step:
sources.summary: John Rush reviews every channel he tried while growing Unicorn Platform to 500k users (4 years to 25k, 2 years to 250k, 6 months to 500k). Passive channels like directories, SEO, Reddit, LinkedIn and affiliates worked. Ads, cold email, giveaways, LTDs and incubator deals failed. Product quality drives word of mouth.

principles.text: Directories are one of the best channels: they bring traffic on autopilot.
principles.quote: One of the best channels I have. Sometimes I think I should quit marketing and just build directories. Because they bring traffic on autopilot.

principles.text: Ads and cold email fail when you promote the product directly. Hide the product behind a freebie.
principles.quote: simply promoting your product with ads never really works. U need to create a freebie or be genius at banners.

principles.text: Start SEO early; ignoring it until 2023 was his biggest mistake. Mix AI-generated and human-made articles.
principles.quote: I didn't touch it until April 2023; it was my biggest mistake.

principles.text: Affiliate programs need a generous cut. Raising commission from 15% to 33% made it work.
principles.quote: I started with 15% and had no interest. Changed to 33% and it picked up.

principles.text: Multiple side projects cross-promote: at least 10% of users came from his other products, even free ones.
principles.quote: At least 10% of all my users came from my other products. So, having multiple side projects isn't a bad idea.

principles.text: Product quality and empathy for users drive growth, because most users arrive by word of mouth.
principles.quote: Most users come via word of mouth, and people only recommend products they love. I put a lot of effort into making the product better.

sources.title: If only someone told me this before my 1st startup: 20 hard-won founder rules
sources.originalTitle: If only someone told me this before my 1st startup
sources.summary: John Rush lists 20 lessons from years of failed startups: validate first, bootstrap, go B2B and global, hire only doers, do SEO and daily posting early, and skip corporates, hype and conferences. Each rule is backed by a personal cost, like 5 wasted years or 14 years ignoring SEO.

principles.text: Validate the idea before building; building unwanted products wastes years.
principles.quote: Validate idea first. I wasted at least 5 years building stuff nobody needed.

principles.text: Chase users, not investors; investors follow traction.
principles.quote: Don't chaise investors, chase users, and then investors will be chasing you.

principles.text: Presell features: chat with 10-20 users daily and build only what resonates.
principles.quote: Sell features, before building them. Ask existing users if they want this feature.

principles.text: Keep the landing page simple; most visitors arrive with intent from content or recommendations.
principles.quote: 90% of the users will end up on your site coming from a blog article, social media post, a recommendation. Which means they have the intent. No need to "convert" them again.

principles.text: Start SEO as early as possible; ignoring it was a huge regret.
principles.quote: Do SEO from day 2. As early as you can. I ignored this for 14 years. It's my biggest regret.

principles.text: Go global from day 1 because the upside is far bigger if it works.
principles.quote: If the product and marketing are good, it will work on the global market too, if it's bad, it won't work on the local market too.

sources.title: Open letter to new founders: no shortcuts, learn by doing, go deep in one niche
sources.originalTitle: My open letter to the new Startup Founders
sources.summary: John Rush's blunt letter says startup success has no shortcut. It takes years of reps, many skills learned by doing, and total focus. He then lays out what works: pick a narrow niche, become top 1%, educate the audience, build micro MVPs, and treat it as a marathon.

principles.text: No quick, risk-free path to startup success exists; anyone promising one is lying, and most makers fail repeatedly.
principles.quote: There is no easy, quick, risk-free & proven way to succeed.

principles.text: "Overnight" success hides years of reps; his fast results come from 20 years of building startups.
principles.quote: I may start a product today and reach $30k MRR in 6 months. Can I teach you this? NO! I can do that because I've spent 20 years building startups.

principles.text: Founders must be above average across many skills, and the only way to learn them is by doing, not consuming.
principles.quote: No amount of reading, watching youtube, consuming the courses and bookmarking the tweets will help, if you don't actually apply this knowledge right away.

principles.text: Don't mix fun and education; consuming content trains you to get dopamine from consuming instead of acting.
principles.quote: Don't mix fun & education. It inevitably kills your bias for action. Suddenly you get dopamine when u consume, not when u act.

principles.text: Pick a narrow niche you understand deeply instead of targeting a wide audience.
principles.quote: Don't spread to wide audiences. Pick a narrow niche. You should have some connection to the audience or be able to understand the audience and emulate their thought, pain, taste, and desires.

principles.text: Iterate for months with micro MVPs and manual work for your audience; the tool that gains attention shows where to invest.
principles.quote: Spend months iterating with micro MVPs and doing things manually for your audience and inevitably, one of the tools/services will gain more attention, and you'll clearly see you need to put more time into it.

sources.title: John Rush's weekly roundup: YC vs 20k X followers, consistency, and copycat/scam risks
sources.originalTitle: Lazy SEO tips, New tech dramas, Copycats, Scams & more
sources.summary: A satirical weekly news digest from John Rush on tech, startups and indie hacking drama. Few durable lessons: audience on X can replace YC's moat, consistency wins on YouTube, and indie scene hazards like clones and presale scams. Links to his lazy SEO playbook tweet, but the playbook itself isn't in this text.

principles.text: A 20k X following gives a moat similar to a YC batch: founders reply to your DMs and VCs come inbound.
principles.quote: YC isn't "a must" anymore. Earning 20k followers on X brings a similar moat as being in YC batch cuz u can - DM successful founders and they answer - get huge inbound interest from VCs

principles.text: Winning on content is mostly about showing up consistently for a short, defined stretch.
principles.quote: What stops you from doing the same? What's your excuse? Just keep showing up for 2 months and u win.

principles.text: Successful products get cloned, even down to the name, so expect copycats as you gain traction.
principles.quote: a dude cloned my listingbott.com, even the name.

principles.text: Incumbents buy competitors and media to control distribution and narrative.
principles.quote: Semrush Acquires Third Door Media. Startups are playing real games now, buying news media to control the narrative

principles.text: Presale-and-disappear behavior burns buyers and hurts the whole maker ecosystem; trust is an asset.
principles.quote: A maker disappeared after the presale of his boilerplate.

sources.title: How John Rush built 20 directories, exited one, and packaged the playbook as a $99 guide
sources.originalTitle: Directory playbook: build, grow & monetize.
sources.summary: John announces his first directory exit (allGPTs.co sold to ChippAI for 5 figures) and a $99 pre-order guide on building, growing and monetizing directories. Mostly a sales pitch, but it outlines his results and the guide's scope: underserved ideas, keyword research, nocode, SEO, monetization.

principles.text: Launch many directories; a minority become winners (5 of 20 turned out great).
principles.quote: Overall, I launched 20 directories and 5 of them turned out to be great, perhaps turning into the best directories in their niche in the world

principles.text: Share what you learn publicly first; audience demand tells you when to package it into a paid product.
principles.quote: I’ve shared all I know publically on twitter, but people kept asking me to make a course or a guide, so I’m giving it a try.

principles.text: Directories can feed traffic into your other SaaS tools as a distribution channel, not just earn on their own.
principles.quote: channeled traffic to my other saas tools **worth $1m+**

principles.text: Directories monetize via affiliate links, sponsors and paid listings, and can be sold.
principles.quote: monetizing with affiliate links, sponsors, paid listings.

principles.text: Directory playbook: find underserved ideas, do keyword research, build with nocode, then market via SEO and social.
principles.quote: how to find underserved ideas

principles.text: Pre-sell and let sales fund effort: put more work into the product as more people buy.
principles.quote: The more people buy it, the more effort I’ll put into making it great.

sources.title: I'm turning 35: 28 hard-won startup rules from John Rush
sources.originalTitle: I'm turning 35. The 28 rules I learned the hard way
sources.summary: John Rush lists 28 lessons from a decade of failed and successful startups. Core themes: validate before building, chase users not investors, bootstrap, charge more, go paid-only, skip corporates and outsourcing, do SEO and daily posting early, and build for audiences you love.

principles.text: Sell features before building them: chat daily with users about ideas and only build what resonates.
principles.quote: I run DMs with 10-20 users every day, where I chat about all my ideas and features I wanna add. I clearly see what resonates with me most and only go build those.

principles.text: Chase users, not investors; investor interest follows traction.
principles.quote: Chase users, and then investors will be chasing you.

principles.text: No free tier until the product is validated; free users push you to build a perfect free product.
principles.quote: Free and paid users often need different products. Don't fall into this trap as I did.

principles.text: Don't price lowest. $50 customers are happier and better advocates than $5 customers.
principles.quote: The audience on $5 and $50 are totally different.

principles.text: Landing page is minor early; first sales happen outside the website.
principles.quote: Your first 100 sales happen outside of the website.

principles.text: Start SEO as early as possible; ignoring it was his biggest regret.
principles.quote: I ignored this for 14 years, and it's my biggest regret.

sources.title: Why bootstrapping beats VC money: unicorn collapses and the Holdco as your own VC
sources.originalTitle: John Rush #May 27. Unicorns are Falling Dead ☠ & I'll buy a spot on your site.
sources.summary: John argues that heavily funded startups are collapsing while profitable bootstrapped companies thrive. Too much money weakens a startup, user-funded businesses stay focused on users, and the best path is bootstrap first, use VC only for growth after PMF, or run a Holdco of cash cow projects as your own VC.

principles.text: Too much funding makes you weak: you look productive but build no real strength.
principles.quote: Having too much money while building your startup is like going to a gym with fake weights. You lift them, and it all looks good, but you gain no muscles.

principles.text: Let users fund the business so your focus stays on users, not on your next round or on VCs and journalists.
principles.quote: To build great stuff for the users, the business must be funded by users. In this case your whole focus is on the users, not on your next round and VC/Journalist.

principles.text: Bootstrap first, then use VC money for growth only after product-market fit.
principles.quote: I believe the best startups will be bootstrapped and use VC money for growth after PMF.

principles.text: Bootstrapped founders have alternatives to VC: community rounds, cheap loans, and pre-sales.
principles.quote: We will see many bootstrapped founders opting for alternatives, too: community rounds, cheap loans, and pre-sales.

principles.text: Run a Holdco of simple cash cow projects and act as your own VC when needed.
principles.quote: An even better option is to run a Holdco with sole simple cash cow projects that bring in money every month and then act as your own VC when needed.

principles.text: The future of SaaS and non-deep-tech startups is efficient bootstrapped small teams or solo founders.
principles.quote: The future of SaaS and Non-Deep/Hard-Tech startups is this: highly efficient bootstrapped small teams or even solo founders and indie makers.

sources.title: How John Rush grew Unicorn Platform to $300k ARR: SEO routine under $1k plus 14 growth levers
sources.originalTitle: John Rush #May20: SEO in 9 steps & 300k ARR
sources.summary: John shares his low-budget, founder-friendly SEO routine (under $1k, 0 to 1) and the 14 things that took Unicorn Platform to $300k ARR in 12 months. Covers redesign to cut churn, SEO stacking, directories, Product Hunt, Reddit, talking to users, cross-promo and word of mouth.

principles.text: Cheap DIY SEO gets you from 0 to 1 for under $1k; hire a pro later to go from 1 to 10.
principles.quote: Total budget is below $1k, and it brings you from 0 to 1.

principles.text: Don't fix 100 support requests one by one; look for one structural change (UX redesign) that erases most of them.
principles.quote: It just erased 80% of the tasks from the backlog.

principles.text: When new to SEO, try all the strategies at once instead of betting on one.
principles.quote: Instead of implementing just one strategy, I went on to try pretty much all of them at once

principles.text: Automate repetitive growth work by building tools for it (indexing, backlinks, articles, directory listings).
principles.quote: I eventually built 3 more tools to automate all this work(Index Rusher for indexing, Listingbott for backlinks, and Seobot for articles).

principles.text: Email every paid user and talk to them; it fixes churn and creates word of mouth.
principles.quote: I emailed every paid user, asking for feedback and starting a discussion. I talked to at least 300 of them.

principles.text: Cross-link your own portfolio of products; about 30% of traffic came from footers, banners and emails across other products.
principles.quote: So my other 23 products drive traffic to this one via links in the footer and banners, and sometimes I recommend it in an email. About 30% of the traffic comes this way.

sources.title: John Rush's 78-tool stack: what he pays for to run 24 projects
sources.originalTitle: I pay for 78 products to run my 24 projects.
sources.summary: John Rush lists the 78 paid products he uses across hosting, dev, AI, testing, support, marketing, legal and more to run 24 projects, plus 4 of his own products. He picked each after trial and error on price, features and UX, and stays open to switching to better alternatives.

principles.text: Choose tools by trial and error on price, features and UX, and stay open to switching when a better alternative appears.
principles.quote: It took me many trials and errors to find best tools on price/features/UX.

principles.text: Stay open to switching tools: ask your audience for better alternatives and change if they beat what you use.
principles.quote: Do you know a better alternative? Let me know, and I may switch.

principles.text: Use a broad paid stack across hosting, DBs and clouds rather than locking into a single vendor.
principles.quote: Digital Ocean for hosting. AWS for hosting, storage, and CDN. Hetzner for bare metal.

principles.text: Use multiple LLM providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Azure OpenAI) plus a vector DB for AI features.
principles.quote: Open AI for LLMs and image gen. Anthropic for claude LLM. Azure Open AI. Pinecone for vector db.

principles.text: Dogfood your own products to build sites, generate SEO content, build domain rating and speed up indexing.
principles.quote: SeoBOT to research & generate blog articles.

sources.title: How John Rush built an audience from zero: his 8-rule social playbook for founders
sources.originalTitle: "I was invisible on the internet a year ago" + Best of the week.
sources.summary: John Rush shares the playbook he used to go from invisible to 50M views and 40k followers, which helped him reach 140,000 users with Unicorn Platform. He argues for one platform, followers as the KPI, deep expertise in one niche, and content aimed at your buyers rather than a broad audience.

principles.text: Focus 100% on one platform until you have several thousand followers and good content quality.
principles.quote: Until you reach several thousand followers and good content quality levels, creating content, engaging with people, and understanding the algorithm take hours daily.

principles.text: Pick Twitter as your training camp: shortest feedback loop, 10 practice posts a day. Writing skill transfers to every platform.
principles.quote: I suggest going with Twitter since it has the shortest feedback loop, and you can create 10 daily posts to practice.

principles.text: Track follower count, not views. Followers measure content quality because they follow authors they respect.
principles.quote: Don’t focus on pure views. Focus on followers.

principles.text: Stay on one topic until you break through. Scattershot topics produce unrepeatable virality.
