principles.quote: The most typical mistake I see around is people trying to throw all sorts of topics, hoping to get lucky and viral with one. Even if this happens, you won’t be able to reproduce it later.

principles.text: Add your own experiments and experience to your topic; become a top 0.1% expert through thousands of hours.
principles.quote: You can’t just repost the known theory. You must add your own personal practice to it. This makes the information valuable.

principles.text: Not every follower counts. B2B founders need followers who buy; entertainment audiences don't convert.
principles.quote: I launched all my product via social media and got way more than 10 sales instantly, while having 20x fewer followers than him.

sources.title: How John Rush built a Next.js boilerplate directory for SEO traffic and sponsor revenue in 8 hours
sources.originalTitle: Anyone can do this (took me 8h)
sources.summary: John walks through his playbook for a niche directory site: spot a hyped topic, validate with Google Keyword Planner, buy a .com, build the directory fast, generate content with AI, force indexing, and monetize via featured spots. He stresses letting a new domain warm up and not launching many pages at once.

principles.text: Find demand first: spot a hyped topic, then check keyword volume for low-competition, decent-traffic keywords.
principles.quote: I saw hype around nextjs boilerplates, so I searched for this term and found low-competition keywords with good traffic.

principles.text: Always pick a .com domain; his tests show it beats every other TLD.
principles.quote: I always start with .com, since after all my tests, .com beats crap out of everything else.

principles.text: Build the first version fast from a template, and put top keywords on the home page.
principles.quote: I used my own website/directory builder (Unicorn Platforms) just out of the template in less than an hour.

principles.text: Seed a directory by scraping existing sources, then let authors submit more listings.
principles.quote: I found about 50 items and got 100 more submitted via the from later by the authors.

principles.text: Let a new site warm up before publishing the blog; don't launch many pages at once.
principles.quote: I didn’t publish the blog right away. I launched the site and let it warm up for 2 months and launched the blog on third month.

principles.text: Monetize directory traffic by selling featured spots to the products listed in it.
principles.quote: the site became attractive for nextjs boilerplate authors, so I made good revenues on selling "featured-spot".

sources.title: John Rush's 2023 recap: idea-to-revenue in 13 steps, what growth worked and failed
sources.originalTitle: Series A Round Killed My Startup + 5 more stories
sources.summary: A newsletter roundup of John Rush's X and LinkedIn posts. It gives his 13-step idea-to-revenue method (SEO and social validation and a waitlist before coding), his 2023 growth results (social media worked; partners, ads, outreach and hiring a marketer failed), and his plan to launch 1000 products on a SaaS OS.

principles.text: Validate before coding: check SEO potential, pick the least competitive niche, get social validation, and build a waitlist first.
principles.quote: 2. SEO potential 3. Pick least Competitive 4. Social Validation 5. Waitlist 6. Organic Promo 7. Paid Promo 8. Directories & SEO 9. Is there traction? 10. Coding MVP

principles.text: Code the MVP only after traction shows up, then turn the coding itself into marketing and iterate before the public launch.
principles.quote: 9. Is there traction? 10. Coding MVP 11. Turn Coding Into Marketing 12. iterate 13. Public Launch

principles.text: Social media was the growth channel that worked for him in 2023; the paid and outsourced channels failed.
principles.quote: Failed - Partners - Newsletter Ads - Podcasts - Outreach - Google/FB/Twitter ads - Hiring a marketing person - Paying influencers Worked - Social Media

principles.text: Share your learnings in public; learning from other bootstrapped founders and then publishing your own lessons compounds.
principles.quote: They’ve inspired me to share all my learnings in public too.

principles.text: He commits to shipping many products on one shared platform rather than a single product, aiming for 1000 by the end of 2025.
principles.quote: By the end of 2025, I’ll launch 1000 products. These products are going to run on a new SaaS OS.

sources.title: Maker predictions 2024-2026: distribution beats code, Google Sheets as DB, directory promo network
sources.originalTitle: Indie Maker Prediction for 2024-2026, got 10 million links clicks on directories, New Experiment, Google Sheet as DB, IndexGoogle
sources.summary: John Rush predicts a flood of indie makers, multi-product makers and "maker labels", where distribution is 90% of winning. He explains why Google Sheets replaced databases for his directories (10M clicks, $0 revenue so far), and his plan for a pay-per-click directory promo network.

principles.text: In the new world distribution is ~90% of winning; big dev teams without distribution lose.
principles.quote: They got large dev force and little distribution force. In the new world, distribution is 90% of what one needs to win.

principles.text: Most makers will move from endless features on one SaaS to many tools for the same audience.
principles.quote: So most realize this and instead of endless feature releases, they go and build more tools, to the same audience.

principles.text: Use public Google Sheets as the DB for directories: free, crowd-editable, transparent, far easier than conventional DBs.
principles.quote: Now all my public directories run on Google Sheets. It's totally free! No matter how much traffic or users I have.

principles.text: Don't build complex moderation software when a public sheet lets users fix the data themselves.
principles.quote: Imagine if I'd spent time building complex software for comment moderation...what a waste that would've been!

principles.text: AI content must be quality, not garbage: spend real money per article on multiple improvement cycles.
principles.quote: We spend almost a dollar on each article, cuz we do numerous cycles of content generation, improvement, research and more.

principles.text: Monetize directories with sponsored spots, matched by software, with a tiny entry price for buyers.
principles.quote: The best way to monetize the directory is to sell "sponsored" spots. But it's not easy to find a buyer.

sources.title: Week one as a maker: viral directories, an acquisition offer, and why PH launches lost value
sources.originalTitle: #1 - John Rush. VC, 0.5M visits, acquisition offer, viral directories and more.
sources.summary: John recaps a week across 20+ projects. Directory sites (allgpts, osssoftware) pulled big traffic, PH launches are losing value versus tweets and HN/dev.to posts, and virality does not equal revenue. He also shares lifetime-deal pricing for indexgoogle.

principles.text: You can't predict what will take off. Ship many projects and let the market tell you.
principles.quote: This shows you never know what will work until you try.

principles.text: Going viral doesn't mean making money. Traffic without paying conversions is not product-market fit.
principles.quote: Going viral doesn't always mean making money - an unexpected learning.

principles.text: Product Hunt launches are worth less now than tweets or posts on Hacker News and dev.to.
principles.quote: I'm stepping back from promoting PH launches as they don't seem valuable anymore compared to tweets or posts on hackernews or devto.

principles.text: Directory sites can pull big traffic cheaply. Offer a directory template so users can build them too.
principles.quote: unicornplatform.com got a big push from our new "directory" template. Users quickly create cool directories at low cost.

principles.text: Signal an exit publicly to gauge price and demand. Then decide using the stats, and keep the asset if the upside is bigger.
principles.quote: hit 0.5M visits & got 4

principles.text: Price some tools as a one-time lifetime fee instead of a subscription.
principles.quote: $99 per domain for life or $199 for five domains. No subscription, just a one-time fee.

sources.title: Why John Rush left VC-backed startups for bootstrapping and building MarsX
sources.originalTitle: Leaving the VC world to bootstrapping - John Rush interview
sources.summary: Short, paywalled interview excerpt. John Rush explains leaving VC-backed startups because founders chase funding rounds, conferences and press instead of users, and VCs act like bosses. He now runs MarsX, a holding company of tools built with Mars IDE, shipping a few products a month.

principles.text: Focus on users and the value you give them, not on funding rounds, conferences or press.
principles.quote: I felt like I was the only one trying to focus on users and value for the users, and everyone else in the VC startup world was obsessed with conferences, the next funding round, and media press.

principles.text: Taking VC money makes you an employee: investors become your bosses and you lose the freedom to say no.
principles.quote: It felt like I was an employee and they were my bosses. Which is in fact the reality for most founders of VC backed startups. You can't say no to VCs.

principles.text: Mix nocode, lowcode, AI and full code to make building ultra productive and ship several products a month.
principles.quote: let’s us build SaaS, apps and directories using nocode, lowcode, AI and full code. A perfect mix that makes the whole process ultra productive. I can ship few products every month.

principles.text: Build a full ecosystem of tools to ideate, build, grow and monetize startups, as a holding company of products.
principles.quote: It’s a universe of products, e.g. a Holdco that aims to create a full ecosystem of tools to ideate, build, grow and monetize startups.

sources.title: I built 30 startups in 20 years: the mistakes John Rush regrets most
sources.originalTitle: I built 30 startups in 20 years
sources.summary: John Rush lists regrets from 30 startups: raising VC and hiring too early, skipping SEO, content and social, building consumer apps, free tiers in B2B, and coding from scratch. His pattern: stay lean, work with doers, validate, and market early.

principles.text: Do most of the work yourself until PMF; hiring too early hurts startups.
principles.quote: Founders should do most of the work until PMF.

principles.text: Raising VC money too early killed most of his funded startups.
principles.quote: Eventually, most of these startups failed by being funded too early.

principles.text: Start SEO early; postponing it forever is a mistake.
principles.quote: None of the people in my network did SEO. We all thought it was something too late, and we kept postponing it forever.

principles.text: Don't assume what the audience wants; validate ideas, because assumptions almost never hold.
principles.quote: I’d always assume for the audience. Anticipate what they need. It almost never turned out to be true.

principles.text: Hire doers, not managers or specialists; one fullstack dev can outpace a big team.
principles.quote: Today I have 1 fullstack dev doing 5x more progress on a project than a team of 12 back then.

principles.text: Don't start B2B with a free tier; if nobody pays, fix the product or find another audience.
principles.quote: If nobody wants to pay for my product, I have to fix it or find another audience for it.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: John Rush walks through his directory playbook live: validate ideas with Google Keyword Planner, buy a keyword-matching domain, launch a minimal no-code site in one evening, promote on Reddit and social, then add SEO. He also covers monetization (sponsors, affiliates, paid listings), selling directories, and using directories as a traffic channel for SaaS.

chunks.heading: Why John says to start with directories
chunks.text:
- He calls directories "one of the lowest risk ways to start a startup" and the best first attempt at an internet business. Starting with SaaS is "the worst idea" because failure is almost certain, and people then feel bad and go back to a job.
- In a directory, failure is hard. With a stable 5K visits a month on a B2B directory, you sell four or five ads and make 3-4K a month, and SEO tends to keep growing even if you do nothing.
- The reason: directory keywords are non-competitive. Nobody pays for them and no VC-backed company competes for them.
- Why directories will matter more: as content grows, quality matters more. People trust a well-curated directory with reviews and ratings, and will outsource decisions to directories as Google results fill with hacks.
- Examples of directories growing big: Starter Story is a directory of starter stories making "a million" a year. Product Hunt began as a plain list of products sent in a newsletter, with no voting.
- Realistic scale: about 5K MRR without luck. His average directory is there, and he believes 15-20K is possible with more time. He sees 20K as the current limit and treats directories as side projects, not main ones.

chunks.heading: Finding and validating a directory idea with keyword research
chunks.text:
- He starts with keyword research, not gut feel: "even if you think that certain idea is great... other people might not think so."
- Tool: Google Keyword Planner (made for ads, but it shows keyword traffic). He spends hours in it every day throwing in ideas.
- Live example: "business ideas" has almost 1 million searches a month with low ad competition.
- The domain should exactly match the keyword. His directory "nextjs starters" was an exact match and had a lot of traffic within three months.
- If the exact domain is taken, use a synonym. Google now matches meaning, not exact words. For "business ideas" he tried small, little, tiny and micro, and bought mini business ideas for $9.
- He never buys expensive domains: "it's always available just be more creative."

chunks.heading: Building the first version fast, with no-code and AI
chunks.text:
- He has coded for about 15 years and still says to go no-code. Reasons: you launch faster, and marketing (landing pages, experiments, A/B tests, blog, programmatic SEO) is built into modern CMS tools. In hardcoded Next.js or PHP, every marketing change is manual, and hiring someone to write pages is harder because it all lives in code.
- He builds on his own tool, Unicorn Platform, which he pivoted into a directory builder because most sites on it are now directories.
- Version one is only a page with a name and items. Ratings, user features and the rest come "later in the month or even a year," since they'd be empty anyway. He told a Discord member (directory makers group) who wanted 20 features for a lawyers directory to skip them.
- He uses AI to generate the structure, menu, text, subtitle and FAQ, then moderates the output for quality.
- Everything is built around SEO: more text, items and pages mean more chances to rank. Featured items can get longer pages than ordinary ones.
- Speed rule: "if it takes more than one evening then you're doing it wrong."
- FAQ method for free keyword research:
  1. Type "how do I..." into Google and read the autocomplete suggestions.
  2. Put each question in the directory's FAQ and answer it. Every FAQ title is a possible search query.
  3. Example: "how to start a business as a teenager" is a keyword he wouldn't have thought of and that is probably poorly served.
- Don't build full pages first. Add a quick item, watch Search Console, and only build a full page for queries that get traffic.
- General approach: do as little as possible to validate each assumption, then put real human time into the assumption that wins. AI is fine for experiments, but humans make the winner great.

chunks.heading: Promoting a new directory in the first days
chunks.text:
He runs these four steps before investing in SEO. Their purpose is validation: if people see the directory but don't click, the idea or the domain is bad.

1. **Reddit.** Google "[topic] reddit", find threads where people ask for places or URLs, and reply with the link. For the business-ideas directory he found over 100 such threads. He plans only 1-3 replies a day to avoid bans, because Reddit has URL rules beyond subreddit rules.
2. **Other directories.** List yours in relevant directories. They are big and can send traffic, but they must be relevant.
3. **Social media replies.** Search X for the same questions and reply with the directory when it truly answers them. Example: Fireship's viral tweet about self-hosted software had about a million views, and John's reply with his self-hosted software directory got about 30-40K views.
4. **Social backlinks.** He says Google does look at social backlinks even though it doesn't say so. After that viral reply, his Google traffic grew the next day across all blogs and items. He says he has seen this about 50 times and that it beats website backlinks now.

He does this search himself each morning, not with a keyword-spy tool, because X search is good and more native.

chunks.heading: SEO for a new directory, including the AI agent and the publishing cap
chunks.text:
- SEO is the key growth channel for directories and comes after the promotion steps above.
- He built an SEO agent that scrapes the directory, researches keywords, proposes article ideas with estimated traffic, writes outlines and articles, and publishes them back to the site. He programmed into it the actions he used to do by hand. Example output: "10 low cost business ideas for 2025".
- He prefers a dedicated tool over prompting Claude or ChatGPT, since SEO is also internal linking, structure and keyword research, not just content.
- Learning tip: watch what an SEO agent does and repeat it manually.
- Publishing cap for a fresh, low-rating domain: publishing many articles at once can look like spam and Google may never crawl them. Maximum about 50 articles in the first month, more in month two. He usually publishes about 10 in month one.

chunks.heading: The 30-day test, then the data phase
chunks.text:
- Routine: day one to build and promote on Reddit and social, another day for SEO and more promotion, then stop and move to the next directory. Come back after 30 days and check traffic.
- Bet on 5-10 directories at once, so one failure isn't disappointing and SEO waiting time is shared. "Never fall in love with the idea."
- If there's no traffic after a month, he says it's very hard to fix, because something is fundamentally wrong (the domain, or a keyword that looked easy but isn't). He has never turned a zero-traffic directory around. Don't "push the dying horse."
- After 30 days he picks the best performer and moves to phase two: data quality. The first 30 days are only for validating SEO traffic and interest.
- Why data matters: experts who open the directory can quickly tell whether you know the topic. His LLM models directory was first filled by a hired person and was missing Mistral. An expert would see that and know the owner doesn't understand the space.
- When the data is high quality, influencers share the directory with their audiences, and it becomes organic as others follow. This happened with all his good directories.
- Ongoing work is small: keep running the SEO agent and check the space weekly or monthly.
- Next growth wave: be early on hot items. He scrolls Twitter daily, and when a new item is relevant to one of his directories he adds it quickly. Google has little else to show for that new item, so the directory can capture the search traffic.

chunks.heading: Ways to monetize a directory
chunks.text:
1. **Banners and sponsor spots (strongest for B2B).** He emailed owners of GPTs on his all-GPTs directory with 30K items, offering to feature them at the top, and many said yes.
2. **Affiliate links**, best when items cost a lot. $10 items need many clicks; items at $500 to a few thousand pay well. His Next.js boilerplates directory uses affiliate links to expensive boilerplates.
3. **Selling data.** Never private data, only anonymized data or insights, sold to corporates interested in distributions and percentages.
4. **Paid listings.** Works where listed parties benefit, e.g. a nannies directory where each nanny pays to be listed (he mentions charging $50 or $500 per listing).
5. **Paid access for buyers.** Show the top five entries without contact data or photos, and charge to unlock the full database, either for life or monthly.
6. **Brand sponsors (his current favorite).** Once a directory is big, big brands pay for affiliation rather than clicks. DevHunt, the biggest after Product Hunt, has ongoing sponsorship deals with brands like Clerk and Supabase. They pay monthly or weekly and likely forever as traffic grows. Sponsor links are smaller and annoy users less than banners.
7. **Channel traffic to your own SaaS.** SEO is much harder for a SaaS with a random brand name competing against VC-funded companies bidding on keywords. He wins traffic on directories and sends it to his SaaS products, and says this was "the best idea I ever had in marketing." Almost all his traffic now goes to directories first, then to products.
8. **Sell the directory.** He sold his all-GPTs directory to cheap.ai (the name is spoken in the transcript as "cheap. a"), which had exactly the same audience.

chunks.heading: Buying and selling directories
chunks.text:
- Why a SaaS should buy one: his math is a directory with 100K views a month grows to about a million views in a year. Channeling at least 3% gives about 30K clicks a year. Paying about 20K for it is under a dollar per click, which he says beats newsletter ads and other channels.
- Prices (from deals he has seen): start at 2K. Small ones go for 2-5K, average ones 15-20K, bigger ones up to about 100K. He has never seen one sell for over 100K. There is no revenue multiple system because revenue is not the main factor; audience and traffic quality are.
- Where to find them: Acquire.com doesn't accept directories because they lack revenue. Smaller marketplaces list them, and he named one as Micro-something (transcript says "Micron iio", uncertain). He says the best way is to research traffic, audience and countries on Similarweb and make a direct offer. Founders surprised by an offer may accept right away, while owners who list for sale often ask a lot.
- He bought the domain selldirectories.com the day before the recording, to launch a marketplace.
- He has a directory guide covering ideation, building, growing, selling and monetizing, at johnrush.me.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: John Rush explains his repeatable blueprint for launching 20+ products: start from your own pain, get a waitlist and presales, deliver manually, then build with a 50/50 co-maker. He covers marketing via SEO, daily social, directories and cross-promotion between apps, plus AI usage, margins and building in public.

chunks.heading: Idea validation blueprint: pain, waitlist, pre-sale, manual delivery
chunks.text:
John uses the same process for all 20+ of his products.

1. **Start with his own pain at work.** He looks for an existing solution first.
2. **If nothing exists, talk about the pain publicly.** If other people reply "I have the same pain, I wish there was a solution," that is the green light.
3. **Launch a waitlist.** The target is 100 signups.
4. **Email the list a 90% discount pre-sale before building anything.**
5. **Build the MVP only after 5 sales.**
6. **Deliver the solution manually, with no product yet.** He ignores margins at this stage. He only cares that customers are satisfied.
7. **Iterate on the manual service until customers like it.** It is easier to iterate with no code, because he only changes his own routine and service.
8. **Find a co-maker, spend two to three months building, then do a big launch on Twitter.**

chunks.heading: Founder-market fit: build for your own work
chunks.text:
- John's advice: "The most important thing when you build a startup is the idea and the founder idea fit."
- He says people go wrong by hunting for random ideas in random spaces. They should build something they understand.
- He went to the extreme and built things for his own work, which he understands "really really well."
- He is sure that any job has hundreds of problems software can solve. His advice is to look around you and find the pain points in your job.
- Building for something you are passionate about or have expert knowledge in gives a head start.

chunks.heading: Co-maker model: 50/50 partners who build
chunks.text:
- Finding a co-maker is as hard as finding a co-founder.
- John befriends other makers over months or years. When he needs a co-maker, he knows who to ask. For a social media tool, he would approach founders who built something similar and failed.
- His pitch is an idea that has already passed validation, with pre-sales done and some users in place. He says that makes it "really easy" to convince them.
- Ownership is split 50/50. John handles operations, legal and accounting. The co-maker handles coding and support.
- To be a co-maker people want to work with, build in public. It lets others evaluate you and see what you have in common.

chunks.heading: Marketing: product first, then SEO, social, directories and cross-promo
chunks.text:
- John says good marketing is a good product. The ideal is a product that drives sales and word of mouth on its own.
- Great products rarely exist on day one. You start with an average product, use "boring" marketing to bring the first users, then use those users to improve the product.
- Channels before the product is great:
  - **SEO** is first.
  - **Social media** is second. He posts on X, LinkedIn, Substack and Facebook, repurposes the same content everywhere, and does it daily. He shares at least 30 tweets a month, sometimes more.
  - **Directory listings** are third. They work well if the product is hot and interesting. All his products are AI-related and easy to package so people click them on directories. A "clickbaity" product drives directory traffic more easily.
  - **Cross-promo** is the fourth, and he calls it unique to him.

chunks.heading: Portfolio cross-promotion: premium tools plus traffic tools
chunks.text:
- John runs 20+ tools. Some are premium tools that make money. Others exist to bring in traffic and channel it to the premium tools.
- Every user who tries one product ends up trying at least one more. Some try all of them. Cross-promo works because people already trust him and know he delivers.
- He does two things:
  - He links tools to each other.
  - He integrates tools with each other. Example: in SEO Bot there is a "boost my domain rating" button that sends users to Listing Bot, which helps boost domain rating.
- Users flow natively from product to product and end up in his whole ecosystem.
- Revenue is concentrated. Seven products bring most of the revenue, and the others bring the audience and channel it to the paid products.

chunks.heading: The portfolio and how he got into bootstrapping
chunks.text:
- Scale: about 26 startups, roughly 1 million B2B users combined, and about $3M ARR combined.
- **Unicorn Platform:** a website, landing page, waitlist and directory builder for busy founders, with 600,000 users. In 2022, after about 10 years in VC-backed startups, he asked the founder to sell him the whole startup and stay on for a year as his bootstrapping mentor. He paid almost $1M.
- **SEO Bot:** about $100K MRR, grown in under 12 months, and one of the first AI SEO agents on the market.
- **Listing Bot:** finds relevant directories and lists your product there.
- **Nova:** an AI project manager he built to manage projects with his many co-makers.

chunks.heading: AI use, tools and margins
chunks.text:
- **Building:** he built his own AI code generator for SaaS products, no-code tools and AI agents. He calls AI coding probably the best application of AI today. His stack is JavaScript and Tailwind, which he says AI handles very well.
- **Design:** logos and images are made with AI, and he mostly does not use designers.
- **Research:** he used to hire people. Now he gives a task to o3 or Grok research mode and gets a complete data table after about 10 minutes.
- **Marketing:** he says this is where AI gains him the most profit, since marketing otherwise consumes a lot of resources. He uses it for SEO, emails, copywriting and ads.
- **Models in products:** he uses Claude, Gemini and OpenAI APIs inside his tools. He keeps switching because the best model changes monthly, so he uses all three and lets users choose.
- **Other tools:** Grok for learning, because it connects to real-time tweets. Discord for chat and project management. Apple Notes for writing, after trying everything complicated.
- **Margins:** SEO Bot earns about $100K/month and pays about $30K for APIs, roughly 70% margin. Non-AI tools have about 90% margins.
- **Support:** he keeps human support in all products. Unicorn Platform's main cost is support agents. His reason: "AI doesn't have the soul." People chat with humans and build relationships.

chunks.heading: Build in public and VC vs bootstrap
chunks.text:
- **Build in public:** he first saw it as free marketing. The bigger value is a direct channel to the audience and users, which helps him build better products.
- **Failure rate:** before building in public, about 90% of what he did failed. After, only about 10% of products fail, because he adjusts them before shipping.
- **VC vs bootstrap:**
  - VC is about exits, and everything is optimized for an exit. Bootstrap is about profit.
  - VC pays for growth. Bootstrap relies on product-led growth.
  - VC grows headcount to raise valuation. Bootstrap cuts headcount, ideally to solo, since then there are no costs.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: John Rush explains how he builds small AI agents and tools as a solo bootstrapper. He covers finding ideas via Google autocomplete and keyword research, validating with waitlists, outreach and discounted pre-bookings, and his five growth channels: social, SEO, affiliates, distribution everywhere, and free tools.

chunks.heading: Building agents that start as internal tools and go public later
chunks.text:
- John says all of his products start as his own internal agent. He runs each one for 1-3 years before it goes public.
- Being the only customer makes a project easier to run. He can move fast, take risks and has no users complaining.
- Once a product is stable and he stops iterating much, he brings in friends who run startups. Then he launches it publicly. "Eventually everything I use internally will become public."
- He deliberately creates "suffering" for himself by doing accounting, design, development, growth and paperwork himself instead of delegating. That lets him judge whether an agent is good enough. He still does his own accounting for this reason.
- His agents are "so simple on the surface and so complicated under the hood". The goal is to turn one on and have it work like a self-managed employee that asks him questions and then goes back to work.
- He has 24 projects, mostly websites, with combined revenue of around $3M. Three products bring in most of it.
- He bet early on AI getting much stronger (he automated things with GPT-2 and GPT-3, and bet bigger when 3.5 launched). He chose to bootstrap small companies and automate the 20% of work that gives 80% of the result: first operations, then growth, then development.

chunks.heading: SEO Bot: an agent with almost no interface
chunks.text:
- SEO Bot is at $1M ARR. It was doubling month over month before summer 2025, then stalled at about $110k a month over the summer. He expected growth to restart in September.
- It runs on autopilot. It sends weekly emails saying what it did: articles, how-to guides, mini tools that drive SEO traffic, and newsletters from collected news.
- It asks him for input only when unsure, for example "I have 10 items, pick five". Over time he moved from involved daily, to weekly, to monthly, to about once a quarter.
- From the start the interface had no buttons, only a checkbox to turn it on. He added controls later because agencies and pro users asked for them.
- He argues people want a lot of control only because they have too much time, such as an employee with eight hours a day for SEO. He believes long term people don't want that much control.
- Setup: give it your URL. It analyzes the audience, finds low-competition keywords, builds an article plan and publishes about one article a day. It syncs with Framer, Webflow and WordPress, so you never have to come back.
- It costs about $20 a month, versus about $5K for an agency.
- To manage SEO churn, he emails weekly KPIs. Views show up within a week and clicks later, so users see things are happening. Results now show in 2-3 weeks, where they once took 2-3 months.
- His customers are mostly busy founders, not SEO professionals.

chunks.heading: Connected products and cross-selling
chunks.text:
- His agents call each other. SEO Bot can ask Rapify (a vibe-coding tool for little tools) to build a tool and send it back, like a marketer asking a developer.
- Roughly half of his new users each month come from one of his other tools.
- Some tools make only about $1K a month, but they are cheap, have trials, and feed users into his other tools. "It's very rare when people leave my universe."
- He does the same with directories. Most make about $1K a month and some make $10K. He values them for driving traffic from people who would not otherwise find him.
- He is not rushing growth. He wants each agent at roughly 100 to 1,000 customers, enough to test and A/B test, and avoids more because of support load and legacy to maintain.

chunks.heading: Finding ideas
chunks.text:
- 99% of his ideas come from scratching his own itch. The second source is seeing what many people ask for.
- Google autocomplete hack:
  1. Type a phrase like "website builder for" and read the suggestions (small business, photographers, artists, nonprofits).
  2. Spend about an hour building a list of 50-60 ideas in a spreadsheet.
  3. Run each through a keyword research tool to see traffic.
- Example: "website builder for artists" showed about 10K visitors a month, with several similar phrases at about 10K each, roughly 100K in total. He also tested "tux heaven" at about 100K searches with low competition.
- Why niches work: VC-backed companies chase the same big markets. Small niches are "not a billion dollar idea" but are enough for a regular person to build a million-dollar business, so many are unserved.
- Don't guess. "The intuition never helps."
- He first asks whether he wants the product himself. If he does, he keeps going even if others don't, and he may shelve it for a year while he works out why.

chunks.heading: Validating an idea
chunks.text:
- He tries to kill the idea. "If you're in love with your idea... you will interpret the data in a wrong way." Better to kill 20 ideas and build the 21st.
- Step 1: build a simple waitlist landing page in a landing page builder (Unicorn Platform, Framer or Webflow), not a vibe-coding tool. Builders have better SEO and are made for landing pages. Vibe-coding tools are for apps with logins. Collect only name and email.
- Step 2: drive traffic.
  - Post on social media and Reddit.
  - Reply to people discussing related topics, even loosely related ones (musicians and software, for example).
  - DM the same people.
  - Cold email them.
  - Do about 100 outreach actions in total.
  - Optionally send paid traffic (he used Google and Meta ads).
- Reading the result: zero signups is a useful answer. One, five or ten signups means you have something. Sometimes it takes off.
- Example: for Dev Hunt (a Product Hunt-style launchpad for dev tools), he tweeted that he'd build it if 100 people signed up. He got 100 signups, and people shared the link to help reach the number.
- Social platforms no longer weight follower count much. Interesting content gets shown to a few people and spreads if it works. He did this before he had followers.
- Step 3: pre-sales. Offer a 70-90% discount to buy now.
  - If under 10% of the waitlist pays, he treats it as a bad sign. It usually means the wrong audience (students, for example, signed up but wouldn't pay a dollar), and he says you'd have to kill the idea.
  - Pre-sales also reveal pricing and model problems. Listing Bot was planned as a monthly subscription, but people wanted a one-time payment. Count Visits was offered as a $100 lifetime deal, but people preferred starting at $9 a month.
  - Emailing waitlist people the payment link gives you a thread where they explain why they're not buying.
- Launch timing doesn't matter much. If you got 100 waitlist signups once, you can repeat it later. He treats first waitlisters as validation, not real users.
- He has never had indicators say yes and then flopped. He has had the opposite: everything said bad idea, then it worked.

chunks.heading: SEO from day one as validation
chunks.text:
- Most people start SEO late. He starts SEO work on day one of a product, then waits a few months.
- SEO traffic is a second validation: it shows whether you can reach attention, not only whether people want the product. He says he rarely sees people fail to build something people want. The failure is reaching them.
- To test several ideas, he publishes SEO articles for each and leaves them for a few months. Some URLs get zero traffic (keywords too expensive to compete on), while others rank easily.
- This can beat keyword research alone, because keyword numbers don't tell you who is searching.
- Put waitlist banners in the articles as another test.
- On skipping SEO because it pays off a year later: "if you would have just done it... it would be paying off by now."

chunks.heading: His five growth channels
chunks.text:
He says these five bring about 80% of early growth.

1. **Social media.** The best channel for small products. Popularity also brings backlinks, newsletter mentions and directory listings, and influencers talk about you for free. Test whether you have talent for it. If so, it may be the only thing to do.
2. **SEO.** Build backlinks and domain rating, and publish articles yourself or with a tool. About one hour a day for a month gives decent output. Outsource to agencies if you have money.
3. **Affiliate partners.** Use a tool like FirstPromoter with a partner portal, unique links and codes. Be "crazy generous" on commission: 50% if the product has no underlying costs, 25-30% if it does, versus the typical 10-15%. He calls it one of his best investments.
4. **Be everywhere.** Directories, launchpads, forums, Reddit, Quora, social media. People may find you, and LLMs crawl those comments, articles and listicles, so you may end up in their answers. Some of his products suddenly got nearly all their traffic from ChatGPT, Claude and Grok in the same week.
5. **Free tools as lead magnets.** For a website builder for artists, build an album cover generator. Users enter an email to get the PNG, and the email promotes your paid product. They click at a high rate because they already trust you.

chunks.heading: Directories and reputation in the AI era
chunks.text:
- Directories made by people with influence will matter more. AI systems rank by backlinks, which are easy to game, and they now use Reddit upvotes to filter. Directories help humans filter out trash when a category has too many options.
- He says to partner with people who own attention and build products around it. A tool built by someone with a reputation stands out when everything built with AI is equally good.
- "Influencer" can be small. In a niche of 10,000 people, talking about it consistently can be enough to go viral within that group.
- Tools: Lovable for prototyping and MVPs (also Bolt, Cursor), his own coding tool for full products, and Make, Zapier and Lindy for automation.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: John Rush walks through building SEO directory sites. Most of the outcome is decided by keyword research and the domain, with data curation second and technology a distant third. He validates keywords with Google Keyword Planner for traffic and Google search for competition, then builds fast with no-code, seeds listings by scraping, promotes, and monetizes.

chunks.heading: Why directories are an SEO game and why most fail
chunks.text:
- John has built about 50 directories (he says "20" at first, then "a lot more like 50"), and about 12 are doing pretty well. He claims over 10 million in traffic and has sold one.
- He runs a product called Listing Bot that finds hundreds of new directories every day, so he watches what others build.
- He says about 99% of directories fail, as with startups generally. It looks easy, but the market is open and crowded.
- The number one reason they fail is too little keyword research.
- A SaaS can find product-market fit by pivoting, because the pain was real to start with. A directory is purely an SEO game.
- People never remember or bookmark a directory. They land on it from a Google search.
- Bad keywords (low traffic, high competition) never win, and he has never seen an exception.

chunks.heading: Keyword research with Google Keyword Planner plus Google search
chunks.text:
John tried Ahrefs, Semrush and others. He always uses Google itself, in combination:

1. Start in Google search and let it help you phrase the keyword. A keyword is always more than one word, and more words make it easier to win.
2. Use Keyword Planner for traffic.
3. Use Google search to judge competition.
4. Check year-over-year growth. Fast growth suggests the space isn't crowded yet, because it wasn't popular a year ago. No growth may mean it's oversaturated.
5. Ping-pong between the two tools, narrowing from the broad term to a sub-term.

Demo: "best tent" showed 10K to 100K searches. "Popup tent" showed 900%+ year-over-year growth. The results were paid ads, a Cambridge dictionary page and e-commerce sites, with no directory and no specialist blog.

- Ignore "high competition" in Keyword Planner for purchasable items. That figure is competition for ads, and people scroll past ads.
- Searchers read URLs closely. A URL like "best popup tents" stands out against unrelated ones.

chunks.heading: Picking a domain
chunks.text:
- Often the keyword is good but the domain is gone, and you have to give up on it. In the demo, a premium domain was listed at 20K. John never pays more than $9 for a domain.
- A .org domain is an advantage when competing with commercial results. You look like Wikipedia, a place for information rather than transactions. He called the .org version of popup tents "just amazing".
- His rule is 80% of a directory's success is keyword research and domain, 15% is data curation (good items) and 5% is technology and design.

chunks.heading: Building fast with no-code
chunks.text:
- Most people reverse the 80/20 rule and spend weeks coding or polishing design. John says to go no-code, using his Unicorn Platform or any other.
- No-code tools give you the ongoing work (promotion, updates) out of the box and ship with templates.
- Nobody cares about brand identity. The plainer and less salesy the site looks, the better, because you are convincing people you're there to inform them and not to take their money. Craigslist is the example of an ugly site that works.
- A Unicorn Platform directory template with big images works for tents. The database is a Google Sheet, and you replace the demo rows with real items.
- Sourcing data depends on the niche. He recommends building for topics you understand.
  - Scrape Amazon or other listing sites.
  - Use Twitter advanced search with a minimum likes filter (he used 30) to find viral posts, since viral items are probably better than unknown ones.
  - He builds one scraper per source (Product Hunt, Twitter, LinkedIn, Reddit, Quora). For one directory he fetched 100 items from Product Hunt into the sheet.
- If building takes more than a day, you're going the wrong way. Finding the idea can take weeks. A first-timer can give themselves a week to a month for research and validation.

chunks.heading: Validation checklist before building
chunks.text:
John's checklist:

1. Search the keyword in Google, so Google helps phrase it.
2. Check there is real traffic. No traffic means nobody cares, or you spelled the term wrong.
3. Check for high growth.
4. Check that you understand the topic, because you need to judge and curate the items.
5. Check that user-generated sites (Reddit, Quora, forums, Twitter, LinkedIn) have active discussion. Use `site:reddit.com popup tent` and repeat for each site, then check views and engagement.
6. Have a promotion plan before you build.

In the demo, the keyword had high traffic, growth, a good domain, and a subreddit with 5 million members. All the boxes were checked.

chunks.heading: Launching and getting backlinks
chunks.text:
- Best launch tactic: find questions on Reddit, Quora and similar sites and say "I built a directory that helps with this".
- Nonprofit directory links rarely get hated, unlike a SaaS with sign-up and pay buttons. Directories are often the only URLs allowed on some subreddits. Be honest about your story, ideally one that comes from your own hobby or interest.
- Reddit gives strong exposure and backlinks. A Reddit post can rank on Google within a day, whereas your own domain takes months or years.
- Example: for his open source software directory he posted on a subreddit with a viral post. The next day he had tons of backlinks, as people wrote blog posts linking to it.
- Two ways to earn backlinks:
  1. List the directory on other directories (directories of directories), forums and blogs, hundreds of places.
  2. Find every article on the topic and drop the URL in the comments. These are nofollow links, but Google still follows them with lower weight.
- Make the data so good that influencers link to it. Update it every month. Most directories stop after launch.
- Pick a niche you love, since you'll update it monthly and already know where the data is.

chunks.heading: Why directories beat blogs and where the opportunity is
chunks.text:
- John says there are too few directories and only about 1% exist that could. He advises against crowded niches like AI tools. Go where nobody is building, such as unsexy niches whose users (campers) aren't developers or founders.
- Programmatic SEO applied to such a niche: scrape everything, create many category pages, and beat affiliate blogs and e-commerce sites.
- He is bullish on directories and bearish on blogs. AI will dominate answers, so people will not open a blog post for something AI already summarized.
- AI will not dominate judgment. If AI says "this popup tent is best, according to the popup tent directory", people will want to open the directory and judge for themselves. He thinks directories will survive the post-AI search era.

chunks.heading: Monetizing directories
chunks.text:
He has a guide with 20 ways and covers the first five:

- **Claim your listing**: email the owners of listed items and offer to update their data, pictures and contact info. Include analytics ("your listing was viewed 100 times this week"). He calls it a no-brainer because you bring them traffic.
- **Affiliate links**: convert every outbound link. It works for high-ticket items. His directory MVP Wizards (people building MVPs) has tickets of about 5K, with 20% commission, so one transaction brings about 1K. His movies directory had millions of clicks on iTunes affiliate links but earned about $100, because iTunes pays very little.
- **Sponsors**: he gets inbound sponsor requests via his social following. Without an audience, use Hunter.io or Find My Mail to find sponsor emails. Look for audience overlap. For popup tents, approach smaller makers where you can reach the founder, not the huge ones. A single sponsor can sometimes pay more than many, and may become a near co-owner.
- **Boosted listings**: charge to be sorted higher, possibly via bidding or an auction for the number one spot.
- **Featured listings**: pay to be featured at the top. On his open source directory he features Listing Bot at the top, which gets a lot of clicks. Buyers come back because you bring growth, and traffic compounds.
- Sponsor retention is possible. For his Next.js starter directory, sponsors pay on a monthly or weekly subscription "infinitely".

chunks.heading: Why start with a directory instead of a paid SaaS
chunks.text:
- John says everyone should have a directory as a side project. Directories need way less talent than SaaS. About one year is enough for an amateur to succeed with at least one directory, but expect to try 10 or 20.
- Benefits: you build confidence, learn idea validation, keyword search and simple promotion.
- Promoting a SaaS gets you slapped in the face, because nobody cares and people hate it. With a directory, people say "cool, nice job".
- Never start with a traditional paid SaaS. Start with a directory, an information site or a free tool.
- A directory in a space you like gives you a ready traffic channel for a later SaaS, so the growth part is covered.
- He offers a Directory Guide (page by page with examples) and a Discord called "directory makers" for buyers of the guide.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: John Rush explains how he validates many startup ideas by pitching them to a large audience he built on LinkedIn, X and Reddit, then building only the ones that draw engagement. Because the same audience uses multiple products, he treats lifetime value as the sum across his whole portfolio.

chunks.heading: Bootstrapped portfolio model: 24 startups, zero employees, 50/50 co-makers
chunks.text:
- John runs about 24 startups with no employees. Each project has one "co-maker" (usually the technical builder) who owns 50/50 with him. John does most of the marketing and product; the co-maker does most of the coding.
- His day-to-day is a Discord server with 24 channels, each with John and one co-maker. He brings roadmap ideas and user feedback, they discuss, the co-maker builds.
- He bootstrapped after about 10 years of VC-backed startups (seed, Series A, San Francisco incubators, exit-focused). He argues bootstrapping works better because "your incentives are aligned with the users not with investors."
- He prefers many small companies over one large one. One large startup "becomes like a job" with a board and employees, and he loses the freedom to pivot.
- Many products also make him safe: if one dies (e.g. ChatGPT ships something), he has many others, so he doesn't need to read the news.
- He doesn't plan to sell the projects. The goal is a holding company of products for the same audience, run for decades.
- He meets all co-makers once a year (usually June), for example a one-month gathering in Istanbul. They run their own hackathons there. One produced an agent store inside Unicorn Platform that turns on all his products with one click.
- He lives in a forest outside Istanbul and takes about 2-3 months off each summer. During one two-month break he posted nothing on the internet and customers kept coming in.

chunks.heading: One audience across all products: busy founders and compounding lifetime value
chunks.text:
- All of John's products target "busy founders": one founder doing most of the job instead of hiring. He sees this as a growing group (even YC-backed startups now brag about small headcount).
- Founders care about outcome, not process. They want few interfaces and ideally one button that gets the job done.
- Because every product shares the same audience, a user who joins one product has a high chance of using five, ten or more of the others. This solves much of his distribution.
- Lifetime value adds up across products. His example: if one product's LTV is $400, then ten products make it $4,000. That lets him spend more on acquisition, and each customer is worth roughly 10x.
- He builds growth and marketing products, not developer tools. Founders paying for growth help will pay and share with friends. Developers "are never willing to pay and they're never willing to share," and VC-backed players subsidize dev tools. He built Dev Hunt, then stopped building many tools for developers.
- Small fees for small problems: a $99/month customer doesn't expect custom demands. Busy founders rarely contact support if the tool works.
- He turns down corporate clients who want SLAs and calls. It costs him money, but he keeps the business small enough to run without that burden, and total revenue across projects stays stable and growing.
- He argues his portfolio can still grow very large because the audience is millions of potential users.

chunks.heading: Idea validation: audience first, then a manual MVP, then a technical co-maker
chunks.text:
- He builds distribution first on LinkedIn, X and Reddit, then pitches many ideas. He takes forward the ones that get comments, likes and questions.
- He validates through story, not code: "It's much easier to [change] your story" than to rewrite code. He shares the product story from every angle, even on podcasts, and discusses ideas for months or sometimes years.
- When people ask "when are you building this?", he recruits a technical co-founder who previously built something similar and failed. He brings them the audience and a full spec (features, pain points).
- The co-maker then does a one-to-two-week hackathon, and users arrive right after release.
- The first version is simpler than people expect. It can be a form that feeds a database while he and the co-maker do the work manually behind it. They lose money on time, but staying manual keeps them agile.
- He tries to launch within a month, then iterates on user feedback.
- His complexity rule: he doesn't want more than one person building it. If he can't build a simple MVP himself with vibe coding, he skips the product, since it would require hiring.
- Pain rule: he does a task manually until it hurts, learns the UX, then builds the product that solves it for himself. He did SEO by hand, sleeping little, before building a tool for it.
- Hundreds of ideas fail at the idea level, but every product that got real code is still running.

chunks.heading: Case study: Index Rusher (December 2023)
chunks.text:
- He saw Twitter screenshots of Google Search Console with pages partly green (indexed) and partly gray (not indexed). The fixes in the comments were all manual.
- He built a waitlist in about 10 minutes, just before Christmas 2023. One button grants access to the user's Search Console. A Discord notification fired, and he manually sent pages for indexing and analyzed why they weren't indexed. The "product" was John behind a button.
- Sharing it on Twitter made it blow up. Once demand was clear, he found a developer to turn it into a real product with no human involvement.
- Distribution: he searched Twitter for keywords like "page indexed" and replied to complaints with the product. People didn't mind because the reply answered their question.
- He looks for small problems, not large products. Scrolling Reddit, Quora or Twitter for a few hours shows many complaints.
- Some products earn little or are free, but they pull people into his ecosystem and then into his other products.

chunks.heading: Vibe coding: speccing and tool-switching
chunks.text:
- For first MVPs he uses Lovable, Replit, or his own no-code tool Unicorn Platform. He says using vibe coding tools is a skill that improves with practice.
- Treat the tool like a human who needs a clear spec. His spec has parts:
  - Business model first: who the user is, why they need it, how often, what they hate about existing products, what they want.
  - Numbered feature list, each with a simplification (e.g. "only email or only Google" for sign-up). AI tries to do things too well and overcomplicates unless told otherwise.
  - A long "do not do" list, his longest section (e.g. no user portal, store data in the browser, use an existing SDK).
- He keeps the prompt in a notes file and refines it over time. He now often gets a working result in one shot with no follow-up prompts.
- He tries the same prompt in three or four tools, because quality varies by day as providers change models and code.
- He moved a learning management portal from Bolt to Cursor when Bolt began breaking things on bug fixes. His view: vibe tools are for MVPs, Cursor is for production, and founders should become more technical and read some code as the product grows.
- Launch MVPs as content, not a pure launch. Teach something about the topic, plug the URL at the end of the thread. On Reddit, describe the problem and the fix without naming the product, and let people ask or click his profile.

chunks.heading: Marketing automation and where growth comes from now
chunks.text:
- He automates marketing to avoid hiring one person per product, since mistakes in marketing are cheap. He uses AI for SEO: keyword ideas, headlines, blog articles, directories and programmatic SEO, mostly with his own SEO Bot tool.
- He uses Lindy AI, Zapier, Make and n8n for sequences. Example: find LinkedIn people who are bootstrapping and mentioned SEO, then DM them genuinely helpful content about their problem, not a product pitch, to start a conversation.
- Social media and SEO are getting more crowded, with VC-backed companies pouring money in and far more AI articles (he estimates roughly 10x more than last year). He wouldn't recommend social media to a new founder as a first channel.
- SEO has changed. New sites can get traffic in two to four weeks instead of six months. But Google favors fresh content, so you have to keep publishing. One of his sites lost its traffic entirely and he hadn't found why.
- LLM traffic is rising. LLMs favor niche directories for queries like "10 best bootstrap founders," and he runs many directories.
- He expects specialized, single-topic sites tied to a trusted human and present across blog, social, podcast and YouTube to win.
- He sees a fragmenting economy of many founders with niche brands, since AI makes money less effective for growth.

chunks.heading: Building a personal brand from zero
chunks.text:
- Personal brand multiplies a good product but can't replace one. His analogy: it's "like a wind on a fire. If there's no fire and you pour wind on it, there will be no fire." Some of his products failed even with his brand.
- His brand feeds other channels: directories list his products and people link to him for free, which helps SEO.
- You can't buy a personal brand. Money makes it look corporate.
- With a few hundred followers, focus on a specific problem, not on yourself. His Dev Hunt launch came at about 200 Twitter followers. His message was that Product Hunt mostly serves marketers and developer tools never win there. It was new and public, and the tweet reached about 100k views.
- Get reach first, without promoting yourself. Repeated exposure makes people recognize your name. Stay consistent on one topic (his are bootstrapping, AI and vibe coding).
- Aim for one viral post. Algorithms now push content from small accounts, you have unlimited attempts, and the only cost is embarrassment. After one big post, the algorithm promotes you more. On LinkedIn he sees posts at about 50 likes and then one at 800 to 1,000.
- Build in public in 2025-2026: share good and bad.
- His social posts are written by him with no AI. Everything else is automated.

chunks.heading: Nova: the AI project manager on Discord
chunks.text:
- Nova is an AI project and product manager that lives in Discord, where his co-makers, partners and some customers are. It acts on his behalf and many people think it's a human.
- Tasks:
  - Pulls product mentions from across the internet daily and posts them in the co-maker channel with proposed solutions.
  - Watches support chats for customer and prospect questions, complaints and bug requests.
  - Replies to customers and solves problems where it can, or sends bugs to the developer.
  - Knows the roadmap; when John shares an idea, it aligns the co-maker.
  - Coordinates cross-product integrations between two co-makers.
- He corrects it in the chat when it errs, visible to everyone. He says it's his biggest time-saver, with vibe coding next.
- He hasn't launched it publicly because he is liable for what it does. He plans to launch next year, probably.
- He expects that in about 12 months work will be optional for him, since everything will be automated except his own ideas.
- He also uses Gamma (gamma.app) for presentations.
- His closing message: "don't trade freedom for money."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: John Rush explains why growth tools beat build tools, how to pick ideas by asking how you'd sell them, and why directories are underrated. He shares a keyword-gap method for validating directories and how he buys micro-influencer posts for $100-300.

chunks.heading: Where John sees startup ideas now: growth and marketing tools for solo builders
chunks.text:
- John sees two trends. More "solopreneurs" build on the side (a corporate job plus weekends and evenings), and others move to cost-effective countries and spend a year or two building in public. He says this movement was very small about two years ago and is at least doubling every year.
- Access to building is the best ever. You don't need to fundraise, find a co-founder or hire a team. You code it yourself, or use no-code.
- His conclusion: "it's easy to build stuff but it's not easy to grow." 99% of makers can build, but only a few can grow, sell and bring in customers.
- So the low-hanging fruit is tools and services around growth and marketing. His own role is to build tools that make this crowd more powerful with fewer resources.

chunks.heading: Micro-tools: start from how you would sell it
chunks.text:
- John's way to find ideas is to start with how you would sell it. Don't build first; see what people are asking for.
- Example from his own path: people kept asking how to get SEO backlinks, how to grow, how to raise domain rating. Others answer with a seven-step list. Busy makers (many with full-time jobs) want to save time.
- He wraps that list of actions into a tool that does one thing. He calls these micro-tools.
- The goal is for people to recommend his tool under those posts: "I did that using this tool." A tool that does one thing is easy to remember and recommend. A tool that does many things is hard to remember.

chunks.heading: Idea: "startup drafts" (validated ideas with a waitlist and prepayments)
chunks.text:
- Problem: more people want to build but don't know what to build. They pick random ideas and fail. John says most people fail right at the start, with no traction and "not even one sign up."
- Idea: someone comes up with ideas, validates them with users, collects a waitlist and maybe prepayments, then sells the "startup draft" to a builder. Much of the risk is gone by then.
- Pricing: people would pay up to $1,000, and with word of mouth maybe $2K, $3K or $5K, to skip the first period.
- Pipeline, with his example numbers:
  1. Generate about 100 ideas through keyword research and hot-topic research on Reddit and Twitter.
  2. Technical validation: check organic traffic, potential, and whether the .com domain is free. About 30 survive.
  3. Human validation: build a waitlist and promote it with ads or paid influencers. About 10 survive.
  4. Ask waitlist members to prepay (his example is a 70% discount). About 3 survive.
  5. Sell each survivor with its audience, prepayments, idea and landing page, for $2,000-$3,000 each (about $6,000 for the ones he used as an example).
- Cost: roughly $1,000-$2,000 to run, so margins are good. Every step can be automated: domains and ads via APIs, landing pages via builders with APIs, ideas via AI and scraping. He says such a system could run 1,000 ideas a month and yield about 30 winners.
- Why it beats marketplaces: on startup marketplaces you get no users, revenue or validation for the same price. Building is the easiest part of a startup. With users, prepayments and validation, he says it is worth at least $10K.

chunks.heading: Buying influencer posts cheaply
chunks.text:
- John prefers paying influencers over ads because it's cheaper. He says you can pay $300 and get 100K views on a post on Twitter now.
- Prices have fallen. Two years ago he saw at least $1K for about 30,000 guaranteed views. He kept asking the same people every few months and prices dropped as more people entered and competition grew. Some deals are now $100 because he buys often.
- How he finds them: direct messages on Twitter and LinkedIn. They reach out to him more often than he reaches out to them.
- Negotiation:
  - They start high (about $700-$800). Bargain down to a few hundred.
  - Even if they say no, they often come back about four weeks later with an empty one-week slot, because $200 beats nothing.
  - Keep many influencers in your pipeline so a slot is always open.
  - After 5-10 purchases, agree on a low fixed price.
- New experiment: pay influencers a fixed amount every month, with a 12-month commitment that he won't cancel without notice. It's like Nike's deals with football stars, but at micro or nano scale. He gets a set amount of activity on their account (a post, part of a listicle, a reply). The price goes very low for him. The risk is that they lose reach, but he hasn't seen an influencer fully disappear.
- He plans a tool around this, which people on Twitter call "reinventing AdSense for micro startups."
- He thinks the cheap-attention window won't last. Influencer supply is growing nearly exponentially. Using social media is also hurting his building time, and he expects many people to turn into full-time influencers. He compares it to Spotify, where the cost of music dropped toward zero. Early users of influencers will still gain momentum over those who don't.

chunks.heading: Why directories work
chunks.text:
- John has been passionate about directories for years. Two years ago his team called them obsolete ("cool in 2017"). He disagreed but only started last year.
- His logic: as quantity grows, the share of quality drops, so choosing gets harder. There are hundreds of CRM tools, tomorrow thousands, and old ones don't get deleted. People want places where selection, categorization or enrichment has been done for them.
- People trust curators who show real experience in a field, and he sees more people starting to charge for good directories. He doesn't charge for his own. His example is Pat's Starter Story, which he calls a directory of startup stories, with Pat picking the best founders.
- A directory doesn't have to be a boring list of items. It can be a list of anything. You can monetize both sides: people who want access and those who want to be listed.
- AI angle: AI needs to find the best items to recommend. Reddit works partly as a directory (reputation, votes, an ordered list). He expects the best directories to be picked by AI for search results, which would give a directory huge power and make people pay to be in it.
- Building a directory takes little tech and a lot of time on content quality and promotion. He says it needs time rather than money.

chunks.heading: Directory idea 1: localize a working directory into another language
chunks.text:
- Many directories exist in English and very few in local languages. Example: it's hard to find a directory of SaaS tools made by French people in France.
- Method:
  1. Find a directory that works well in the US.
  2. Search for the same thing in another language (e.g. French) on Google.
  3. If nothing good ranks on top, build it.
- Reputation is solvable over time: learn the topic and the tools, make podcasts with founders of the tools, and so on.
- He argues non-English speakers are not "not in tech." Many prefer their own language, build in it, have large markets, and go international later.

chunks.heading: Directory idea 2: pick the niche by keyword data, not intuition
chunks.text:
- Method:
  1. Use Google's free Ads Keyword Planner to search keywords around random topics.
  2. Find a keyword with high traffic.
  3. Search it on Google. If no directory is on page one (only blog posts), build a directory around it.
  4. Google likes directories, and he says you eventually reach the top.
- He uses no personal judgment: "my intuition never works." The directories he had high hopes for failed and the ones he didn't succeeded. His theory is that if he likes an idea, many others do too, so it gets built by everyone.
- Keyword ideas come from ChatGPT. He tells it which products he has (he launched directories to drive traffic to his dev tools such as Dev Hunt and Flat UI) and which audience he wants, asks for 20 ideas, tests all 20, and found one great one.
- Run about 10 ideas because it's cheap and fast. Drop seven and push harder on three.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: John Rush explains why he bootstrapped after a VC-backed decade and built agents that replace teams. He covers when an agent is good enough to ship, why founders should avoid popular ideas, how to validate via services, why directories are the easiest first product, and why startups take about 10 years.

chunks.heading: Why John went bootstrapped and solo after 10 years of VC-backed startups
chunks.text:
- John ran VC-backed startups from 2010, with large teams. They raised money, ran in the USA and scaled internationally. This lasted about 10 years.
- His biggest pain was managing people. He says he likes people but not at work, because "at work you have to tell them what to do", and people use niceness as an excuse not to do things.
- All his companies had fewer people than competitors, and he always automated what he could, first without AI.
- Around 2020 he tried an early GPT (he thinks GPT-2 or GPT-3) in a B2C "concierge for tourists" startup. It connected to local taxi and pizza systems and translated on the fly. COVID lockdowns and closed borders killed it, so he moved to B2B.
- He left VC because he disliked the model and the San Francisco meetings. His thesis for competing with VC-backed startups: "90% of the money goes into the people in early stages", so automate the people with tools.
- His first project was automating coding itself, because it gives the biggest leverage for building every other tool. He spent 2020 to 2022 on it, then entered the market in 2023.

chunks.heading: The solo-founder bet: build software for founders, not employees
chunks.text:
- He bet around 2021 that attention was shifting to a world where talent matters more than money. Ads are expensive and getting more so, and people trust authentic content over paid.
- His prediction: solo founders and tiny, talented teams will out-compete giant companies with hundreds of people and millions in funding.
- Second assumption: almost all software is built for employees, who have time to learn tools. Nobody builds for founders, who never have time and want to "click the button, that's it".
- His approach: build the agents for himself, iterate until he is happy, then ship. Because he is "such a good representation of the new audience", others from that audience love the product.
- He tests across his many projects (corporate, consumer, directories) so the tool does not only work for one use case.
- He has had a fixed list of things to automate since 2021. He only reorders it by which one brings the most gain. In 2023 SEO across about 20 websites was the biggest pain, so he built that agent first.
- Status as of the interview: 2 years fully in, 7 agents on the market, about 26 projects in total. Some agents are, he thinks, best in class and growing faster than he can handle. He has slept under five hours for about a year and treats the pain as a signal of what to automate next instead of hiring.

chunks.heading: Agent timing: ship only when the tool saves about 90% of the time
chunks.text:
- He accounts for LLM progress so he does not build what the model will soon do out of the box (e.g. RAG, JSON output). That is why he kept many early tools unlaunched.
- Founders need to at least double productivity to change habits. His bar: the message must be "it saves you 90% of the time". Early agents were 50/50 or 70/30 human oversight, which was not enough.
- Timeline: everything in-house in 2022, closed in the first half of 2023, some agents opened in beta at the end of 2023, most opened publicly in September 2024.
- GPT-4 (April 2023) convinced him the bet was right, but it was unstable for systems that must run predictably. Function calling and JSON outputs arrived in summer 2024. He says stability matters because agents run on autopilot.

chunks.heading: Where agents work and where they don't: creativity and social content
chunks.text:
- Agents are least suited to creative work. AI is good at average creative output, but "the average never wins" in the attention world, and algorithms reward the best content even more over time.
- Even if AI gets funnier, humans move higher. He compares it to chess: AI plays, but people still watch humans, and people will care about the origin of content.
- Not all content needs creativity. SEO content just answers a question, so it suits agents.
- He runs social media mostly himself. His agents only help distribute content he created.

chunks.heading: Content strategy: long-form compression and the chat-driven workday
chunks.text:
- He does not think attention spans are shrinking. He thinks people are lazier and want content that is easy to read and also useful.
- Content that is both fun and educational is hard to make. He bets on long-form, partly storytelling, partly jokes, with things readers did not know and will bookmark. He says he was one of the first to do long tweets and deep dives on X.
- Compression wins attention: people share content that saves them time. But compressing requires real understanding. He can compress agents and startups because he has used them 10 to 20 times across scenarios.
- His day is about 90% chatting. He answers short questions from his agents (yes/no, pick one of five) and prompts tools. Replies on Twitter arrive in the same channel, so content creation fits in without a separate block of time.
- For learning his material, he points founders to his X Highlights tab, with a week of reading including the replies.

chunks.heading: Why solo and micro startups will multiply
chunks.text:
- Implementing today's agents everywhere could lay off perhaps half the workforce. Many of his products out-compete companies of 50 to 100 people.
- He argues new niches open up. If a product takes a month to launch and costs about $1K a month in agents plus his own salary, markets once too small (below a billion dollars) become viable. He cites roughly $1M a year as a fine ceiling for a niche product.
- He estimates 99% of the world is not powered by software, and expects the number of people building startups to rise from perhaps 10 million to hundreds of millions. His guess is most people will build startups or be a single employee overseeing agents.
- He compares it to Instagram. People once thought few would create content, but over 50% of social users now do, and he estimates about 20 in 100 do it seriously.
- Today the market punishes founders (no incentive, no insurance perks). He expects that to flip as agents lower corporate salaries and raise requirements.
- Niches the best founders skip stay open, like rabbit YouTube content that is average but sells pills. Small niches mean little competition from top talent.

chunks.heading: How to pick what to start: unpopular niches and services first
chunks.text:
- Most people pick what is popular (AI wrappers, chatbots) and face heavy competition. His rule: avoid competition today and tomorrow, since being first means little when others enter and prices drop.
- Pick an unsexy niche you are willing to understand deeply, such as flowers, schools or tractors, and aim to be among the best in it.
- His method: sell a service to the niche first. Services are easier to sell than products (one transaction, price-first buying). While doing them you learn which part to turn into a product, and you pitch ideas to real buyers.
- He says coming up with an idea in isolation almost never worked for him. Validation: buyers keep asking "when is it done?" Then failure risk is very low. Without it, failure risk is very high.
- Details matter: the audience, format and size, not only the one-liner.

chunks.heading: Getting the first sale and the founder mindset
chunks.text:
- Services solve the credibility gap. You can do the work free before being paid, like a designer redesigning a site and tagging the owner, or an SEO expert writing an article or roasting a profile and sending it.
- He says to expect about one in five recipients to buy. Once someone buys a service, you are "in their house" and they trust you enough to buy a product even with no users.
- Mindset: it is a 10-year game and the first 3 to 4 years are a "training camp". Fast success stories are, he says, mostly luck, perhaps 1 in 99 or worse.
- Do not pick big fights early. Like a boxer, spar with the punching bag first. Starting too hard means a near-certain early failure that makes it hard to continue.
- Easier fights: services, free products, non-AI products, directories and job boards. In year one, chase attention before revenue, then go for small-ticket revenue.

chunks.heading: Directories as the easiest starter product
chunks.text:
- A directory lists items in a niche (AI coding tools, MVP builders). In a world of infinite choice, people who help others choose are useful.
- He predicted in 2020 that directories would be big, because AI makes building easy, so near-identical alternatives multiply and buyers fear picking badly.
- Value comes from curation: good descriptions, highlighting the right things, filters and categories that narrow 500 items to 50, 5, then 1.
- Why he is bullish:
  - Easiest tech product: it can start in about half an hour with no-code or AI code, then takes time to collect items and write descriptions.
  - Easiest to promote: SEO. No Twitter audience or cold sales skills are needed, and the items themselves act as content for Google.
  - Competition is avoidable with the right niche, and the traffic is free, so the only cost is time.
- The monetization logic: connect buyers with sellers. Find buyers through content or directories and sellers will come to be shown to them.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: John Rush explains why he went all-in on directories after years of being told they were dead, why crowding shifts the win to quality, and why LLM search will send more clicks to directories than blogs. He also lays out a simple LLM SEO playbook: Reddit, top Bing and Google rankings, and social mentions.

chunks.heading: Why John started building directories and why they last
chunks.text:
- Friends and partners told John for about five years that directories were "yesterday's thing". In 2023 he decided to build one anyway, because directories kept surviving and every year some new directory got the traffic while he owned none of them.
- His first directory was a GPT directory, built right after the OpenAI demo day. It went viral, and he then built many more.
