- Early on, he says, only about five people in the world had built more than one directory, so whatever you shipped beat nothing. Now there are many boilerplates, tools and no-code tools (he counts "hundred of them"), plus directory courses from people who never built one.
- His conclusion: when a space gets crowded, the best quality and best work wins and the rest lose.
- He compares "directories are dead" to the "Drop Shipping is dead" argument. A directory is just a website model, and as long as websites exist, directories will too.

chunks.heading: Spend the most time on thinking, not building
chunks.text:
- John says he spent months or years thinking before building anything. Once he started building, it went fast.
- His process: whenever he sees something relevant on Twitter, he adds it to the idea and keeps shaping it until he knows what the directory must be built around.
- The core questions he settles are:
  - What should the directory be organized around?
  - What should it sort by?
  - What is the most important missing information about this type of item that people can't find anywhere?
- If you put that missing information in one place, people can judge the whole list well.
- He says he struggles to explain this to people who arrive with an idea and just go build it.
- Scraping, enriching and implementation are "so easy nowadays" compared with the thinking.

chunks.heading: How LLMs treat directories and why they help them
chunks.text:
- John argues LLMs make basic information easy to find, so demand moves to the best-quality source on a topic. LLMs and directories improve together.
- Three years ago, some directories won just by having some items. Now low-quality data comes from an LLM, so winning directories need really good data.
- A directory owner has one topic and unlimited time for research, so LLMs will always lag on depth.
- His prediction: deep search is slow (about 50 seconds) and costly for LLMs, so they will increasingly pull from one place known to be great on a topic and act as a proxy, citing the source.
- He thinks directories benefit more than blogs from this. If someone asks for dog parks in their town and the LLM cites a directory, there is "almost 100% chance" they click through to browse and filter. A blog link only loosely intersects the query, so people rarely click it.

chunks.heading: How to get referenced by LLMs (LLM SEO)
chunks.text:
John separates two cases.

- **LLM without web access (training data only):**
  - Every LLM has its own training set. OpenAI used a lot of Reddit and has a deal with Reddit that he describes as a "billion dollar deal".
  - He verified this on his own products. The ones the LLM knew about were the ones he had on Reddit, a "100% correlation".
- **LLM with web search (Grok on X, Perplexity, OpenAI):**
  - They run a regular search, often Bing because of the Microsoft deal. They take the top 10-20 results, crawl them, put the content in context and answer.
  - Grok does the same with tweets.
- **His checklist for all LLMs:**
  - Be on Reddit.
  - Rank on Bing.
  - Rank on Google.
  - Be present on social media, e.g. a tweet answering "what are the best dog parks" that links to you or describes you.
- He says SEO now brings LLM visibility as a by-product, because LLMs only started using search about three months before this recording.
- Caveat: the LLM doesn't just take the top-ranked result and doesn't trust ranking blindly, since that would be easy to manipulate. The picking logic is live prompting that can change any day, so the basics (Reddit plus top rankings) are what hold up.
- He sees user-generated content as the signal LLMs trust most, because it is hard to manipulate.
- He has seen social impact on SEO directly. When a tweet for one of his directories goes viral, the site jumps in traffic the next day.

chunks.heading: Directories as a game for millions of people
chunks.text:
- John argues the main reason people join a product is to be entertained. He thinks most directory builders already have income elsewhere and want to do something on their own terms.
- Job of the tool or course: keep them in the process, one thing at a time, "not too complicated not too easy" so they neither feel overwhelmed nor postpone it.
- Some people will be entertained, some will actually build something, and nobody knows in advance which.
- He thinks the audience for directories may be bigger than for SaaS or agents, because convincing someone with a main job to build SaaS is much harder than convincing them to build a directory.
- Google Search Console impressions keep beginners moving. Impressions arrive long before clicks, so analytics alone shows nothing early on. He sees people with no earlier success get excited about their first Google traffic.
- Even about $300 a month is "amazing money" in many places, and it is enough to stay in the game and build more.

chunks.heading: Winning a niche and building something to be proud of
chunks.text:
- John asks whether you can become the best educator in a narrow sub-niche, directories. He says it's "100%" possible to be number one, because the existing competitors are the old generation and the market wants a new generation to own it.
- His own directory course and tools sell every day and bring income, but he says it is "nothing spectacular" and not something he would be proud of at 70.
- He says he knows how to turn it into something bigger, but it takes more work than he can spend right now.
- His goal is bigger than revenue: own the space worldwide and let millions of people run a small business of their own. He says that if that isn't the end goal, "then it's just like project to make some money but it's not that interesting".

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: John Rush explains how he left VC-backed startups to run solo with AI agents. He prototypes ideas in Lovable and tests them with users, uses specialized agents for real work, and runs SEO content at volume, then improves only the winners. He also shares views on directories, SEO vs AIO, and agents as autopilot.

chunks.heading: Running a near-zero-employee company with AI agents
chunks.text:
- John ran VC-backed startups with large teams for about 10 years, got tired of working with people, and went solo once AI tools arrived.
- He handed his VC-backed startup to a CTO and a CEO he hired, then left and started building small workflows, then agents, to automate the repetitive work he used to do himself: accounting, paperwork, design, coding, marketing, sales.
- His goal is to be the first to automate the whole organization so it runs on just him and AI. He says he is "about 80% on the way", with 20% left.
- He did his own tax paperwork and accounting with AI this year. Professionals checked it afterward and found no mistakes.
- He treats the agent's job as removing work from the user. His target user is the busy founder who doesn't want to become more productive, but wants to "do nothing and the whole thing happens."
- He argues most agents still look like old SaaS tools that help teams be productive. He wants agents that run on autopilot, with the user acting like a boss who gives feedback and doesn't do the work.

chunks.heading: Validating ideas with AI prototypes (Lovable instead of Figma)
chunks.text:
- When he has an idea, the first thing he does is open Lovable and pitch it. He uses Lovable instead of Figma and says this is a habit now.
- He spends the day talking to Lovable about the idea and treats it like a human employee. He explains why the idea matters, who the users are and why he wants to build it. He says this gets more creative UX back.
- He builds around 10 different prototypes in one day, with different ideas, designs and UX. His example was an inbox bot that unifies email and LinkedIn messages and drafts replies.
- Testing process:
  1. Find friends willing to give an hour.
  2. Send them the 10 links and get on a call with screen share.
  3. Tell them "Try that. Don't talk to me. Just try them all." Ask no questions.
  4. Watch which prototype they understand best. That gives one winner, which he builds into a real product.
- His iteration cycle with Lovable is about 3 minutes, versus about 3 days with a designer for the same cycle.
- He says he can test ideas "literally in hours" and gets through roughly 20 ideas a week, though most don't work out.
- He says adding politeness and emotion to prompts tends to give better output. He cited research showing "please" gave about 7% more accurate answers.
- Selling at least 10 licenses is his signal that an idea works. Only then does he find a co-maker to build it further.

chunks.heading: Picking AI coding and building tools
chunks.text:
- He has compared about 40 AI coding tools, trying each as it appeared.
- His rough map:
  - Prototypes and front end (replacing Figma): V0 and Lovable.
  - Full-stack apps: Replit, which he calls probably the most powerful. He runs things built with it in production.
  - Heavy business logic: Cursor and Windsurf. They are great for logic but need coding knowledge.
  - Bolt: the middle option, good at front end, real apps, vibe coders and coders alike.
- His favorite is Lovable. UX is usually the most time-consuming part of a product and often decides whether it wins.
- He prefers specialized agents over general ones. People have fixed the corner cases in specialized tools. Unattended general agents like Manus or Genspark "do some stupid mistakes pretty often."
- His workflow is to start with a general agent to get data in and prototype. For real work and full data, he moves to a specialized agent.
- Unicorn Platform is his website and directory builder. It only builds what is in its template gallery (like a waitlist or an Airbnb-style site). If your idea is in the gallery, results beat Lovable because experts made and secured the template.
- For automation workflows he uses Zapier and n8n out of habit. He thinks Lindy is better for non-coders, but he prefers writing code for agents because it lets him make them smarter.

chunks.heading: Coding with co-makers and a studio-style process
chunks.text:
- He runs about 20 projects. He builds the MVP himself, and most die because nobody wants them.
- Once an idea gets attention and sells at least 10 licenses, he finds a "co-maker". This is someone strong with AI coding tools who also codes for real.
- The setup is just him plus one coder per project. He does everything that isn't coding.
- He says he is the human who improves the output later. Early on, cost matters more than quality, and a human can be brought in once something works.
- He suggests corporations should run an internal "AI factory". Pick the most creative person, let them crank out about 20 ideas a week, expect one good one a month, then turn it into a business unit.

chunks.heading: SEO Bot and the "fund 100, double down on 3" content method
chunks.text:
- He built SEO Bot (seobotai.com) as a true agent. You give it a URL, it researches the site, finds low-hanging keywords, checks Google search traffic, and proposes about 10 headlines with estimated clicks (for example 1k clicks for one article, 2k for another).
- After the user clicks proceed, it builds articles, sends them to the website and keeps doing so every day until turned off. The user only watches it work.
- His quality method works like a VC fund:
  1. The agent generates about 100 articles a month for one product. This is the "seed funding."
  2. On the last day of the month he checks analytics for the 3 best-performing articles.
  3. He spends an hour improving those 3 articles. This is the "series A and B."
- He argues that people who say AI content is low quality are right that AI is not as good as humans today. But in a first run quantity matters more than quality, and humans can add quality later.
- He expects quality to improve as new models arrive, for example "20% better and cheaper."
- On Unicorn Platform he lets people hire agents inside the platform. One example is an agent that pitches a site's potential sponsors and lands a sponsorship deal. He thinks agents and humans will compete for work.

chunks.heading: Directories, SEO and optimizing for LLMs
chunks.text:
- He believes directories have a big future. LLMs answer well only if they have good data to pull from (their RAG and context), and a directory is months or years of curated work, not an evening of work like a blog post.
- He expects the race between LLMs to become a race for data, and says whoever supplies the best data "can charge for it" and monetize it.
- Evidence: he asked Grok for indie makers, it linked to Indie Maker List, which is his own directory, and he clicked through. He expects people to still visit directories after LLMs surface them, to browse directly.
- On optimizing for LLMs, he thinks the game is very similar to SEO. He rarely sees an LLM answer with a link that isn't on top of Google or Bing.
- His playbook is the same: good content, a link that answers the query, people sharing it, and backlinks. He thinks hacks might work briefly but "the best data will win" long term.
- He tested social signals. A new site with zero backlinks except one viral tweet got a lot of Google traffic the next day. He concluded Google counts backlinks from social media and popular profiles.
- He notes that Reddit, LinkedIn and X are being flooded with fake comments, and nobody knows what to do. He thinks X is best placed to fight this because it has its own data on who replies, follower counts and verification.

chunks.heading: Views on AI progress, kids and the future
chunks.text:
- His most controversial belief is that we will not get to AGI using LLMs. He says LLM progress has gone nearly flat or linear since GPT-4 in 2023, and that the jump from GPT-3.5 to 4 was bigger than anything after.
- As an API user in his own tools, he hasn't seen a crazy change since GPT-4. He thinks the felt progress comes from the software and agents built on top.
- For kids, he thinks what they learn matters less than training their "brain muscle." He calls coding the best way, "almost like lifting weights," and addictive without the downside of video games.
- He promotes having kids to founders. He says AI frees up the time, and he lets his kids prompt Lovable and give random ideas that make his work more creative.
- His 2050 view is that robots and AI make everything very cheap and eventually free. Humans then invent games, and online games win over offline ones.
- He shares what he does daily on X, LinkedIn and Substack. Each month he posts his plans, and on the last day he posts what he got done.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: John Rush explains his bootstrapped studio model: he builds the first MVP, pairs with a 50/50 co-maker, and holds every product forever as part of a cross-promoting ecosystem. SEO Bot reached about $120K MRR with two people. He also covers his growth split, pricing ladder and SEO backlink advice.

chunks.heading: John's agent portfolio: revenue, team model and equity splits
chunks.text:
- John says he is at around $3.5M ARR across his AI agents. He launched the first one a bit more than a year before this interview (Nov 2025). Before that he spent time "in the trenches just experimenting and building stuff."
- A few products carry most of the revenue: SEO Bot, Listing Bot, Unicorn Platform and a few others. The rest are free or just starting out.
- SEO Bot: almost $120K MRR, "been doubling month over month after the launch." It had about 6 months of closed beta with people he knew, then a public launch about 12-14 months before the interview. Plans are $19, $49, $199 and $499 a month, with about 4-5K customers. At the time of the Stripe screenshare the product had been at roughly $100K in a month.
- Team model: every product is a team of two. John comes up with the idea, builds the first MVP, runs the pre-sale, and designs the UX. Then he finds a co-maker, usually on Twitter or in his network, to build it with him. The co-maker builds and John promotes, and they help each other.
- SEO Bot is split 50/50 with his co-founder Vitalic (CTO, with John as CEO).
- Listing Bot is built by John alone. A co-founder handles moderation (watching the AI, fixing mistakes, catching hallucinations) on a 90/10 split in John's favor.
- He holds products forever and does not sell. His reasoning: each product is part of an ecosystem that drives people to his other tools, even if it earns nothing.

chunks.heading: Growth channel mix and the user-chat flywheel
chunks.text:
- John's SEO Bot growth breaks down as roughly 30% SEO, 30% cross-promotion, 30% social media (building in public, users sharing) and 10% everything else.
- Dogfooding: he uses SEO Bot on all his other products, shares the results, and that helps both the product he shows and the tool he used. Example: he launched lmodels.org from zero and grew its clicks with his own tools. Because he keeps launching new products from zero, he can show fresh results each time.
- Cross-promo works because all his tools target the same audience. A customer of one product ends up using the others.
- He says he has never asked users to post screenshots or tag him, and thinks asking would "maybe 10x my revenue over a few months."
- Customer loyalty comes from listening. He says he has almost 1,000 chats going on with users, "I don't think anyone on earth has more chats than me." He comes back with fixes and improvements, and users become ambassadors.
- He builds for builders first because they give good feedback and effectively join the product team. Once they love it he raises the price and moves toward teams and companies.
- He treats directories as marketing channels. He owns 25-35 directories, most make no revenue, but they drive traffic to his other tools.

chunks.heading: Listing Bot: one-time pricing as a deliberate start
chunks.text:
- The tool does two things: deep research to find every web directory relevant to a product (ranked by relevance and domain rating), and web automation that registers and fills out the forms to list the product.
- Directory database: about 20K directories now, with at least 500 new ones added each month. He estimates about 100,000 directories exist, including niche ones for e-commerce stores, mobile apps and pet shops. The goal is to find them all.
- Revenue: over $50K a month, one-time payments, "basically thousand people buying it every month." There is no recurring revenue, so it needs new buyers every month.
- He ignored advice that he must have recurring plans. It began as an experiment with a Stripe payment link, so users pay before seeing the next step. He calls this a "really high bar" that few people pass, and it still brings in a lot of users.
- Version two, coming soon, lowers the bar: $50 a month for 20 directories listed each month.
- His strategy is "just like Tesla started with Roadster": start expensive with a really good service (AI plus human review of everything), then reduce human labor, go fully autonomous, drop the price, and let users moderate themselves.

chunks.heading: Capping products at about $100K MRR and fixing support first
chunks.text:
- John's pattern: grow a product to $50K MRR, pause and move to other tools, come back and reach $100K, then pause again.
- He deliberately avoids going much past $100K because it would force him to move upmarket to enterprise clients who want demo calls and his time. He wants products fully async. He returns only once he can automate the bottleneck.
- SEO Bot's bottleneck is support: "almost 80% of our time go for support." Customers connect their CMS and "everything just falls apart all the time." Nothing new gets built or marketed.
- His fix is a support agent that acts rather than just answers: it tries to fix the problem, gets into the database and changes things.
- SEO Bot sells credits that customers load and spend on articles. Revenue comes through two Stripe channels: self-serve and enterprise invoices.
- Revenue per employee: with two people on SEO Bot, the host computed roughly $720K a year per employee.

chunks.heading: Tiny Ads: building an ad network because paid growth never worked
chunks.text:
- John says he had only done organic growth. Every time he tried paid on Google or Facebook, it never worked, so he built his own B2B ad network for small B2B startups so he could spend on growth.
- Result: it launched April 15 and reached $5K MRR and $10K revenue in 35 days, with almost 1,000 publishers joining to serve ads.
- He ignored people who said an ad network is "a dream for big guys." He compares it to 2022, when people said developers would never leave VS Code for an AI coding tool.
- His view on the model: Google's ad game runs on VC money, where spending $10 to get $5 back is fine. He asked why not build a system where you pay $1 and get two back and the other side makes money too: "you serve the ads you get paid. The other side just pays for the traffic."

chunks.heading: Why John bootstrapped and built Mars X first
chunks.text:
- Background: studied computer science, AI and UX, then spent 10 years in VC-backed companies. He started seven as CTO with co-founders in Norway, then went to San Francisco (500 Startups, Altimus).
- Why he left: he felt his whole game was to serve investors and chase exits, when he wanted to serve users and chase a legacy, a generational company that lasts beyond him. As a bootstrapper he doesn't optimize for an exit or next round. He owns it all, funds himself from profits, and uses profits to build the next product.
- Vision from 2020: an ecosystem of 100 tools run with almost no people. His first step was an AI coding tool, Mars X (marsx.dev), because building 100 products otherwise requires thousands of people.
- He spent 2-3 years building it alone on weekends and evenings while running a VC-backed startup, had a working version in 2022, then used it to build all his later products.
- End goal: every tool a busy bootstrap founder needs across building, operating, growing and monetizing.

chunks.heading: SEO advice: page-level backlinks, internal links and AI search
chunks.text:
- Context: the host's site has about 35,000 programmatic "[company] revenue" pages. They rank well but clicks fell about 50% as AI results raised impressions. John says AI made it easier to enter the SEO game, so far more people are competing and traffic is harder to win.
- LLM search: almost all LLMs now use live internet search (mostly Bing), so ranking on page one of Bing means showing up in most of them. They no longer need to be in a training set. John's long-term bet is that all LLMs will search the web in a similar way, so focusing on topping Google solves the other problems too: "the SEO game is also LLM game at the same time."
- Page rating beats domain rating: a site with a poor domain rating can have a high rating on a specific page, and Google looks at the page's URL rating first. Ahrefs data for a URL is often incomplete, so don't trust a zero.
- Backlink tactic: pick a query where a competitor outranks you, then build backlinks to that exact URL using the exact anchor text of the search query. John says he has done this several times and eventually took the number one spot. He calls it "the most typical serious work you can do on SEO": go page by page and beat competitors with backlinks to that exact page.
- For programmatic SEO at scale, he suggests owning a network of websites and automating the backlink part.
- Internal links: "go crazy with links." More internal links is better than fewer. Create blog posts that link back to the company profile pages, and link any mention of a company name (like Zapier) to its revenue page, giving hundreds of internal links. He noted dynamic pages may not be seen by Google.
- Ranking logic: good content gets you onto page one. To reach the top you need precise anchor links to the URL, both internal and external.
- Citations from AI tools may be nofollow links and won't necessarily send traffic.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: John Rush argues indie hackers should go deep on one project instead of launching many MVPs, and learn every founder skill over time. He covers lessons from buying an $800k product (Unicorn Platform), pricing so customers actually need the product, SEO as both traffic and copy, and not quitting your job.

chunks.heading: Depth over breadth: learn every founder skill on one project
chunks.text:
- John says the common indie hacker belief that launching many MVPs will eventually produce a winner is wrong. A founder who builds MVPs for 20 years only learns to build MVPs.
- He argues founders must learn all the skills: building, SEO, cold sales, UX, design, copywriting, marketing, distribution. With every skill, the odds of success go from about 2% to 20%, then 50%, eventually close to 100%.
- Experienced founders like himself, Peter Levels and Marc Lou rarely launch projects that fail, because they have learned the skills.
- Tactic: try at most three projects, pick the one you like most, and go deep for years. Once the product is built there is no more code to write, so you are forced to do marketing, content, SEO and sales.
- If you do launch several projects, push a different skill in each one (development, design, SEO).
- His own path: one cinema software company for 10 years, then one project (Unicorn Platform) for almost 2 years with no other launches, then more projects. He did not build 24 projects at once. "Never build second project unless your first project is successful."
- Imitate the process, not the outcome. He stopped posting MRR about a year ago because it makes beginners feel they are missing out and copy the wrong thing.

chunks.heading: When to quit a project and how to read early signals
chunks.text:
- John says quitting too early means success depends on luck.
- Give a project a few months and watch the signals. If after 3 months you have shared it widely and nobody signed up even once, the idea is bad or you can't present it well. Either way, drop it.
- Most makers build something that already exists and makes money, so the idea is already validated. The real test is whether you can promote and communicate it.
- If you get some signals, keep hammering: change the wording, narrow the features, pivot the positioning slightly.
- Example: an analytics tool becomes "analytics for e-commerce store owners". Same technology, different positioning, and it starts spreading in that community.
- Waitlists and MVPs are good at the start to test whether you can promote the project. After you reach the market, focus on making the product really good instead of building another one.

chunks.heading: Build what the business needs, not what you like
chunks.text:
- John's tweet: the best way to fail as an indie hacker is to keep doing things you like. Successful people say they love what they do, but not that every daily task is their favorite.
- Stages he describes:
  1. Talk to customers first. You can't predict what people want, "if you could predict what other people want, you could predict stock market."
  2. Then build an MVP and put it in their hands, because people can't imagine a product from a description.
  3. Expect them to hate the first version. Send new versions "ideally tomorrow", then the day after, every day, until they get happier.
- Founders who "worked hard for a year and it didn't work" usually worked on the wrong small tasks (a favorite SDK, a new Tailwind kit), not the wrong project.
- Customers don't buy features, they buy solutions to problems: saving time or money. Features are the vehicle.
- Distribution vs product: he used to think distribution mattered more. He now says it's false. "If my product is not doing well, it's because the product is bad, not because the marketing is bad." People who say they have an amazing product but are bad at marketing have a product that isn't amazing.

chunks.heading: Pricing: a $49 price tag filters for real need
chunks.text:
- John says if customers pay $49 a month, they actually need the product and their business benefits from it.
- At lower prices ($9, $19), people buy products they don't need. If people won't pay $49, it's not because it's too expensive, it's because they don't need it. Making it cheaper just gets you customers who still don't need it.
- Customers who don't need the product don't share it, don't become ambassadors and give poor feedback.
- Indie hackers rarely pay more than about $20 a month, which is too little for a sustainable business, so you need many users. He says people need to pay at least $50 for the product to be sustainable.
- Real businesses with a real use case pay for expensive software, don't tweet about it, and simply use it to solve a pain. Those customers are outside the indie hacker community.
- Product Hunt and indie hacker testimonials: friends and fans are testers, not users, even when they pay. A good project has users from outside the indie hacker community.

chunks.heading: Lessons from buying a product for $800k (Unicorn Platform)
chunks.text:
- Goal: enter the bootstrap world fast by buying an existing popular project instead of building from scratch. He followed Laravel projects for a year, picked a small one with good press, DMed the founder and agreed the sale on Telegram.
- Problem 1, churn: indie hacker users are attached to the founder, not the product. When ownership changed, churn hit 15% a month, which means losing all users in about 6-7 months. There was no SEO traffic and word of mouth was too weak.
- Problem 2, stability: the product had constant downtime that nobody had reported because the previous buyers had no real users. When he brought in real users with real websites, they left. At one point he brought 10 users in and 10 left the next day.
- His conclusion: it was his own failed due diligence, not the seller's fault. Most users of an indie product are friends and fans who never complain and don't run serious businesses.
- Fix: it took more than 2 years to stabilize the product and build organic channels outside the indie community. It now has 250,000 users (100,000 when he decided it was good enough to launch other projects), low churn and stable revenue.
- He plans to compete head-to-head with Webflow and Framer next year.
- Exits: he doesn't congratulate people on exits. About 90% of projects die after being sold, usually to inexperienced buyers who can't maintain them. Indie hackers selling to each other creates no outside economy, so he now calls himself a startup founder instead of an indie hacker.
- Audience: posting "zero to 30k MRR in 3 months" content attracts people who want fast money and cancel after 3 months. He now aims content at founders playing a long game.

chunks.heading: SEO: traffic plus better copy, and how to start
chunks.text:
- John says SEO matters for two reasons: traffic, and the fact that writing for search intent makes your page text match how people describe the problem, so the copy converts better.
- In some of his products over 50% of traffic comes from SEO, in others about 10%. High-intent search traffic can convert very well. He started SEO only the year before and regrets not doing it earlier.
- SEO is a lot of simple, repetitive daily work: content, keyword optimization, backlinks (to the site and subpages), internal linking, technical readiness. He compares it to going to the gym and says it's boring for developers, which is why he built SEO Bot AI to automate it.
- Recommended method: AI plus human. Use a tool as the draft maker and act as chief editor. He produces content with SEO Bot, then manually improves the pieces that get views.
- How to start: connect any AI blog generator (there are hundreds), generate 10, 20, 50 or 100 articles, let it run for a month or two and check Search Console. He says 10 AI articles won't get you punished by Google, and seeing traffic is addictive, so you'll want to do more.
- Long term: SEO is zero-sum, so if everyone uses AI content you need manual work on top.

chunks.heading: Hiring, social media, and not quitting your job
chunks.text:
- People: he has employed hundreds over his life. After 3-5 years employees lose steam because it's a job to them, not their business. Someone who must care for a decade has to be a co-founder. His current goal is to automate more so he needs fewer people, who then do better work on less volume.
- Social media: he used to think it was a waste of time for businesses like his and only started using it about a year before. It opened doors to people, friends, partnerships and marketing. He says new founders should be social media native from day one.
- Content experiments: he tried drama recaps in a fast, funny stand-up style on X and got millions of views. He studies stand-up comedians and meme makers to find new formats, since copied formats lose attention. He follows Hormozi's content daily.
- Tools: a chat AI (ChatGPT, now Grok for real-time data) as a co-founder, and Discord for chats, project management, support and community, because a chat feed keeps all context in one place.
- Advice not to follow: don't quit your job. No one replaces a salary with indie income in 3 months, and zero to revenue in 3 months is only possible for people who have done it for years. Keep your job and build on evenings and weekends. If you can't get mild traction in two days a week, five days won't help, and less time makes you focus on the right things.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: John Rush explains his bootstrapped playbook: build an audience in public, sell before building, ship a tiny MVP with no-code tools, and split 50/50 with a technical co-maker. He also covers directories, AI agents, automating toward one-button tools, and staying productive by skipping unimportant work.

chunks.heading: How John builds startups: validate by hand, then split 50/50 with a co-maker
chunks.text:
- John built 26+ products in about three years, serving almost a million users. Unicorn Platform has 600,000 users; the other products combined have about 400,000.
- He spent 10 years building VC-backed startups and concluded he doesn't like it. In 2022 he switched to self-funded, bootstrapped startups: "I want to please the user not the investors."
- His process:
  1. Find an idea from his own work or frustration.
  2. Share it on social media and see whether people resonate.
  3. Build a very simple MVP himself with no-code or vibe-coding tools. Sometimes he builds nothing and does the job by hand: "I'm the tool."
  4. Sell it to about 10 people to check they will pay.
  5. Deliver the service and watch whether they like it, want to keep paying and bring friends.
  6. If so, find a builder (usually on Twitter or in his friend circle) and offer a 50/50 split as co-maker. John does product and distribution; the co-maker does coding and support.
- Most products are John plus one person. They hire no one until at least 50k MRR.
- Neither John nor the co-maker takes a salary. They split revenue or profit, and the only real cost is AI usage, which appears once there are users and revenue.
- He says he has no system for idea generation: ideas come randomly out of his own frustration, he fixes the problem for himself, and he launches when he's happy with it.
- Running many products removes risk. If OpenAI ships something that kills two of his startups, he doesn't mind because the others survive. He says he reached financial freedom "a long time ago" because costs are low.
- He sees more founders heading toward owning many small and mid-sized tools.
- Without VCs or employees, he says he can follow his intuition: "my best ideas and best products. I couldn't explain them at the start."

chunks.heading: Building in public: why it works and which platform to start on
chunks.text:
- Building in public means sharing everything (good, bad, the process) before you even have an idea. John compares it to a reality show.
- It became popular 2-3 years ago because customer acquisition costs got so high that attention is expensive to buy with ads. Social media is where the attention is.
- By launch you already have an audience waiting. Followers are loyal and forgiving because they watched you build, and the marketing is a byproduct of sharing the process, with no extra campaign needed.
- He started in 2023 with SEO Bot, which grew popular, then repeated the model for every later product. His latest, Tiny Ads (a small ad network), crossed $10k in revenue in 50 days, also built in public.
- He argues introverts do better. Extroverts come across as salespeople who oversell, while an authentic, clunky, shy builder inspires other builders. "People don't want to see perfect stuff anymore."
- Start on X, not Reddit or YouTube. Anonymous commenters there are harsh, and the build-in-public community on X is supportive because everyone is in the same boat. Go to Reddit and YouTube only when you're big. For the same content he gets very few bad comments on X.
- LinkedIn has copied X's algorithm, so it is now interesting and rewards entertaining content. Two years ago he had to repurpose content for LinkedIn; now the same post works on both.
- Rule: focus on one platform until about 4-5k followers, then expand to all platforms. He set 4k because the smallest profile among the 20 most popular people in his niche had 4k followers at the time. He thinks it's around 10k now.
- Why one platform first: growth needs engagement as well as content. Post, reply to your own replies, then reply under other people's posts. "You have to create this social currency where you give first and then you get back."
- He has answered every DM and reply he has received, about 50,000 answers, and says he will keep doing it.

chunks.heading: Directories as a first product, and his AI growth stack
chunks.text:
- He recommends starting with a simple product like a directory before anything ambitious: "Don't start to building Apple right away." Small steps give frequent small wins, and he says people enjoy the process more than the outcome.
- He has built at least 35 directories. They take roughly one evening to launch, then improve over time with more items and information.
- Build a directory on a topic you know better than anyone, such as motorcycles. Group items, add filters, and make them easy to search so a less expert person can find what they need. Niche content spreads quickly within its niche.
- His own AI-tools directory works because he tries AI tools daily and can rank them well among many similar tools.
- A directory also builds an audience, because it shows you understand the topic and gives people visible results rather than claims.
- His stack for directories and growth:
  - **Build:** Unicorn Platform (AI website builder). Framer and Webflow also have AI now. You can skip hiring designers and do the MVP yourself.
  - **Distribution:** Listing Bot, a web agent that finds forums and directories where a product fits, registers and submits the product. Web agents control a browser (forms, bookings, purchases) and are slower than a human but good for repetitive work.
  - **Content:** SEO Bot generates blog articles on autopilot from a URL and sends them to the CMS. Cheaper alternative: ask ChatGPT or Grok for articles and paste them into the CMS yourself.
  - **Data:** an AI scraper visits a list of URLs, pulls pricing, features, pros and cons, and outputs a CSV for the CMS. Previously he hired people on Upwork, who often did good work on the first items and sloppy work after.
  - **Monetization:** Tiny Ads finds sponsors and advertisers for a directory, reaches out to them (emails, social accounts), lets them place ads, and the owner collects the money. Manual sponsor outreach is a lot of work.
- His refund workflow in Zapier: every support email goes to an LLM that detects refund requests, checks the database for a real user by email, and refunds automatically if they are in the first 30 days, no questions asked. Complicated cases are forwarded to him with the details.
- Make, n8n and Zapier all have AI that builds the workflow from a plain description, so he says you don't need a course.

chunks.heading: One-button products and automating the work
chunks.text:
- Every product he builds aims at "one button" or none: SEO Bot has no real interface, you turn it on and it does everything. He says he is "super lazy" and is the user of his own tools.
- His obsession with automation comes from watching his entrepreneur parents work extremely hard. His goal is to make sure business owners don't have to.
- He estimates 75-80% of his work is automated now, targeting 90% by the end of this year and 95% by the end of next year. The remaining job would be the creative part: coming up with ideas and directing AI agents as if they were tireless employees.
- His pattern: build with AI, drive traffic with AI, monetize with AI. All 26 products use AI to some degree; some, like Listing Bot and SEO Bot, are heavily AI.
- He runs no calls, only chats.

chunks.heading: Productivity: no system, a pitch-first focus
chunks.text:
- He uses no project management software, documents or plans. His rule: use memory to prioritize. If he remembers a task the next day, it deserves work. If he forgets it, people didn't complain enough or it wasn't important.
- His only tool is Discord, with one channel per product where he and the co-maker talk. It keeps a scrollable history.
- He doesn't do calls (a "15-minute" call becomes an hour) and replies to emails with short messages. He says nobody has ever called him rude for it.
- Don't spend effort on things that don't matter yet:
  - Logo from ChatGPT or a stock library.
  - First landing page from a template in about five minutes, while he knows people who spend weeks. A new website is invisible, and anyone you send it to has already bought the idea.
- Put about 90% of early effort into the pitch, because most pitches fail and nobody ever sees the product. Practice the pitch heavily.
- Principle: "Put 1% effort, get something out, don't care. Be embarrassed. It's fine." Then focus on whatever matters at the current stage, which changes at each stage.
- He doesn't chase billion-dollar outcomes, so he can relax some days and let growth be slower. He launches products, then works long hours when traction hits (Tiny Ads brought bugs, support tickets and features) to keep momentum.

chunks.heading: Validating an idea: audience first, product last
chunks.text:
John's reverse-order steps, from his answer on coaching someone with an idea such as a voice agent for children:

1. Start with the audience. Check whether you can build one for the idea, since that is harder than building the product. "Try something that's hard first."
2. Try to sell before you build. You'll learn you need more skills, and may need to test 100 versions of your pitch.
3. Talk about the topic on social media. If the content gets no attention, nobody cares about the problem or your pitch is bad. Even with few followers you can test on Reddit by finding the relevant subreddit, sharing the idea, and changing the pitch until people upvote and ask questions.
4. Expect this to take years, not weeks.
5. Talk to the people who respond until you know exactly what to build.
6. Then build a very simple MVP yourself with no-code or vibe-coding tools, even if the final product is complex and will need real developers later.
7. Bring it back to your audience and iterate for about a year based on feedback.

- After traction exists, anything is open: keep building solo, hire, raise money or find a co-founder. "As long as you have traction everything will be open all doors will be open."

chunks.heading: Skills, luck and keeping up with AI news
chunks.text:
- Skills: build one superpower you know better than others (design, coding, business), be a lightweight generalist elsewhere, and find the intersection of that skill and technology. His own was coding, then business knowledge from many failed products (most of his first 15 years failed, which showed him typical founder problems). He suggests that fields like biology, chemistry or agriculture combined with tech may beat crowded computer science.
- If you think you're not great at anything, he says you haven't tried enough things.
- Luck: he has seen lucky people make a lot of money and end up depressed, doubting they deserved it. He prefers earned results, which give self-respect. Throwing many darts and staying in the arena produces results that are only partly luck.
- His AI news posts, in three steps:
  1. Remember the week's events and list them from memory.
  2. Give the list to his tool Social Boat to research details and exact numbers (for example, the price of Windsurf's sale to OpenAI).
  3. Rewrite it himself so it is interesting. AI makes things boring, and AI-written irony overshoots, so he adds the strange, funny, sarcastic tone himself.
- Sourcing without doomscrolling: every few hours he opens X's Explore tab to see what is hot and leaves without entering threads or the feed. Daily on Reddit he uses the "best today" filter.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: John Rush explains his 10/90 approach (10% of action gives 90% of outcome), why AI agents beat copilots, and why he keeps agents to a single "turn on" button. He also covers how adoption needs viral show-don't-tell demos, why most launches die, and why founders should solve problems they see around them.

chunks.heading: Do everything quick and not perfect: the 10/90 rule
chunks.text:
- John has been building since 2009. He says it got easy after about 10 years.
- His key skill is finding the "10 to 90" split: 10% of the action gives 90% of the outcome.
- He applies it to every task, even writing an email: "I do everything quick and not perfect."
- The compound effect is that he ships in days, not weeks or months.
- He found that this is easy to say and hard to do on every task. So he turned the habit into specialized AI tools, one per task, that other people can plug into their own process.

chunks.heading: Agents beat copilots
chunks.text:
- John says most people use AI as a copilot. He thinks that is a good use but won't make a founder "crazy 100x". Used as an agent, it "works when you sleep".
- Copilots are like any other tool: users have to learn how to use them. AI raises expectations, so one mistake and people think "I do it myself next time". John says most copilots are abandoned quickly.
- An agent is a black box. You give it a task, it does everything without interference, and it asks you only when it lacks data or answers. You wake up and the work is done, which keeps impressing people so they use it more.
- He compares a good agent to a good employee or an obedient child.
- A year earlier he predicted agents for everything within six months. Twelve months later he says the only agents on the market are, probably, ones he built. His agents are viral and people pay for them.

chunks.heading: Keep an agent to one button
chunks.text:
- John says the hardest part of building an agent is resisting the urge to add buttons, form inputs and interfaces.
- The only button an agent needs is "turn on".
- He says other agent builders started well, then added many buttons and drifted back to a regular UI. He has kept his agents to one button so far.
- Users will scream for buttons because they have never used a tool that works on autopilot. John says "never listen to the users" on this. His intuition is that once they see the value over days, weeks and months, they stop asking.

chunks.heading: Why people don't adopt AI, and how to fix it with demos
chunks.text:
- John says people talk about AI far more than they use it, roughly 99 to 1. They repost, ask and sign up, but don't use it, because changing habits is much harder than people think, even for a 100x productivity boost.
- On Unicorn Platform (AI website builder), most users did not use the AI much at first.
- Usage jumped after he built something that went viral and recorded how he did it, including entering the prompt and the AI producing the whole page. People who had seen AI before then started using it.
- His conclusion: people who have tried AI keep using it, while people who never tried hesitate until they see something viral that shows exactly how to use it. "Show, don't tell."
- He says real AI adoption is still far off.

chunks.heading: Mars X: reuse micro-apps, use AI to connect and modify them
chunks.text:
- Mars X is a dev platform where you build from micro-apps. You never reinvent existing pieces; you only invent the new part or connect pieces in a new way. He says this saves about 99% of the time.
- Most things already exist, but people rebuild them because they can't discover them.
- Inside Mars X, AI is used for discovery, for modifying pre-built micro-apps (his analogy: you need a 30-inch wheel, not the existing 20-inch one) and for connecting them.
- His pitch is "code plus no code plus AI".

chunks.heading: How John gets launches seen
chunks.text:
- He is very active on Twitter, so he can push something out and get an initial reaction fast.
- He also posts on other platforms where he has followers. He says his audience is smaller than most, but it reacts quickly, and good products then spread.
- He credits virality to a mix of this audience, the one-button agent design and demos.

chunks.heading: Expect nothing from launches, enjoy the process
chunks.text:
- John says most products he launches "will die and fade into oblivion". About 95% of the code he has written never saw the light of day, especially in his first years as a maker.
- He advises people to expect nothing from launches. His analogy is a parent: you hope your kids do well but aren't sad if they don't. He is happy during the process and very happy when something works, because his expectations are zero.
- Money as the reason to build is, in his view, "the best way to fail". He stays motivated by problems: seeing something that can be improved and isn't yet. He says he has to resist starting a new project every day.

chunks.heading: How to find what to build
chunks.text:
- Entrepreneurship in tech is about solving problems: see something inefficient, add code and AI, make it more efficient.
- He tells young people who ask for an idea to look around rather than invent from inside. Younger founders bring ideas "from totally inside" and he pushes back.
- Get bothered by real problems in daily life. He says he is bothered by about a hundred things a day, so if you aren't bothered by any, you aren't looking around.
- His closing advice: "Build stuff fast."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: John Rush explains how he left VC-backed startups for bootstrapping 24 products and grew on X from 72 followers. He covers niche-first strategy, never asking for feedback, turning his own problems into products, and buying back time with tools.

chunks.heading: Why John left VC-backed startups for bootstrapping
chunks.text:
- John spent about 20 years working with startups, starting at 15, mostly in the VC-backed scene: raising money, joining incubators, hiring many people, going to conferences, bragging about headcount, then raising again.
- He found that cycle boring and too far from actual users. He wanted love and feedback "directly from users", not from journalists.
- He discovered Build in Public and scrolled the feed for about 10 hours. He liked that people bragged about having few or no staff, because fewer people means better margins and easier running.
- He dislikes employing people because "you're taking some Freedom away". VC investors also expect layers and structure. That was a key reason he left.
- He builds one product every month or quarter and keeps adding. He ended up with 24 products and about $2M in yearly recurring revenue (the host's figures, which he did not dispute). One product, Unicorn Platform, had 130,000 users at the time.
- He says he has never had more passion than in the past two years, because users send real screenshots and kind words.
- His big goal is not revenue. He wants the bootstrapper/indie scene to go from well under 1% of the SaaS world to 10-20%.

chunks.heading: Growing on X from 72 followers
chunks.text:
- He never used Twitter before. He started because he wanted a direct, real-time channel to people, with quick feedback.
- Step 1: copy what accounts with big followings did. He used Twitter's filter to see their old posts, and found it easy to repeat. This got him to roughly 2,000 followers.
- Step 2: after that, "become yourself". Post things that are interesting about you, not just the content.
- Don't post what you don't want back. A joke or a Google-bashing post can go viral, but it attracts the wrong followers. People follow others who look like them.
- Decide who you want as followers (for him, founders who care about users) and post what they would also post.
- In B2B, don't worry about people outside the indie bubble. Indie makers run all kinds of businesses (a coffee shop, a cinema). "Build it and they will come" doesn't work; "build a good product and they will come" does, but others have to say it's good, and their outside networks bring more users.
- To protect against account loss (his X account was suspended for a week in May after a post with about 5M views), he is building a newsletter and a LinkedIn audience of about 10,000 people. He thinks LinkedIn people take things more seriously.

chunks.heading: How John gets feedback and builds with users
chunks.text:
- Building in public shortens the feedback cycle, and he believes shortening the cycle is the only way to build a great product. Indie makers are rough in DMs, which helps.
- Feedback from free users, friends, and people you ask is bad for you. Someone asked for feedback "becomes like a professor" and tries to sound smart. Good feedback comes from people far from your circle who volunteer it.
- He never asks for feedback. He creates a channel instead. Most of his products have no public sign-up page, so people DM him on Twitter for an invite. That opens a conversation, and almost everyone eventually gives feedback (maybe tomorrow, maybe in a year).
- He talks to about 100 people a day, and calls them his unofficial product team. His Twitter chats are mostly about what he is working on that day. He shares what he does rather than asking questions.
- Small decisions matter more than people think, because product quality is the quality of hundreds of daily decisions.
- Everything is in his head: no notes, no diagrams, no Notion-style tools.
- He moved his own YouTube habit out of the way because it was the real focus-killer, not the Twitter tab.

chunks.heading: Bugs, Sentry and launching early
chunks.text:
- He has used Sentry for 10 years and runs it on all his products. Sentry sends errors to a Discord channel where he chats with his developer, so errors appear in the middle of conversation and can't be ignored.
- When he forgets to set up the Discord webhook, the bugs get reported by users first, and he hates that.
- Fixing a bug before the user writes is a trust builder: "bugs are good if you kill them in front of the user". Replying "a fix is already on the way" makes him look ahead of everyone.
- He leaves small imperfections, such as spelling mistakes on landing pages. He doesn't create bugs on purpose, but he isn't afraid of them. Bugs bring people into your chat, show how you respond, and make them comfortable sending feedback and feature requests later.
- Launch early versions. If someone can try it, everyone should be able to. New people are born every day.

chunks.heading: Niche strategy and Unicorn Platform
chunks.text:
- Building for a large market is a lottery. Narrow as much as you can: one problem, one type of company (team or solo founder), age, and so on.
- No market is below about $1M a year, and in a niche you may win 50-100% of it. Wide markets have 1,000 competitors, many funded and buying ads, and even SEO is paid and hard.
- Grow out of the niche by adding features. For example, start with individuals, then add team, collaboration and permissions features. The first group are word-of-mouth ambassadors, and some get hired into large companies and bring the product along.
- Unicorn Platform was a niche product that eventually hit the ceiling of that niche and stopped growing. He then removed filters, widening to a bigger niche, and it started growing again. His image: with 20 filters you find one person on earth; removing one filter gives 20, and you keep eating the market from inside out.
- Nothing he builds is disconnected. The vision is a toolset for busy founders who are short on time. He bets this group will take over the SaaS world because they build personal "startup machines" that can move faster than teams.
- He does not plan to look for other niches. He bets this niche becomes the mainstream and he powers it.

chunks.heading: Product ideas from his own problems, and buying back time
chunks.text:
- He runs each new product internally for a long time before releasing it, because release brings support and uptime burden.
- If something takes him 10 hours a week or month, he swaps it for a tool. "My problem is my fuel." Without a problem, his ideas would be guesses.
- He tries to be the best example of his user, because no one is busier than him, so if he pleases himself he pleases everyone.
- Pay to buy time back. He mentions a friend with many followers who refused a $100/month tool and would do it by hand. He calculates the hours lost against $100.
- Developers do too much by hand because they love building. He has no time for that.
- He asks "how can I do this 100 times faster?" task by task. He says productivity and innovation go together, using the analogy that New York to London takes five hours because transport was invented, not because horses were beaten harder.
- At 25 he would stubbornly push a wrong approach. Now, with less energy, he asks a minute in whether he needs to do it at all. He thinks rich founders are not young, and says "you are 47 when you can make a million".
- He says he works about 6 hours at the desk plus about 4 hours of loose work (DMs, comments, thinking in the shower). He wakes around 10, spends time in the garden with kids, and stops to see friends.
- His advice: the long-term goals should give you joy, while short-term actions should be somewhat painful. "Don't do things that you like doing" in the small moment.
- He regrets many times hiring people for skills over character. He now only works with people he would be comfortable hugging, and says he failed "maybe 100 times, at least" by ignoring that.
- He A/B tests his Unicorn Platform landing page daily and records conversion, which is stable with high traffic. A recent test showed templates moved higher (not just examples of what others built) converted better.
- As a joke, he said he grew his button one pixel per day until conversion reversed.

chunks.heading: Where VC and startups are heading
chunks.text:
- VC will shift from pre-seed and seed to companies with traction and revenue. Successful bootstrappers will mostly end up raising, which then works as a liquidity event rather than a necessity: take cash out, and delegate more.
- He is not raising, yet says more VCs have contacted him than ever, saying they are bootstrapper-friendly, with no board seat or even a board.
- He doesn't need money because he doesn't spend on growth, and building is cheap.
- Startups used to be built around a product. Now the founder or the machine is the product. Products may become uninteresting within a year, so founders who can keep producing relevant products win. He compares this to Elon Musk building the Gigafactory, the factory rather than one car.
- He expects investors to back people (like a founder who can build anything) rather than one product.

chunks.heading: Product Hunt, Dev Hunt and an Indie Maker Village
chunks.text:
- He built Dev Hunt, and takes Product Hunt's direction seriously, as indie makers' success is his success. He believes Product Hunt should act like a community with real, taggable people who engage in complaints, not a black box that spits out winners.
- He argues indie makers are a small share of the population but drive a big share of activity: comments, good ratings, real feedback. Without them "the party may turn so boring" that nobody dances.
- On low-effort products (e.g. a Notion-page template made in an hour), he partly agrees with the CEO, but says the community should decide, not moderators. Moderators can be fooled with a pretty website.
- On Dev Hunt, voters must add social handles. They remove votes from fake accounts and fake handles, and the voting rules are public. His recommendation to Product Hunt: work much harder on the quality of votes, remove cheaters and fake accounts, and let the community decide.
- He thinks indie makers should be more open to cross-marketing, because otherwise they are "small kingdoms" a big enemy can destroy.
- He predicts a burnout epidemic among makers, because they sit at the same computer for work and leisure. His answer is a physical Indie Maker Village. He built a small version in Turkey years ago, with about 20 people.
- The plan has three stay types: up to five years' residency (many makers from developing countries want a passport path), 3-month incubation stays, and short hackathon weekends.
- Residents would do shared real work together (build a house, plant vegetables). Villagers do one activity together, so people copy each other's doing, rather than learning theory.
- He plans to presell days (one day costs X, refundable, usable later) to gauge interest and says he already has a list of hundreds of people who would come. He aims to build many such places around the world.
- Success would be measured by combined MRR and website traffic of residents, like Mark Lou's leaderboard.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A conversation prompted by Stripe acquiring LemonSqueezy. John Rush argues indie makers can build wrappers on top of big platforms, win with niche boilerplates, and beat VC-backed teams by launching early and talking to users. He also covers why good products always find users and why Europe suits bootstrappers.

chunks.heading: Why the Stripe acquisition of LemonSqueezy is mostly good for indie makers
chunks.text:
- John sees three upsides:
  - Indie makers can now sell to famous companies. Micro-acquisition platform deals are "usually below 1 million" and rare. He guesses this deal is worth "maybe 100 maybe 50 maybe 200" (million), a guess, since the price isn't public. He thinks it will inspire people to bootstrap in order to sell later.
  - Building in public on Twitter makes makers visible to VC-backed startups, investors and corporations, not just fellow makers. He expects acquisitions like this to become normal.
  - Makers who join a corporation keep their indie connections and become a bridge into that world. He cites KP joining Paddle.
- The main downside is cultural. Many bootstrappers privately would raise VC money or sell if the offer were good, but don't say so because it "makes us look cheap".
- Selling a payments company is easy to defend. It is "nearly impossible to bootstrap a bank or a payment provider".
- He expects the bubble to be "happy and proud", like a friend getting accepted "into the cool league".

chunks.heading: Why Stripe bought LemonSqueezy and what happens next
chunks.text:
- John thinks Stripe bought the team, not the audience. Stripe's pitch was about merchant of record, and the internet had been asking Stripe to handle tax, which Stripe didn't know how to solve.
- He guesses LemonSqueezy people will build merchant-of-record and tax handling inside Stripe, and the LemonSqueezy brand may disappear.
- He also thinks Stripe wants to stop merchant-of-record products like Paddle and LemonSqueezy from owning the customer relationship. Most LemonSqueezy users don't know Stripe powers it, so LemonSqueezy could swap Stripe out at any point.
- He says "at least 90% of all acquisitions kill the whole underlying product they bought", so he is pessimistic about LemonSqueezy's survival.
- A possible exception: Stripe may keep LemonSqueezy as a separate entity with extra KYC, so it can keep serving countries Stripe can't, such as India.
- Taxes are the biggest unanswered question for indie makers. He says most "simply ignore the taxes and hope for the best".
- With Stripe, Paddle and LemonSqueezy all big or VC-backed, he sees room for a new bootstrapped payment or merchant-of-record product to fill the gap.
- He prefers bootstrapped vendors because "founders never really change their vision", while a VC-backed company can hire a new CEO who changes everything.
- For a boilerplate today he would default to Stripe: best known, best API, and tax isn't relevant to beginners yet.

chunks.heading: Small products on top of big platforms: wrappers as a strategy
chunks.text:
- Indie makers win with small products. LemonSqueezy used Stripe as the processor and built a layer on top because it had few resources.
- That makes such products attractive acquisition targets for the platform they build on. Shopify acquires apps and folds them in as features, and he thinks OpenAI-wrapper startups will be bought too.
- He rejects the idea that being a "wrapper" is bad: "everything is a wrapper and the higher level it is the smarter you are". Users care about the experience, not the underlying layer.

chunks.heading: The indie bubble as a free accelerator
chunks.text:
- John argues the indie maker community is a launchpad, not a dead-end bubble. Makers sell to each other first.
  - They are good early users: critical, they pay, they use the product themselves and give feedback.
  - The iteration cycle is fast. You can launch and iterate daily, and once the product is great it moves outside via SEO and social media.
- Plausible is his example. It started in the indie world and is now used by many VC-backed startups too.
- He compares it to YC, where startups first target other YC companies. He calls the indie bubble "better than YC bubble" because there are more people, companies and product types, and no lottery or acceptance limit. It is "a global decentralized acceleration program" that is free.
- He thinks the Stripe deal and press coverage like TechCrunch will make indie hacking much more popular.

chunks.heading: SaaS boilerplates: why he is bullish
chunks.text:
- He calls boilerplates "the best thing that happened to the indie maker world" and says SaaS innovation speed has maybe gone "10x".
- He expects boilerplates to get niche-specific: no-code landing page builders, PM tools, chat apps. He says "don't do the generic one" because you won't beat Marc Lou's ShipFast, which makes about 100K per month (the host's figure, which John did not dispute). Build for a niche instead.
  - Examples he sees launching on DevHunt: boilerplates for directories, Chrome extensions and iOS apps. Many show MRR.
- Developers used to be too arrogant to pay for someone else's code. Now they want to save time.
- Boilerplates suit individuals, not teams, so VC-backed teams won't adopt them soon. That helps indie makers move almost as fast as startup teams.
- He would personally take a boilerplate and move fast, even if he doesn't know all the code, because "the advantage looks heavier than the disadvantage".
- Iteration speed matters for newcomers. One iteration a week versus one a month is a 4x difference. People who don't use boilerplates will quit sooner because they won't get users in time.
- For beginners, the real value is the "aha" moment: a launched product on a domain with a brand within a week or two. For experienced makers it matters less, since the bottleneck becomes decision-making, not development.
- His platform Mars has many micro-boilerplates you can combine. A single boilerplate rarely fits all needs. He says he had this idea in 2018.
- Future makers will mostly be attention-winners, not introverted builders. With no TechCrunch, VCs or accelerators picking winners, you have to win an audience yourself on social media, and the extroverts will win it. He thinks "maybe 90%" of millions of makers will be attention-winners.

chunks.heading: Selling on a famous maker's brand, and why great products win
chunks.text:
- Selling a boilerplate through the founder's success story is ethical in his view. It is how brands work: the James Bond ad for BMW, Apple's "be different".
- The line is a 100% guarantee. Courses promising 10K a month are "pretty much just lying".
- Being inspired, educated and kept in the mood of making stuff is a big part of entrepreneurship. He credits Marc Lou with doing the most to keep people making things.
- On free alternatives like T3: details make the product different, like a Chinese phone that looks like an iPhone. He hasn't tried ShipFast, but expects its developer experience is better because Marc Lou gets thousands more feedback loops.
- He says he has "never seen great product without users". He tries more products than anyone on Earth, daily, and sees UX and landing-page quality go together: a really bad landing page means a bad product "like 99%".
- In the bootstrap world you win by real marketing, not ads, so great products almost always rise and bad ones rarely do.

chunks.heading: Why Europe could become the capital of indie making
chunks.text:
- US: VC culture is dominant. Founders see lots of money, "demand creates supply", and being an indie hacker there "means you're a loser rather than you are smart". Cost of living and health insurance push people into jobs, and there are few part-time or short-hours jobs.
- Europe: founders believe there is little VC money, so they look for alternatives. Work-life balance leaves time for side projects. Cost of living outside capitals is low. John lived on a 2,000 euro a month stipend in Holland. Some people live on social benefits for a year while building a startup.
- VC money can hurt. VC-backed founders build in a bunker and launch late. Bootstrapped founders "launch you talk you launch you talk and you iterate". John says paid growth has stopped working for him over the past three years: expensive, bot traffic, no retention.
- Small, focused startups win against wide ones. He thinks Europe should aim for "the next million average companies with 10 people or 100 people", not the next Google, since huge companies move to the US anyway.
- He sees European design taste and the "ability to be irritated with something so that you want to fix that thing" as an edge, especially among Dutch, German and French makers.
- Problems: Dagobert Renard, an indie maker from France, told him indie making in Europe is "terrible". People don't understand it, and renting an apartment is nearly impossible without a regular job contract. John argues products can solve this, as SafetyWing did for nomad insurance, and Stripe and Mercury now give loans based on transactions. He expects makers to use their indie profile as proof of income for rentals and mortgages.
- Policy prediction: nomad visas and remote-worker tax laws are multiplying, "exponential" in his view, like COVID rules spreading in three months. France has a four-year visa where you only need a startup. He expects most countries to have such rules by the end of next year, then to extend immigrant tax perks to local indie makers so they stay home. The US will do nothing because it already has more immigrants than it needs.
- He urges makers to keep posting about this on social media, since politicians are on it too.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: John Rush walks through his methods for finding startup ideas: replying to public complaints with a solution, tweeting many ideas, cloning across markets, keyword research, automating your own job, and splitting out one feature of a big tool. He argues for starting with safe, simple ideas, being patient, and building for trends before they get big.

chunks.heading: Start with B2B pain people already complain about, and offer the solution on the spot
chunks.text:
- John calls this the single best way to find an idea: find a pain many people mention that has no solution, then reply with a solution right where they complain (X, Reddit, blogs, comment sections).
- He prefers B2B pain over b2c. In b2c, "consumers are really bad at changing their habits", so even a solved pain often goes unused. In B2B, better tools mean more profit, so people change habits more readily.
- He says people don't see ideas because they don't browse with their eyes open. They should put their brain in "hunting mode" for weeks, build a long list, and not stop at the first idea.
- Example 1: a tweet about open source alternatives to paid tools led him to build an open source alternatives directory. He shipped it within hours and it went viral because he answered the problem fast.
- Example 2: a tweet asking who builds MVPs on a fixed price drew many "I'm looking for that person too" and "I'm that person" replies. He saw the whole marketplace in one thread and built a directory.
- If the build takes days or weeks, put up a waitlist. John says people overestimate intent: most won't click, they bookmark, and those who click are happy to see a waitlist.
- He says you can also mock up low-fi screenshots and say "leave your email to be told when it's launched". He sees validating before building as good for everyone.

chunks.heading: Tweet many ideas, and don't fear having no followers
chunks.text:
- Pitching an idea publicly beats DMing it to one person: one person can't say if it's good, the market can.
- If you try 50 ideas, one will probably be good, and you don't know which.
- No followers is an advantage: if a tweet goes viral without an audience, the idea is good.
- His Devun launch (open-source Devin alternative, in his words) went viral with very few followers. Before it he had tried about 20 other ideas with no reaction.
- Bad tweets cost nothing: if nobody sees them, there is nothing to be embarrassed about, and you can delete them.
- He never schedules tweets, because he has to be inside Twitter to feel the right mode.

chunks.heading: Clone what works into a new market, or tweak a proven idea
chunks.text:
- **Localize:** find a hot new tool in the US (new there means unlikely to exist elsewhere), then clone it in a market where it doesn't exist and localize it. Examples: Airbnb and Uber clones in local markets, or a "where to watch this movie" app built around a country's own streaming services.
- Clone the whole app, with all its best details, not just the idea. US apps usually have strong design and UX.
- Idea for a service: a daily email of the top 3 new apps from every country, each app sent only once and only apps missing from your market. He says it would also show trends outside your bubble.
- Travel is another source: he says nearly every founder story starts with "I went there, saw that, came back and did this".
- **Tweak a proven idea:** change the pricing (monthly to one-time, expensive to cheap, no trial to trial) or change the audience (dog lovers to cat lovers, makers to flower sellers). He has also made something more expensive and says it worked really well.
- Examples of cheaper clones: many Shopify-style competitors, and an open-source Bloomberg terminal alternative (Bloomberg was around $1K a month, in his words) that went viral.
- He would do this safe route for a first idea today, and says the longer something has no competitor, the lower the chance that anyone builds one.

chunks.heading: Keyword-led ideas using Google Keyword Planner and autocomplete
chunks.text:
- John uses Google Keyword Planner (free), Google search and autocomplete only. Other tools make him less creative, because they suggest so much that he loses control.
- Spend hours, not five minutes. He says he spends at least an hour on it daily and sometimes a full day.
- Start with seed words you know. If you have none, ask ChatGPT for 100 variations. You need domain familiarity to judge ideas.
- Look for high traffic and low competition. Then Google the keyword: if the top 10 is only SEO blog posts, nothing real exists.
- Directory idea: he seeded "directory", saw "directory submission services", realized people pay for what he did by hand, and built listingbott.
- Emailer example: he searched email-related words, found a domain "s emailer" available (from "s email" with high traffic) and built a simple email tool for himself.
- Autocomplete trick: type part of a sentence such as "landing page builder for" and read the suggestions. He also mentions AnswerThePublic for questions.
- Domain exact-match plus related long-tail keywords can also win traffic.

chunks.heading: Automate your own job, and get a first customer from inside it
chunks.text:
- John says millions of ideas live in jobs. Any job can be improved with software, and his own ideas came from automating his work (landing pages, blog articles). His end goal is to automate himself out of his work.
- Any job works, even manual labor. He gives a kindergarten teacher losing track of children's belongings and scheduling events as examples.
- Being an insider means you can use the tool yourself, and bosses usually say yes to a free trial.
- B2B tools don't need a catchy pitch: if they save an hour a day, users tell colleagues.
- Think about your first customer before the idea, because ideas never work as imagined without real users. Ads "almost never work" for an idea without its own traction.
- His first idea was a marketplace for student books at his university.
- Caution: solving your own problem is risky if you lack experience. The habit you replace must be weak enough, as with note apps vs Apple Notes.

chunks.heading: Single-feature micro tools and a descriptive name
chunks.text:
- Find a popular tool, find where its users talk, and look for a group using only one feature. Talk to about 100 users: roughly 5 use just one feature.
- Build a micro SaaS with only that feature, price below the big tool, and name it plainly. His examples: listingbot, and a simple visit counter named for counting visits.
- Why it works:
  - the idea is validated before building
  - the name matches the search query, which helps SEO
  - it's easy to remember and recommend
- People recommend focused products: "people don't send you to a restaurant that also serves coffee, they send you to a coffee place".
- Example: browse Webflow users' profiles, find people building waitlists on it, and build waitlister.com. They feel they overpay and won't recommend Webflow for that.

chunks.heading: Ride tomorrow's wave, not today's hype
chunks.text:
- John rode crypto and NFT waves and said it nearly worked, but the swings wrecked him. His friend's AI website builder boomed and then fell. He says most AI tools have about 10 times less traffic than a year ago.
- His rule now: "always work on things of tomorrow". Build in something small today that he expects to be big in a year or two.
- OpenSea was founded in 2017, was ignored until late 2019, and in 2020 was a huge share of NFT trades. The winners predicted early.
- His own bets: bad no-code (2018), boilerplates before people knew them, and directories, where he became an expert as the wave grew.
- Being early builds expertise, then content, then audience, and you know what to build. The market respects whoever was there before it got hot.
- He says he works about 5 hours a day of "exercise" work plus relaxed thinking, and has no stress because he has no competitors. His biggest regret is working too much.

chunks.heading: Start easy, play the long game, and use ChatGPT as a negative filter
chunks.text:
