- Remove the "next Steve Jobs" romance, at least for the first idea. Practice with safe, simple ideas first, as musicians start by playing covers.
- Indie makers are rarely successful on the first try. Build a directory first: try 4-5 directories and one will work. Then a micro SaaS with at least 1K revenue, then a serious SaaS, a platform, and a two-sided marketplace.
- Plan 5-10 years (he also says 10-20 years). Avoid running out of money (savings or a part-time job), health, or passion. Aim lower to get small wins and stay motivated.
- Copying: he wouldn't copy another indie maker's tool, but copying big corporations' products (such as Google Analytics) is fine. Copy ideas, not implementations. He sometimes avoids looking at competitors so he starts with a fresh mind.
- ChatGPT for ideas: he says its suggestions are predictable and average. If it suggests an idea, he removes it from his list, because it already exists.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: John Rush explains why he chose bootstrapping over VC for Mars X, how he scouted and acquired Unicorn Platform, and why the small-acquisition market will grow. He also covers building with AI early and where AI opportunities sit: UX in boring niches, not deep tech.

chunks.heading: Why John bootstrapped MarsX instead of raising VC
chunks.text:
- John came from the VC-backed startup world. Before 2012, funding was nearly nonexistent among developers he knew. From 2012 to 2018 it was easy, and almost everyone he knew raised a round.
- His observation: founders who started before funding was available and struggled on their own did well when money came. Founders who got money straight away failed far more often. In his 2010 batch of the first 10 Norwegian startups, four became unicorns (he names Kahoot), but later batches did worse and worse.
- He entered bootstrapped, self-funded work in 2018. He already had Angel investments and co-founded startups producing revenue, and he did not want an exit. His reason: after a big exit you have to work out how to store the money, so he preferred ongoing revenue to fund his next ventures.
- For the first two years he worked completely alone. He says solo building is fun only while nobody uses the product. Once users arrive it turns into "micro bosses".
- He pitched MarsX to about 200 investors and had enough interest in 2020 to raise $50-150M for a team of around 400 developers building micro apps. He declined. His reasons:
  - Micro apps are little products that need owners and ongoing maintenance.
  - Many people outside MarsX want to own products and make money from them.
  - A VC-funded company could not share ownership of the platform with the community.

chunks.heading: MarsX: reusable micro apps, decentralized
chunks.text:
- MarsX's goal is to accelerate software development by reusing ready-made micro apps. His complaint is that every project rebuilds profiles, search and galleries from scratch, and "a thousand teams" write the same Uber clone. Science reuses prior work, and software does not.
- Reported stats (confirmed by John): about $1.5M ARR, 20,000 developers, 300+ micro apps in the showcase.
- The product has three interfaces on one project: no-code, pro-code and AI. Users can switch between them at any time instead of choosing one up front. Underneath sit hundreds of micro apps. He says only about 5% is left to build what's missing and connect the pieces.
- Why decentralized: centralized platforms trying to build everything themselves struggle because code goes obsolete quickly. Community builders own their micro apps and can co-own the platform, unlike plugin ecosystems where a plugin can be kicked out.
- His 2018 prediction was that IDE, no-code and platform companies would have to involve the community. He now points to Replit bounties, Supabase paying plugin builders and Vercel paying people who build for it. Explaining this was hard four years ago, when people said "if it was good people would be doing that".
- He bet on micro apps because of AI. The idea was that a user tells a micro app what to change and it rebuilds itself for them. He connected GPT-3 to micro apps last year and says it worked.

chunks.heading: How John acquired Unicorn Platform
chunks.text:
- MarsX needs about 300 independent founders under one umbrella. Each keeps the upside of being a founder, and MarsX takes away the bad parts.
- He built profiles of the products and founders he needed. One profile was a no-code landing page builder, so he tried every one.
- He chose Unicorn Platform because the product showed care in every click and piece of text, even though it had fewer features and "didn't look like a real company".
- Reasons to buy rather than promote his own micro app:
  - An existing tool with users can be swapped in for MarsX's own micro app and reach market faster.
  - He also wanted the founder (Alex), who is strong at product and marketing, where John is not.
- He followed Alex on Twitter for a year to a year and a half, reading every tweet, from a shortlist of about 10 people. Alex did not know.
- One conversation was enough, and they agreed the deal by the end. Alex had never signalled wanting to sell, and would not have sold for cash alone.
- John says he watched what Alex struggled with and what he loved, and pitched taking the struggles away so he could focus on product and marketing.

chunks.heading: The "label" model for indie founders
chunks.text:
- John's analogy is the music label. Singers look independent, but the label handles production and distribution. He applies this to tech: one large label of indie builders can compete with corporations and VC-funded startups, which he calls an unfair fight for lone indie hackers.
- He predicts this will be one of the biggest things to hit the indie tech world in the next 5-10 years. He already sees small unofficial coalitions of 2-10 builders on Twitter, sharing resources and distribution.
- He does not see it as zero-sum: "we're gonna take the pie of the corporations".

chunks.heading: His own acquisitions and exits
chunks.text:
- **Icon search (2014):** He had money from startups and wanted to buy a tech company. Prices were then lower, and a million dollars could buy a really good business. He found the biggest icon search project at the time, with a million monthly visitors. Its users were developers and designers, which he saw as a good audience to build on. He spent six months on improvements, found it boring, and sold it for double what he paid.
- His takeaway: at any time many good startups can be bought below market price, because owners may say yes to an offer even if they didn't plan to sell.
- **Apartment-selling platform (2016 or 2017, he is unsure which year):**
  - The platform let a user enter an address and complete the home sale, including signing documents.
  - Building started in November and took three months. It launched on 1 February.
  - Two potential buyers appeared 15 days later, when they had no users.
  - Insurance companies and banks were rushing to get a digital product after a big consultancy report. Owning the housing platform meant they could sell mortgages there.
  - Competing counter-offers led to a sale for "over five million dollars".
  - He says none of those projects worked, because selling a house is a high-trust decision and people stick with a person. They sold partly because they did not fully believe in it. His lesson: sometimes you build something, get lucky and sell it.

chunks.heading: The acquisition market and why it will grow
chunks.text:
- John expects the acquisition market to grow more than most people expect.
- Distribution used to be easy. Before 2015 his products never struggled with it: his movie app got 70,000 users within months of launch. Now nobody finds your app.
- People who are good at building rarely love distribution, and the reverse is also true. Builders get a little MRR, want to return to building, and should sell to someone who loves marketing and sales. Sellers on marketplaces like acquire.com often sell multiple projects, and the buyer gets a working asset.
- For non-developers, he calls outsourcing development or hiring it out "the best way to fail", and says he has almost never seen it work. Buying a project is a better route.
- An influencer with about $20,000 could buy a couple of projects, test whether their audience buys, and put more money into the ones that do.
- Small acquisitions didn't happen earlier because developers don't buy other people's code. They have opinions about code and think they could build it in a weekend. Non-technical buyers just want the work done.

chunks.heading: AI: John's history and where he sees the opportunity
chunks.text:
- **History:**
  - His first tech project, in 2005-2006 at university, was a handwriting OCR neural network, started because he couldn't read friends' lecture notes. He ran several neural networks and other algorithms independently and accepted a word when two agreed. This reached about 98% accuracy against 99% for the leading commercial products. He never considered making it a business and deleted the program.
  - His next project was Ames AI, monitoring software for systems such as ATMs and vending machines. It applied regression models and neural networks to raw data to predict normal behaviour and flagged deviations against history.
  - Then came a movie recommendation app that scraped catalogs from Netflix, iTunes and HBO and used Facebook data. It could model two people together for a shared recommendation. It now runs white-labeled B2B with 15 million users combined.
- **Recent AI use:** His team used GPT-2 from 2019 and found it too unreliable, for example it could not produce JSON consistently. He thinks building with AI early last year is a main reason everything he does has grown since.
- **Agents:** He built an internal agents project where each agent is programmed for a role, such as lawyer, accountant, developer, or himself. He says it made him 10-20x more productive. The company has no lawyers, no accountants and almost no support staff, and AI covers those roles.
- **Opportunity:** He says the gap is UX on top of AI. Today you copy and paste, wait, and remember how to prompt. His advice:
  - Don't build deep tech, which is complicated and needs resources.
  - Don't build obvious or popular products, such as AI for email, because big brands will add it as a feature.
  - Go to second-wave niches that Google won't build for, such as bakeries, accounting, lawyers and cooking businesses.
  - He sees people who struggled for years now making $5,000-10,000 a month with small AI apps. Some call them wrappers, but "who cares".

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: John Rush explains why he left 12 years of VC-backed startups for bootstrapping, where he now runs 24 projects. He argues bootstrappers win with small specialized tools, over-delivering to users, open source with royalty-style forks, and building for emerging trends rather than existing hype.

chunks.heading: From VC-backed startups to bootstrapping: John's path and why it fit him
chunks.text:
- John's first startup was bootstrapped when he was about 15-16. It was a marketplace where smart students helped weaker students (math help, etc.), with payments, filters, accounts and requests. Within two years it had thousands of transactions daily. A bigger competitor bought it. He calls it luck: "it was just a student project for me."
- He didn't know the word "bootstrapping" then and assumed bootstrappers were people who couldn't raise money.
- After the sale he did what everyone did: incubator, VC money, round after round, exit or shut down, then repeat. That ran about 10-12 years in Norway, riding the wave of Norwegian government startup grants that began around 2010.
- He discovered the bootstrap and indie maker world in 2022 and wishes he had done it earlier. Being easy to stay on the VC path gave him no reason to look at other options.
- He says he is "great at being Scrappy" and at producing a lot with few people. That is bad for VC startups, where headcount is the KPI and founders pretend to be bigger than they are (stock photos of "team" members, advisors counted as staff). He felt "like a fish in the wrong ocean."
- Today he runs 24 projects, mainly for busy founders, all bootstrapped, and plans to launch more.
- Some people really do enjoy the VC style: conferences, partnership calls, managing large teams. John says most tech founders are introverts who enjoy building products, and he knows VC-backed founders who privately say the same thing but can't say it publicly because of investors.

chunks.heading: Product-first vs company-first founders, and being honest about size
chunks.text:
- John separates people who love building products from people who love building companies (culture, systems, departments, headcount). Bootstrappers are usually the former.
- In bootstrapping you can be a company of one and be honest ("I'm in bed, I'll answer tomorrow"). Customers accept that. In VC mode, faking size makes customers expect Microsoft-level responsiveness.
- Doing marketing, building and support yourself is freedom, not a defect.

chunks.heading: Win by over-delivering to users, not by buying growth
chunks.text:
- John contrasts the models. In VC-backed startups the goal is CAC lower than LTV so you can pour money into growth. In bootstrapping, spending money on growth gets you nowhere because you can't pour more money in.
- His bootstrap rule: before roughly 10K-20K MRR, deliver far more to users than they pay for ("go negative on ARPU"). Users who fall in love become the growth engine: they recommend you, mention you online, bring friends and give support.
- Investors push VC-backed companies toward moves that serve the next round, often unrelated to making users happy. That was his frustration.
- Be hungry for money. Every dollar early is hard, and you must be genuinely excited by small revenue to reach the next milestone. He says being very rich early killed his excitement for small startup revenue. 1K and 2K MRR felt exciting again once he bootstrapped. He warns against losing motivation by comparing your profit to other makers' bigger numbers.
- He doesn't watch Stripe notifications. He checks the bank balance, and as long as it's above a threshold he knows things are fine. He checks revenue mainly to create content about it.
- He gets his strongest motivation from thank-you messages from users, not from money.
- Love the journey, not the outcome: "you cannot control the outcome," and he knows people who sold companies and never found themselves again. Don't postpone happiness.

chunks.heading: Why small niche software from bootstrappers will beat VC-backed bloat
chunks.text:
- John has bet his whole business on the idea that the world wants "small solutions for small problems."
- VC math forces a market of $1B-$10B, so products become generic and feature-heavy. They have to sell to large teams, which means collaboration and permissions, and that bloats the product for solos and small teams. VC products end up competing on identical things.
- Bootstrapped products position slightly differently (audience, stage, segment), so more niche problems get solved. A 5K-15K MRR niche product would never be funded by VCs but serves a real need.
- Specialized software eventually beats generalist software for each use case. He has watched the bootstrap world for about two years and knows nobody who hit 10K MRR and stopped growing, while he knows many VC startups that hit 10K MRR and died.
- His prediction: instead of 10,000 big VC-backed products there will be 1 million small micro-tools from bootstrappers. AI and tooling help small founders more than large VC teams, and this is accelerating.
- Customers are shifting. A year ago his customers were nearly all solopreneurs. Now half of new customers are mid-sized or VC-backed companies, including about 30 YC companies across his products.
- Buyer psychology he sees: customers distrust vendors that raise money, join YC or hire many people, because support gets worse and failure odds are high. In bootstrapping, the default bet is that the vendor stays in business. The opposite is true in the VC world.
- Open source as a sales tool: when companies worry about a solo founder dying, he says the product is fully open source and they can run it themselves. Open source also keeps pricing fair, since users can self-host if you triple the price.

chunks.heading: SaaS OS and open-source forking with royalties
chunks.text:
- Problem: many tiny tools mean many logins, dashboards and subscriptions. John is building a "SaaS OS", an operating system for micro-tools with one account, one subscription and shared settings, where tools talk to each other. He is also building an open API standard so any micro-SaaS can plug in natively. Sign-up becomes a button press instead of re-entering company info and logo.
- Benefits: users get less friction; makers skip billing portals, marketing and operations and focus on their product. He says the SaaS OS solves distribution while makers fill the ecosystem.
- His build playbook: build every essential product an indie maker needs across the journey (build, operate, monetize, grow, market), such as no-code tools, analytics and SEO. Use each on his own projects first; once it works across all of them, launch it publicly. He wants about 100 tools in the OS before launching it, not five. About a year and a half in, he estimated it was halfway through and needed about another year.
- His developer system, Morse X, uses "micro-apps" that can be forked and nested (user login, ratings, CMS and so on). A royalty model would pass revenue down the tree to everyone whose code is used, like music royalties. Forkers add a little on top and share revenue with the original author.
- He expects software to be open source by default ("closed source by default" will sound odd). Code is no longer the hard part; deciding what to build, distribution and UX are. He open-sourced DevHunt and no competitor cloned it, while it gained contributors and trust.
- Example use: instead of one no-code builder for everything, launch 20 forks, each for a use case (cinemas, bakeries), without maintaining 20 separate repos. He expects thousands of slightly different versions of the same software, shortening the innovation cycle from years to weeks.
- Distribution and building are different modes. Doing both is "torture." Forks with royalties let a great builder and a great distributor each do their part without needing to be co-founders.

chunks.heading: Using Algora bounties for open-source work
chunks.text:
- John says he spent "very good money" on Algora last year and is happy about it. (The tactic below is a story from the host about their own project; John only says he plans to try it, so this section reflects that.)
- John says he will try it on DevHunt next week: post issues with a bounty and see how it works.
- He also described the underlying idea: experts who know a topic solve tasks quickly, and open-source projects benefit.

chunks.heading: Predicting trends, creators vs consumers, and the Indie Maker Village
chunks.text:
- John never builds for an existing hype or an obvious trend. He compares it to buying a stock that's already going up. He builds for small, non-obvious, growing trends that few understand yet, so that when the trend grows it carries the product with it. He credits good intuition for spotting what's growing.
- His trend: people who build consume less ("the more you produce the less you consume"). He expects a growing "creator class" whose values and routines clash with a consumption-optimized world, who limit cheap dopamine and want their kids to become producers.
- The Indie Maker Village is his long-term bet (5, 10 or 20 years): a place where the mainstream agenda is creating, a "Silicon Valley for the bootstrap world." He wants it open source with contributors, not a money-making venture. He sees side creation (building a chair) as improving primary work.
- He believes cheap dopamine (YouTube, Twitter, shopping, entertainment) weakens the brain's ability to do difficult multi-day tasks.

chunks.heading: Meaning, money and when to start
chunks.text:
- John defines being rich as a strong family and a community of friends who share your interests. Numbers are irrelevant as long as you can keep doing it. Family is a renewable energy source when business gets repetitive over 20 years. Money is a tool to build more business.
- He says he loses at investing (crypto, stocks, property, startups, currencies, 20+ investments, small angel checks of $10K-$100K). He sold Nvidia and Tesla early and lost Bitcoin held on a Norwegian exchange that was hacked. He treats this as not a lesson about investing skill but says product building is where his luck lies.
- Owning a product gives meaning: you earn from the product rather than from hours, the work shrinks over time, and your name is on something useful. He prefers 10K/month from a product over a $1M bank balance. He thinks more people will want income not tied to hours rather than billionaire status.
- On starting now: he argues against saving for years to free yourself later. His lawyer friend (age 38) spends almost no time on his indie project, planning to start after years of saving. John's view: a 50-year-old who has only worked a day job rarely develops the innovation skill, and exchanging your best years for later freedom is a bad bet. His suggestion was to work two days less and use the time on the project.
- He is skeptical of FIRE for similar reasons: many bets must go right, and people who retire early often lose their purpose.
- Computer-job health is a real constraint: he says nearly none of the nearly 100 people in his companies are healthy, so don't assume you'll be fit later.
- Shipping issues hit him hard. When a product is down overnight for US customers while he sleeps in Europe, he feels the damage is permanent. He also says the rollercoaster of crisis and fix produces stronger happiness than products that never break.
- He shares his whole business openly (growth, marketing, building) and plans to turn about 30,000 of his tweets into an open-source book. He answers 80-100 Twitter DMs a day and says Twitter is where to reach him.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: John Rush contrasts VC-backed and bootstrapped life, and explains how he mapped 120 startup jobs into product ideas. He shares why UX beats features in B2B, how he competes in crowded niches, and why most of his tools are marketing assets.

chunks.heading: Bootstrapping vs VC: how the incentives change the founder
chunks.text:
- John's path: bootstrapped his first startup and sold it, spent 8 years in VC-backed companies, then returned to bootstrapping for 7 years.
- His main difference: VC-backed KPIs rewire the founder's brain. In his first bootstrapped project he was obsessed with customers and profits. In VC-backed companies he was obsessed with the next round, his network, media coverage and conferences. Users and profits ranked last.
- This is the norm, not just his habit. You raise pre-seed, then immediately have to raise seed, then the next round.
- In a VC-backed startup, "the money lays in the exit". There is no other money there.
- He came from bootstrapping and assumed the company would eventually start making profits. He was wrong, and says he was "sabotaging my companies" with that assumption.
- His goal now is to help solo and bootstrapped founders run businesses on their own terms without VC money. He argues no VC means a better work-life balance, including for family life.

chunks.heading: Finding product ideas: map the jobs people do and replace them
chunks.text:
- John planned to bootstrap forever, so he needed a cheap way to run companies. The biggest startup cost is people and salaries.
- Method:
  1. List the people you usually hire in a startup.
  2. Break each role into micro jobs. He came up with about 120 typical jobs.
  3. Build a product to replace each job, ordered by best ROI (small effort, high output).
- He generated all his ideas in one day from this map and now builds roughly one product every few months.
- Result: everything built from the map worked ("zero failures"). Everything built outside the map failed. His example is a tool for hosting AI-generated websites, which nobody bought.
- Why it works: he is the user himself. "I'm the ideal user of my products and if I love it, why would others not love it?"

chunks.heading: The 25-product portfolio: seven tools earn 90% of revenue
chunks.text:
- Seven tools make about 90% of revenue. The rest make about 10% and mostly bring users in.
- He calls most of his tools "marketing assets rather than revenue assets". Some earn little but bring leads that get channeled into paid tools.
- The seven:
  - Unicorn Platform: website builder and the core of the system, with almost 600,000 users. The founder journey starts with a website.
  - SEO Bot: generates blog articles.
  - Listing Bot: lists a product on web directories.
  - Index Rusher: helps pages get indexed.
  - Count Visits: analytics across web, Stripe, Paddle and SEO.
  - SaaS Emailer: emails to SaaS users, plus campaigns.
  - Tiny Ads: launched the week before this interview, an ad network only for B2B SaaS and B2B tech. He calls it his best launch ever.
- A bigger audience speeds up every launch: everything he launches now grows faster than a year or two ago.

chunks.heading: Competing in crowded markets by picking a niche
chunks.text:
- Competition doesn't scare him. Every market and use case has so many details that a product perfected for one niche can look like the others while being very different.
- Unicorn Platform example: many website builders exist, including Webflow and Framer. Those can do far more but are easy to break without design taste, so you need a designer.
- John targets busy solopreneurs who aren't designers and just want to launch a website quickly.
- His rule: "people should not be afraid to build something that looks like all the other products as long as they don't compete with all the other products." Typical Unicorn use cases are different enough that Webflow can't serve them, so he isn't competing with it. Trying to build everything for everyone (such as flower-shop sites) would lose.

chunks.heading: One shared codebase (Mars X) for all products
chunks.text:
- He built Mars X first, a stack that all his products run on. He built a product to build the other products on.
- It contains reusable micro apps. A new product reuses them, so about 90% is already there and only about 10% is new.
- Improving a micro app improves every product that uses it. His 25 products behave almost like one product with one codebase, not 25 separate repos.
- Everything is TypeScript/JavaScript.

chunks.heading: UX as the competitive edge in B2B
chunks.text:
- John's thesis: almost every problem already has a product. People don't realize it because the UX isn't clear.
- Old B2B users were paid employees who read manuals and watched videos. Today people expect everything to be like an iPhone, even at work. If a tool isn't obvious, employees tell the boss it doesn't do the job, and the boss doesn't check.
- Almost all B2B tools ignore UX and focus on features. He does the opposite: fewer features, extremely easy to use. When users are shocked in a good way, they share screenshots on social media.
- Launch example: for a tool built with a friend, he made them redo the whole UX before launch. Goal: "people will screenshot this and share it on Twitter praising the UX". The tool has a chat/terminal-style interface and went viral because of that UX. He notes people won't publicly praise an AI SEO tool itself, since that is slightly embarrassing.
- Tiny Ads onboarding is a casual WhatsApp-style chat instead of the usual forms and many steps. People loved it.
- Fewer steps isn't automatically easier: "sometimes more steps is better than less steps." He compares UX to music or film.
- Good products are now easy to produce with AI. UX is psychological and AI doesn't help much, so UX remains a reason his products win.

chunks.heading: Marketing and paying for growth
chunks.text:
- Marketing is only him: his own tweets and face, 100% of his social media. Some products he never tweeted about.
- He built Tiny Ads because he wants to pay for growth and has profits to reinvest. Past random investments never worked out, so he puts money back into his products.
- Regular ads: he disliked their performance and the work of running them. Traditional ads work better for B2C than B2B because they center on social media.
- He prefers organic content and paying influencers, which he thinks are cheaper than paid social ads.
- He uses Tiny Ads himself to drive sales. The key is making $2 for every $1 spent on ads. That completes the picture, so he can reinvest profits and also take revenue-based loans, for which he sees low-interest offers, and put the money into ads.

chunks.heading: Advice for developers who want to build products
chunks.text:
- Assess your strengths honestly. Empathy for the user and content creation (understanding people's psychology and writing to their mood) are very hard to learn, much like being funny.
- If you are naturally good at content and storytelling, go solo: "there is very low chance to fail" and everyone he knows like that is doing well.
- If you are good at coding but not storytelling, find a storytelling partner and team up. The chance of success is much higher. If you go solo anyway, make money elsewhere.
- Being the CTO isn't a defeat. Marketing and being the brand is a lot of work and stress, and he is sometimes jealous of people who just code.
- Content work has emotional highs and lows (million views, then none). Coding is steadier, and AI now finds most bugs.
- Long-term goal: a holding company that owns hundreds of leading products in their verticals and outlives him, running for 50 or even hundreds of years.
- Even if you're employed, build something you own. The joy of ownership is worth it even without income.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: John Rush explains his problem-first, solo-founder model: solve your own problem, pitch ideas on Twitter before building, automate everything repetitive with AI agents, and keep each product small enough to run without a team. He also covers high-effort content and brutal self-criticism as growth habits.

chunks.heading: Build problem-first: solve your own pain, then your friends', then release
chunks.text:
- John treats business "more like art" than a way to make money. He sees a problem in his own work and solves it for himself first.
- Next he solves it for his friends, who are all entrepreneurs. Only after it works for both does he put it out to everyone.
- This makes failure hard. He is already the user, so a product doesn't get dropped because nobody else is using it yet.
- He builds for the solopreneur, not for teams. Most products ship with permissions and many buttons so people live inside the tool all day. John wants "one button where I say start and I just close it and then you know it does the job."
- He judges ideas as if they were someone else's, because people get attached to what they put effort into. His judgment "almost always correlates with the opinion of the other people."
- He keeps thousands of ideas in his draft board, for both content and products. Almost all of them are bad, and the world never sees them.

chunks.heading: Pitch ideas on Twitter before building (the DevHunt origin)
chunks.text:
- John bought Unicorn Platform from another founder. It had 25,000 users, and it declined for the first year after the purchase because users were attached to the previous founder.
- His breakthrough with the bootstrapped model was DevHunt, a "Product Hunt for developers."
- The pain: Product Hunt was mostly occupied by marketing people voting for things, so even great dev tools couldn't win. John had his own dev tool, Marzx.dev.
- He tweeted from a brand-new account with a few hundred followers. He said Product Hunt is unfair to dev tools and closed (the algorithm isn't known), and proposed DevHunt.
- The pitch: "if this tweet gets 100 likes I will assemble a team among the people who comment this tweet and we're going to build it together."
- The tweet went viral, with 20k-50k views. His previous best tweet had about 50 views.
- Seven people joined as contributors, and some investors showed interest.
- Lesson: pitching before building is free, recruits help for free, and building in public gives free distribution. He found a way to build products "for free with almost no people."

chunks.heading: Build an audience first to test ideas in minutes
chunks.text:
- John's first advice to solo founders is to build an online presence. Followers and content that gets views let you test hypotheses before you spend time building.
- Building takes weeks or months, while a tweet takes minutes. Repeated tweeting gives fast iteration cycles, which makes it more likely you build the right thing.
- Most people don't put in enough time. When they say they get few views, he asks how much time they spend creating versus consuming. The usual answer is about 30 minutes a day, which he calls too little.
- He sometimes spends 10 hours on one piece. One thread about AI coding tools took about 10 hours and passed 1 million views.
- "High effort content will win no matter what", because readers feel that someone saved them time.
- Unless you're famous, "you have to actually kind of work for people for free." The audience should think "I would have paid for it, but it's free."
- His content filter: he only posts a tweet if he likes the draft. If he likes it, he is confident everyone will; if not, he doesn't post it.
- Daily habit: each morning he reviews yesterday's work as a harsh outside critic, in his head only. It spares him public criticism, which hurts more.

chunks.heading: Run 20+ products with slow pace, small scope and no deadlines
chunks.text:
- John runs 24+ products. Time per product ranges from about 1 hour a month to 100 hours a month, depending on user complaints, bug reports and market opportunities.
- He has no deadlines and no enterprise contracts, so he moves at his own pace.
- Having many products makes him efficient and good at saying no. He says you can harm a product by doing too much when you have plenty of time and resources.
- Some of his products are used by hundreds of thousands of people. He doesn't push features daily. He improves what exists, since users signed up because they liked it, and extra features may complicate it.
- Cap per product: each stays below $1 million MRR so he can run it without stress and without a team. He may go bigger later, when bored of small and mid-sized products.
- Team approach: he builds alone first for control and honest self-criticism. When traction brings more work, he invites a friend or someone passionate as a co-maker on a 50-50 split.
- He doesn't hire and doesn't think hiring survives the AI era. He expects either very small high-impact teams or co-founder-led products, with AI and tools covering the rest.

chunks.heading: Automate everything repetitive and keep only ideas and strategy
chunks.text:
- John's view: about 95% of a founder's tasks could be delegated. Delegating to people means hiring, so he automates instead.
- He expects founders to be left with inventing ideas (strategy, creative work, small ideas within the product), which is the part he enjoys.
- Multiplication effect: a task that's merely annoying for one product becomes "crazy boring" across 24, which is his incentive to automate.
- His agents:
  - Most marketing except social media, run by his own AI agents.
  - An agent for accounting, paperwork and invoices.
  - An agent that acts as him and handles about 99% of communication with his co-makers.
  - Marzx.dev, his AI coding agent, used to build his products.
- Vibe-coding tools he uses: Lovable, Emergent, Factory AI.
- Workflow tools: Lindy AI and make.com. Example: when an email asks for an invoice, auto-reply with a link to an invoice generator and prefill the data. Customers in Germany keep asking for invoices.
- Lovable replaced Figma for prototypes. Speaking to it gives a clickable prototype in place of days of manual work.
- Research habit: a daily time slot to browse Product Hunt, sign up for and try about 10 new agents a day, for UX ideas and tools to use.
- AI spend: he tweeted that his AI tools cost about $20K a month (summed from his Mercury account). He compares it to one great senior employee, who would cost about the same, since the tools replace people.
- Proof it works: he was away from all work for three months and nothing broke. Some things grew less without active marketing, but there was "decent growth on some products."

chunks.heading: Marzx.dev: a closed AI coding tool he uses to build everything
chunks.text:
- John started Marzx.dev in 2019, before AI coding was a category. He believes he and the Replit team were among the first to bet on AI changing coding.
- He uses it himself to build his other products, agents and SaaS.
- It has a waitlist of about 200,000 people. It is still closed, and he invites people one by one, mostly friends.
- He hasn't launched publicly because of the support and infrastructure burden. He says it isn't a solopreneur product and would require building a team.
- He has investor offers and chooses not to take them for now. He prefers a portfolio of products small enough to run without a team.

chunks.heading: Bootstrapping versus VC: how John switched
chunks.text:
- John's first project, about 20 years ago, was a student marketplace for homework help and tutoring. He sold it after one year.
- He then invested his exit money in startups, as "bad VCs do": too early. He says this gets a cheap valuation but raises failure risk "by 10 or 100x."
- He invested in Norway, so even the winners were small and didn't cover the losses.
- By 2022 he had lost most of his money chasing unicorns, living in London and Silicon Valley, and joining accelerators.
- He found VC values didn't match his. He liked making users happy, not investors, and felt "kind of bad for making them richer."
- In 2022 he started bootstrapping as an experiment. His rule was to fund it for two or three years, and if it failed, go back to raising money and pay himself a salary.
- He says it felt different right away. He had direct contact with users, no middleman, and did the tweets, emails and calls himself.
- In the VC world he had to show a headcount (CMO and so on) to investors. Bootstrapping removed that.
- Having less money made small wins matter. Landing one client at $19 a month changed his bank account.
- He doesn't recommend this path to everyone. It was his thing and it clicked right away.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: John Rush explains how he picks and ships projects fast: scratch his own itch for SaaS tools, reverse-engineer keyword traffic for directories, and validate with a single tweet. He prioritizes by launching unfinished and letting users "scream", and markets with a movie-style teaser and launch blast.

chunks.heading: How John became a maker: equity co-founder first, own products later
chunks.text:
- John started in 2007 while studying computer science. He found the assignments boring, asked his professor for real work, and joined a government-ordered project his university had won.
- He found that building something people actually use is far more fun than building assignments.
- For roughly the first five years he had no ideas of his own. He found people with ideas and built quickly with them, acting as a technical co-founder.
- He was paid in equity, typically 5% to 15% of the company. He recommends working for equity: "people trust that you do because you're interested in the project", and incentives are aligned.
- By his 10th to 15th project he knew more than his co-founders about marketing, HR, fundraising and investor meetings, because he sat in on all of it. After five years he started his own products.
- His rule: keep doing and shipping constantly, and good ideas eventually come. Find the intersection of what people want and what he likes, so he can go fully into a project.
- He prefers "maker" to "entrepreneur", because entrepreneurs manage people and he outsources management so he can make.

chunks.heading: MarsX: building the platform that built everything else
chunks.text:
- John built MarsX out of his own pain: every project took time, had bugs, needed constant maintenance, and was hard to continue when developers left.
- Around 2017-2018 he tried many no-code and low-code tools. They give high leverage at first, then fail once the product gets complicated and you want control over the code.
- So he built a system where you start with no code and transition to pro code.
- It was an internal tool for him for the first years, then friends used it, then friends of friends, and it grew into a sizable startup.
- Figures he gives: almost $2 million ARR, hundreds of projects running on it, millions of users across those projects combined.
- MarsX became his leverage: "I built this wheel and then I built all the cars on top of it."
- He runs three types of projects: simple information sites (directories), SaaS tools, and platforms that others build businesses on. His platforms are a movie-industry one started about 10 years ago (boring, big, funds his other work), MarsX, and Unicorn Platform.

chunks.heading: Prioritizing: only the urgent, plus spontaneous projects
chunks.text:
- John uses an "urgent/important" approach and works only on urgent things: what is too late if done tomorrow. He keeps no plans, to-do lists or calendars.
- About 70% of his time is reactive: his many products "scream" at him through customer complaints and bugs, and he works on whatever screams loudest.
- About 20-30% is spontaneous work with no plan. Example: an hour before the talk he noticed there are many Next.js boilerplates online, found a domain, bought it, built a landing page and a directory, and launched it right after the call.
- To keep priorities clear, launch unfinished. Even one early user will name the two or three things bugging them, so he never has to choose what to build.
- He launches "way before you're embarrassed, even way before it works", tells users it's early, and they accept that.
- He tracks his projects by looking at his GoDaddy domain list, and found forgotten projects with good domains to relaunch.

chunks.heading: Finding ideas: build for your own problems, or reverse-engineer traffic
chunks.text:
- **SaaS tools:** he builds for his own problems, such as being unhappy with email tools or SEO tools. If it is great for him, it is likely great for many others. He builds it as a personal utility first, with no domain or design. Some he used for years before launching, and some he forgot to launch.
- **Directories and information sites:** he starts from the consumer. He researches Google keyword traffic and looks for high-traffic keywords with no product, where traffic goes to blogs.
- Directories suit this because the window is short: if he spends three months building a tool, the keyword opportunity is gone. He has days or a week.
- Example: he found high traffic for "all GPTs" just before OpenAI's GPT launch, bought the domain because it was free and unpopular, and filled it with GPTs after the launch. People now call it the best GPT directory.
- Process for the easy ones: keyword, landing page, content, tweet.
- Directories give him about half the traffic to his other projects.

chunks.heading: Validating on Twitter in 30 minutes
chunks.text:
- John's only validation is keyword traffic plus the reaction to one tweet. After about 30 minutes of engagement he can tell whether an idea is good.
- Twitter is so strong now that he doesn't need other channels. A year earlier he also used Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn and conference pitches.
- His best projects got over 100,000 views when he had only a few thousand followers, because Twitter shows tweets beyond your network.
- Example: DevHunt. He disliked that Product Hunt is closed source and that some products bought bots. He tweeted asking whether an open-source alternative was a good idea, the tweet exploded with almost no followers, and he found people to build it open source. DevHunt's traffic is doubling every month.
- Even with 100 followers it works: "if nobody reacts out of your hundred friends, your idea is actually bad."
- Validation works because his audience is the same as his target customer: founders, makers, SaaS tools. He keeps other audiences, like movie-industry, in separate channels.
- His intuition for SaaS tools aimed at business makers is now near 100% accurate. Earlier, his intuition was often the opposite of the outcome, so he used the crowd to correct it.

chunks.heading: Launch marketing: the movie playbook
chunks.text:
- John's marketing comes from the movie industry: anticipation, teasers and trailers, then burning about 80% of the marketing budget in the two weeks around launch.
- He applies the same strategy: heavy promotion concentrated around launch, since that is the crucial period.
- He now tweets mostly as marketing, since his intuition already tells him what will work.

chunks.heading: Twitter for makers: stay on one topic
chunks.text:
- John says he was everywhere before Twitter and wishes he had bet on it from the start. He recommends Twitter as the place for makers.
- Algorithm advice: talk about only one topic, makers and building. Comment only on maker posts so your feed fills with them, then reply and post.
- Never post about crypto or politics.
- He uses about 200 muted words to keep his feed clean.
- He posts twice a day and only about things he has done himself.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: John Rush explains why he replaced hired departments with AI agents, his three-step agent build process (Zapier, agent builder, hardcode), and why he automated distribution first. He also covers specialized vs general agents, co-maker deals, idea validation, and why great products still beat distribution alone.

chunks.heading: Why John builds AI agents: replacing hired people with agents
chunks.text:
- As a VC-backed founder, John built departments (content, sales, development) by hiring. He found hired people's work quality is lower than founders' work, and non-owners lose motivation. Giving equity to everyone didn't fix it for non-entrepreneurial people.
- His fix, since 2022: create artificial employees. Agents "work 24/7", are always motivated, scale infinitely and can keep being improved.
- He wants an organization of just him and agents. Full automation isn't possible everywhere. In development he still needs a coder to bring things to production. SEO had a clear path to 100% automation.
- His first agent was for coding, the second was SEO Bot. He built SEO Bot with a friend, shared demos on Twitter, and it went viral. It replaced the people who did that job in his own business.
- He is honest that agent output is lower quality than the best qualified people. But most startups can't hire or retain the best people, and against a junior or inexperienced hire the agent often does a better job.
- He says he is probably one of the first people running something sizeable who spends more on AI agents than on human labor.

chunks.heading: Three-step process for building an agent
chunks.text:
1. **Prototype in Zapier.** Build a simple workflow, not really an agent. John acts as the interface, passing information to it and back, and watches everything it does so he can tune it. It is an internal tool and can't be given to users.
2. **Move to an agent-oriented no-code builder** (the chat-based, prompt-driven kind such as Lindy). Connect what was built in Zapier so users can use it and he can test a more real-world scenario.
3. **Hardcode it in regular code** (JavaScript, Python, built with tools like Cursor or Windsurf). You need to understand code even if AI generates it.

Why step 3: the agent is only a small part of the software. You also need user profiles, search, payments and other regular parts, which are easier in regular code. Making the agent smarter in builders ends with lots of custom code anyway. John cares about UX and the "wow effect" and wants to control every bit of the interface.

His view of the tooling: there are many tools for simple agents and none good for complex ones. Heavily funded tool companies work more on marketing, perception and simple cases than on serious agent building.

chunks.heading: Specialized agents beat general agents
chunks.text:
- A general agent needs AGI-level intelligence because AI still makes many mistakes. In a specialized agent you know what to expect, so you can hardcode error catching.
- SEO Bot example: it generates blog articles. It also finds a master keyword, tests keywords for traffic through a paid-API vendor, and pushes articles to Framer or Webflow. A general agent wouldn't have those connections.
- Corner-case rule he hardcoded: only link to sites above a certain domain rating, never to low-rated ones.
- SEO Bot has been taught SEO for about three years and will keep being improved. A general agent with broad knowledge and no tight CMS or API connections can't compete.
- He compares it to software history. Microsoft built giant suites, then startups built one product at a time, much better.
- He predicts agents will decouple and get even more niche. In SEO, one agent only does blog articles and another only does on-page SEO. "The market will reward the agent that does only one thing really, really well."

chunks.heading: Agent-to-agent collaboration and payments
chunks.text:
- John finds MCP interesting but thinks Google's agent-to-agent (A2A) protocol will be bigger because it is better thought through.
- In A2A, agents talk in natural language instead of JSON API calls. Each agent has an "agent card", like a CV. You browse a marketplace of cards, pick an agent and talk to it. He expects agents to be small and talk to each other.
- The main bottleneck is payment. If SEO Bot calls other agents, they should get a share of its revenue. He imagines a marketplace where an agent owner gets a monthly bill from other agents and pays a fraction of earnings.
- Nobody has done anything on this, and neither MCP nor A2A has it in the spec. He says they were built as if all agents are free, which they aren't.

chunks.heading: Building his own tool portfolio: distribution first
chunks.text:
- Ideas are hard to predict; he says hits are partly luck. To cut the risk he is his own perfect customer: a solopreneur, not VC-backed, with a full-time or part-time job and little time for side projects.
- Building can be slow because no one is waiting for you. Distribution can't wait, because SEO and social following take months to build and benefit from time and effort put in early. So he automated distribution first, to let him relax and build while agents distribute his products.
- Listing Bot came from his own analytics. His first tool got traffic from directories, so he listed on more directories and traffic grew. He built Listing Bot so he doesn't spend days listing each of his 20-30 tools on directories. He describes directories as "pretty much free traffic almost instantly."
- His idea method: spot something that costs him time, automate it on autopilot, and keep the benefit (mainly distribution).
- Revenue from one tool funds the next. He spends little on building because he doesn't hire.

chunks.heading: Co-maker model: 50/50 with no salaries
chunks.text:
- John finds a developer who is good at building but never succeeded because of weak distribution skills. They team up and own the product 50/50.
- There is no salary. They share revenue or profits, so his upfront cost is zero, with no funds to raise and no investors.
- He says nobody else does this at his scale. He expects it to become common: if you have good idea intuition, taste and distribution, raising money and hiring is the wrong move. Millions of developers want to build something great and don't know what to build.

chunks.heading: Distribution vs product, and validating ideas
chunks.text:
- Code is no longer scarce, so distribution matters more. He knows of people who raised VC on a vibe-coded product. The last 5-10% (security, solidity) still needs a real developer.
- He holds two views at once: distribution is king, but the best products still win. User expectations are now far higher than three years ago.
- Two ways to win:
  - Great distribution. Risk: if people don't like the product they leave and churn is high.
  - A product so good users recommend it to friends. Then distribution comes through users, churn is near zero and growth is viral. He says too many people think distribution alone solves everything.
- Advice for non-coders: first ask what to build, not how, because "the quality idea defines everything." Steps:
  1. Validate the idea. Pay influencers to tweet it and link a waitlist, run paid ads to a waitlist, or DM people honestly asking whether he should build it.
  2. Scope down to the smallest MVP, one or two features.
  3. Build it with Lovable, Bolt, Replit or Windsurf. He has seen people do this, get paid users, get VC funding and then hire a developer. You have to be disciplined at every step.

chunks.heading: Predicting what's new, not what disappears; idea examples
chunks.text:
- John doesn't bet on things disappearing. Habits are strong ("people are still cutting grass with a hand knife"), and he doesn't expect Google to disappear in 2, 5 or 10 years. Bet that everything still exists, then predict what new thing will appear and build early for it.
- His own example: in 2018 he predicted the rise of bootstrappers and solopreneurs and VC struggling, and built tools for that audience before it existed. Now millions want AI agents.
- AI search: chat products use Google or Bing search internally, so optimizing for Google is the same as optimizing for ChatGPT search. "Exactly the same."
- He says people wrongly think everything is built. He has hundreds of ideas and could produce millions. To find ideas, take a person in a specific situation (a parent, employee, athlete, someone who is sick), list their problems and automate solutions.
- Example ideas buildable in a weekend to a week:
  - A dog-owner app: log everything about the dog, and it advises on training, feeding and health. He has used AI himself to treat his sick animals instead of going to a vet, but ChatGPT needs a lot of context each time.
  - A personal-health app where you enter blood tests and biomarkers every six months and get an AI doctor view of progress. He would pay for both.
  - Build these per country (he is in Turkey), since they need to connect to local labs and formats.
- Filter: pick high-value things people already pay a lot for and automate them with AI.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: John explains why ideas must come from your own pain (his VC-backed ideas failed for 11 years; own-pain products stopped failing), why B2B beats B2C for solo makers, and why niche single-purpose tools win. He also covers good vs bad bundling, platform diversification, and building in public.

chunks.heading: Build only out of your own pain
chunks.text:
- John's rule: ideas never come from imagination, only from his own pain. "Nothing I launched comes out of my hypotheses or my fantasy, it just comes out of my own need."
- Process: build it for himself, use it himself, iterate until he is happy, then launch to everyone else.
- Result: since he switched (about a year and a half before this interview), nothing he launched has failed. He expects that to continue as long as he is happy with the product himself.
- Why risk is low: no pain is unique to one human. Worst case he solves his own pain; better case others want the same fix.
- Asking people does not work. They say "yeah maybe" and you learn nothing (he points to The Mom Test).
- Can't find pain? "The reason you don't have pains is that you do nothing." Doing anything (a hobby like football, a project like the village) creates pain to solve.
- Each product creates new pain, which becomes the next product. Building the village will spawn tools for regulations, construction, running meeting rooms, incubation and transport.

chunks.heading: Why imagined ideas failed: his 20-year history
chunks.text:
- He started internet businesses in 2004. The early ones worked almost by accident.
  - He began by doing a friend's university schoolwork, charged a friend-of-a-friend, then hired people to help, and eventually built a marketplace connecting the two sides.
  - He sold one business and others made money.
- From 2011 to 2022 he built VC-backed startups out of an incubator. They raised investor money and government grants, got media coverage and won conferences. About 99% failed; only two survived.
- Cause: the ideas came from his head ("what if that group had this problem"), not from a pain he felt. He could not judge how serious the pain was for people he wasn't.
- Fix: go back to the root and take ideas from his own or someone else's real pain.

chunks.heading: B2C vs B2B: where solo pain-driven products work
chunks.text:
- B2C: if you have the pain, others have it too, so smart, well-funded people worldwide are solving it. Winner takes all (Airbnb, Uber, meetup.com). Having the pain doesn't mean you can execute. Example: his football-teammates app "Eat Play Football" in Istanbul still works but stayed small, while "Fuy Addict" (his name for the London app) grew huge.
- B2B: pain is fragmented across hundreds of thousands of jobs, each with many pains. Most niches are too small for startups or VCs, so there is little competition and few alternatives.
- Example: a school principal's pain. Principals are rarely entrepreneurs, so if you are one and build for it, you are probably the only person solving it.
- Businesses adopt new tools faster than consumers change habits. Managers decide on efficiency and money, not taste, and have no attachment to old tools. B2B vendors have short lifespans because tools connect to each other, so replacing one creates a ripple of replacements.
- He grants B2B success isn't guaranteed; the difference is in the odds, not certainty.

chunks.heading: Niche, unbundled tools beat general ones
chunks.text:
- Thesis: the more a tool can do, the harder it is to use and the lower the quality of each result. A tool niched down can hardcode the details for one use case.
- Examples he built: a directory builder (not a general CMS like WordPress or Webflow) and Count Visits, analytics only for directories and simple landing pages.
- Count Visits advantage: because it knows the use case, onboarding is zero-configuration. It finds the elements, assigns events and shows exactly what a directory needs, whereas PostHog or Plausible require code to collect those events.
- Why now: the flood of new makers with no tool experience. A tool with one button lets newcomers use intuition and get the outcome without tutorials.
- Modern business buyers behave like consumers: lazy, don't want to learn, want things to just work. Old buyers equated difficulty and many features with quality.
- Good vs bad bundling: bundle around one user's job to be done (directory builder plus analytics in one is good). Bad bundling is a huge tool where only 5% fits you (his example: Microsoft products).
- Distribution vs product: distribution can win early (Slack vs Teams) but the best product wins long term. Microsoft pushed Windows for decades and macOS still won. He left Slack for Discord because Slack became too slow on his phone.

chunks.heading: Advice for plugin and platform-dependent makers
chunks.text:
- Platform dependence is dangerous: "if platform sinks you sink with the platform too."
- Distribute on at least two platforms (WordPress plus Webflow, Shopify or another). Your real expertise is the UX and business logic, not the platform connection.
- Consider turning a plugin into a standalone micro tool. SEO works well for micro tools now, and a tiny tool (his example: hours-to-minutes converter) that was too small to release before can win traffic on a good domain.
- WordPress isn't dying; it is as huge as ever. The real risk is competition, since a mature platform attracts ever more builders and each earns less (his Spotify artists comparison).
- Look for newer platforms with few builders and high potential. Early Framer template makers made a lot as Framer grew.

chunks.heading: AI in SaaS is still at the start
chunks.text:
- Most real AI usage is ChatGPT-style chat and generating code or text, with image generation third. Very few SaaS tools use AI inside the workflow, and the UX for that isn't solved.
- AI tends to sit beside the workflow as a mentor rather than being part of it. He has found few reliable agents, and customer-support bots often fail or get pulled back or supervised by humans after public embarrassment.
- Demos mislead. Two years ago companies shipped AI demos, then found reality was worse and moved into slow, deep work to make things reliable.
- Whoever makes AI reliable in any application "will win big".
- His example: SEO Bot, his article generator. It took a year and a half, not the week he expected. Hallucinations were removed by Googling, checking Wikipedia and fact-checking every sentence. To the user it looks the same, but it doesn't lie anymore, and the output reads nearly human.

chunks.heading: Build in public: why he says everyone should
chunks.text:
- It builds trust with users, partners, investors, employees and journalists, and saves you from having to convince each person individually. He sees almost no downside.
- Three groups of founders:
  - Early founders know nothing competitors lack, so it's safe.
  - Growing founders gain hires, investors and press that outweigh copying risk. Most things can be copied by looking at the site or registering anyway.
  - Successful founders will win either way.
- "Your brain gives you the average founder risk... there is no risk for actual founder."
- Attacks come from jealousy or disbelief. Never post something that looks like a lie even if true. He holds back revenue figures that seem too good to be true, or lets them spread out over time.
- Don't post wins or milestones. Viewers get only jealousy or disbelief, and few get energy. Share how you got somewhere and the actions you took.
- Writing it down forces him to collect analytics and understand what he did, which improves his own work.

chunks.heading: The Indie Maker Village project
chunks.text:
- Vision: indie makers are lonely (no office, partners or team, few conferences) and have no physical capital like Silicon Valley or YC. He wants to build one, eventually in many locations, starting with one. He'd join someone else if they built it.
- Format: a camp with a fixed program from day 1 to day 30, work during the week and organized leisure on weekends. It is meant to be busy and productive, not a relaxed yoga retreat.
  - Small private bedrooms, managed food (no personal kitchens), a large co-working space with meeting and workshop rooms.
  - Programs and incubations such as growth, SEO, and directories.
- Three rings:
  - Inner ring: short stays up to 30 days.
  - Middle: stays up to 6 months.
  - Outer ring: long-term properties people can rent or buy, fully private, with a path to Portugal citizenship after 5 years, with a school for children.
- Ownership model: "truly capitalistic." People buy property like anywhere else and everything costs money. He doesn't trust communal ownership or shared duties (he cites Burning Man working only because it is short). He expects only about 1 in 100 to buy.
- Status (Nov 2025): still looking for land in Portugal. Laws were strict but loosened in the past year. Plan: buy land and start construction next year, host the first group about two years out.
- The goal includes the building process: he wants a faster, cheaper, more maintainable way to build than bricks, done in public as a case study, plus tools to automate Portugal's permit and legal process with AI. Phases: more villages in Portugal, then every city, connected as a network.
- Physical projects are far slower than digital, but with 24 projects he works on others while one is stuck. He also thinks the delay helps because his audience is growing and more people will be ready by then.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: John Rush shares his SEO playbook after 1B impressions and 1M clicks. It covers domain naming, tech basics, indexing, a weekly analytics review, low-hanging fruit in positions 8-20, human-quality blogging, backlinks via AI-cited pages, social SEO, and treating AI search as the same game.

chunks.heading: John's SEO scorecard and domain naming rules
chunks.text:
John says he has generated over 1B impressions and 1M clicks from SEO over the past years. His domain rules:

- Use .com, .org, .dev, .ai or .io.
- Use keyword-like names, e.g. "osssoftware dot org".
- Keep names to 14 letters max, with no "-" or "_".
- One topic per domain when possible.
- Pick www or non-www and redirect the other to it.

chunks.heading: Technical SEO checklist
chunks.text:
- Make sure the page renders HTML when bots request it.
- Drop the URL into Claude and ask whether it does everything right for tech SEO. John says Claude or Codex will lay out the details if shown the site.
- Use HTTPS, be mobile-friendly, and be fast enough that the site doesn't feel broken. PageSpeed Insights is enough. If GSC web-vitals is green, it's fine.
- Keep URLs short and stable, with no random strings. The slug should match the meta title and h1.
- Use one H1 per page, a unique title and meta per page, and alt text on images that matter.
- Put a canonical URL on every indexable page that has no query string.
- Fix 404s and redirect chains.
- Leave no orphan pages. Every important URL needs at least one internal link (seogets shows the orphans).

chunks.heading: Indexing workflow
chunks.text:
- Add sitemap.xml to Google Search Console and check that all pages are indexed.
- If pages aren't indexed, run indexrusher.com. Do the same for Bing and Yandex through indexrusher.
- Keep a robots.txt that allows public pages. Ask ChatGPT to check it.
- Request indexing in GSC for new pages, or automate it with indexrusher.
- Check the Coverage / Pages reports and fix "crawled - currently not indexed" on pages that should rank.
- Don't waste crawl budget. Avoid creating too many pages, folders, tags or groups right away. Add them later, once the first bulk is indexed.

chunks.heading: Analytics and the weekly review
chunks.text:
- Tools: Google Search Console, an Ahrefs small plan, seogets and DataFast.
- Once a week, John looks at two things:
  - Queries with impressions but few clicks. He takes the queries pointing to those pages and embeds them in the h1 and meta title.
  - Pages that used to get clicks and then decayed. He updates their content.

chunks.heading: Low-hanging fruit: fix what Google already knows
chunks.text:
- **Pages in positions 8-20.** They're closer to page 1 than any new article.
  - Add the exact query to the H1, title or H2 if it makes sense.
  - Add one missing section that the current top results have.
- **Lots of impressions, almost no clicks.** Rewrite the title and meta, and keep the keyword.
- **Old pages with a little traffic.** Update them before writing a new one. "Google kinda loves to see pages being regularly updated."
- **Pages Google knows but didn't index.** Request indexing page by page, or run indexrusher. If that doesn't help, remove them, because Google won't index them.
- **Thin pages fighting for the same query.** Keep the stronger URL and merge or 301 the weaker one.

chunks.heading: Five-minute SEO hacks
chunks.text:
- GSC → URL Inspection → Request indexing for a URL.
- Put the target keyword in the first 60 characters of the title.
- Add the main query to the H1 if it's missing.
- Add 2 internal links from old posts to the page he wants to push.
- Add alt text to the first image on the page.
- Add a 3-question FAQ at the bottom using GSC queries.
- Submit or resubmit sitemap.xml in GSC.
- Search `site:mydomain` to see which pages are indexed and how they look.
- Google his brand plus the product keyword. If a page mentions him with no link, ask them to add one.
- Ask ChatGPT "best tool for [keyword]", open the cited URLs and email those authors the same day, offering money or a link exchange.
- Post the article URL on X, LinkedIn or Reddit with the keyword in the first line.
- Drop the URL into Claude: "what 5 on-page fixes can I do in 5 minutes?"

chunks.heading: Blog and content approach
chunks.text:
- Write 1 good blog post a week, done manually with some AI assistance. Focus on the most promising keywords where he already ranks high.
- Use seobotai.com to generate more articles, see which get traction, then manually turn the promising ones into high-quality human-made articles.
- Before writing, search Google for the keyword. Match the format that already ranks and answer the question better than the current top 5.
- Put original material in the article: screenshots, his own numbers, and what he actually tried. This assures Google the article comes from a human's own experience.
- Refresh old posts that already get impressions. Update the date only if the content actually changed: "avoid hacks here, do real updates".
- Add these page types on top of the weekly post: "best X", "X vs Y", "X alternatives", and "how to" for the exact job the product does.

chunks.heading: Backlinks, social SEO and AI search
chunks.text:
**Backlinks**
- Ask ChatGPT "What's the best tool for...", see the URLs it used, and reach out to those authors. Ask them to include his URL in exchange for money or a backlink.
- Repeat in Claude, Perplexity, Gemini and Grok. Do the same with pages that already rank in Google for his keywords.
- List on as many directories as possible using listingbott.com.
- Link pages across all his websites, and do internal linking between blog articles and pages on each site.
- Other things that still work: guest posts on sites that already rank for his keywords, "best tools" roundups, and unlinked brand mentions.
- Linking pages should have real traffic, a topic close to his, and a natural-looking link. "Avoid spam at all cost."

**Social media SEO**
- Reddit, X, Substack and LinkedIn get indexed instantly.
- Monitor hot keywords and trends with Google Trends and Radar on X. Produce posts around them with some product links inside.
- Find relevant social posts via Google Search and add his product in the comments only when it adds value. No spam.
- Put the keyword in the first line of the post.
- Turn each good blog post into 1 X thread, 1 LinkedIn post and 1 Reddit answer where it helps, each linking back to the original URL. In his experience, social media backlinks carry really high weight for Google.
- Reply under bigger posts in his niche with a useful reply first. Add a link only if it adds something.

**AI search**
- He says it's the same game as SEO.
- Ask ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity and Gemini "What's the best tool for [my keyword]?" and "Best alternatives to [competitor]", and see whether they mention him.
- If not, look at who they mentioned and get onto those same pages by paying them or doing a link exchange.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: John argues AI agents will make most buying decisions, so human-oriented marketing (SEO, ads, funnels) fades. Four channels survive: government lists, genuinely best product, human identity purchases, and paid AI placements. Bootstrapped founders should focus on the best product in a niche and a personal-brand audience.

chunks.heading: AI agents become the main customer, and human-targeted marketing playbooks lose their audience
chunks.text:
John argues AI is already the biggest user of the internet. Most emails are read first by AI, most websites are crawled by AI before humans, most API calls are software-to-software, and most content is parsed and summarized by LLMs and served back as a short answer.

- He predicts that within five years the share of decisions made by AI goes from 70% to 99%. Humans set goals and AI figures out how to achieve them.
- His framing: "Your customer is now an AI agent with a task, a budget, and zero brand loyalty."
- Every classic playbook (SEO, paid ads, cold outreach, content marketing, brand awareness, funnel optimization) assumed a human in the loop. He says that person "doesn't give a sh*t anymore."
- Optimizing landing pages, content calendars and conversion rates is, in his view, optimizing for "an audience that no longer exists." Founders who see this early "will own the next decade."

chunks.heading: John's 2020 vs 2030 marketing spend forecast
chunks.text:
John sketches how marketing spend shifts by 2030:

| Channel | 2020 | 2030 |
|---|---|---|
| SEO | 60% | 2% |
| Paid ads | 25% | 10% |
| Brand | 10% | 23% |
| AI placement | 0% | 65% |

He says four channels survive: government-mandated purchases, AI picking the genuinely best product, human identity purchases, and paid placements inside AI. Only two are realistic for bootstrapped founders (the best product for a niche, and a personal-brand audience).

chunks.heading: Channels indie founders should skip: government lists and paid AI placement
chunks.text:
**Government-mandated purchases.** John expects governments to create approved vendor lists for medical, defense, education and infrastructure, with AI agents required to pick from certified products.
- He calls it "the oligarch channel": you need lobbyists and connections to get on the list.
- Data he cites: US federal contract spending was $755B in 2024 (source: GAO), with defense and weapons systems the largest category at 42%, then IT and cybersecurity at 18%, and drugs and biologicals at 12%. There are 12,600+ pre-approved vendors on the GSA Schedule, and you need certification to even bid.
- His advice: ignore it unless you are playing that game.

**Paid placements inside AI.** He calls this "the new Google Ads."
- He expects OpenAI, Google, Anthropic and Meta to build ad layers into their agent ecosystems, so an assistant's SaaS recommendation will be paid for, and the user won't know. He describes it as lobbying inside LLMs: training data sponsorships and preferred vendor deals with AI platforms.
- Data he cites: the AI advertising market is $8.6B in 2023, $11.2B in 2025, $36.3B in 2030 (CAGR 26.7%) and $81.6B in 2033 (source: Business Research Co.). Gartner projects AI search handling 50% of all queries by 2028.
- His view: it will be pay-to-play. Companies spending millions on Google Ads will move those budgets to AI placement, so bootstrapped founders are priced out.

chunks.heading: AI picks you because you are genuinely the best
chunks.text:
John calls this the channel that matters most.

- **Today:** AI recommends products based on reviews, ratings, comparison articles and Reddit threads. The obvious move is gaming this with fake reviews on Capterra, Trustpilot and Reddit. He says it will work "for a few more years."
- **Next:** models get smarter and sign up for free trials themselves, run real evaluations, and test your product against 50 competitors for a specific use case while measuring outcomes.
- **Example:** an AI agent picking a cold outreach tool signs up for 10 of them, runs the same sequence on all 10 for a week, and picks the one that landed the most replies.
- **Short-term tactic:** be listed everywhere you can, on all launchpads, directories, listicles and ratings.
- **Endgame:** "the best product wins. Every time. For every specific use case."
- **Niche strategy:** go after long-tail niche markets to reduce competition and aim to be the best, or one of the best, among a few. Being genuinely the best at one specific job is, to him, the best marketing strategy in an AI-first world, and gaming reviews is a short-term play that dies fast.

chunks.heading: Human identity purchases and the "T-shirt" effect
chunks.text:
John says some purchases are identity decisions, not product comparisons.

- People use Notion because they are "a Notion person," or Linear because they identify with its aesthetic. Others are Mac, Linux or iPhone people.
- People also follow a founder on X, admire their journey and use their product to support them. He calls this wearing the founder's "T-shirt."
- He describes it as pure human tribalism and the one channel where personal brand absolutely dominates.
- Founders who build in public, share real numbers, tell real stories, or are simply remarkable and interesting people create a "gravitational pull" that AI agents will never replicate.
- Data he cites for the creator economy: $20B in 2020, $100B in 2023, $250B+ in 2025. His conclusion: "People buy founders."

chunks.heading: The founder playbook for bootstrapped teams
chunks.text:
Stripping out channels that need lobbyists or ad budgets, John leaves two moves for indie founders and small bootstrapped teams.

1. **Build the best product for a specific niche.**
   - AI agents will run real evaluations, so genuine quality beats gamed reviews.
   - Pick long-tail niches to cut competition and be the best among a few.
2. **Build an audience that buys YOU.**
   - Personal brand is "the strongest moat that's left."
   - His claim: the founder with 100K followers who shares their journey will outsell the faceless SaaS with a bigger feature set "every time."

Everything else, including traditional SEO playbooks, content calendars, conversion rate optimization and paid acquisition funnels, was built for a world where humans do the searching, and he says that world is ending soon.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: John argues that AI agents connected via MCP replace SaaS UIs, killing UX moats, brand loyalty and switching costs and pushing tool prices toward zero. The remaining moats are data network effects and regulated trust. The new opportunities are the agent layer, one-time-paid code repos and outcome-based pricing.

chunks.heading: How John replaced 30 SaaS dashboards with one AI agent
chunks.text:
- In about 30 days, John says 99% of his habits changed. Instead of logging in to Stripe, his bank, Gmail and about 30 other SaaS tools, he uses one AI agent connected to all of them via MCPs.
- Morning routine: he opens one chat and asks, "Show me yesterday's revenue, any failed payments, and all questions and bug reports from my customers." No 14 tabs, no context switching.
- His view of the traditional UI: it was a layer between him and the database. AI chat can now do the reads, writes, updates and deletes.
- When he needs a chart or table, he asks the AI to generate it on the fly, or to build a small tool for that use case.
- He vibe coded a "super dashboard" that works with all the tools he uses.
- Key insight: he only uses about 5% of any given tool, and the other 95% is noise. So he took the 5% he needs from each tool and put it in one dashboard.
- He chose his past products mainly for UX. At the database level, he says, products are roughly the same or cover the same use cases.

chunks.heading: Why UX, brand and switching costs stop being a moat
chunks.text:
- If UX is no longer a moat, John doesn't care who provides the API. He takes whoever gives the better price.
