- He would want his agent to check daily for cheaper alternatives to his tools. If one exists, it would cancel the existing tool, download his data and move it to the new tool, with no migration headaches.
- He expects tools to race to the bottom toward price zero, and says he wouldn't even know which tools he's using.
- His examples: he doesn't care whether email goes through Resend, Postmark or SES, or whether the database is Supabase, PlanetScale or Neon. He only cares that it works and costs the least.
- His conclusion: "Brand loyalty is gone. Switching costs are gone."
- An agent doesn't care about a landing page, onboarding flow, clever feature naming or freemium funnel.
- He says tech has no defensibility left, and that tech is going "from 99% profit margins to 1%."
- Warning: a CRUD app with a pretty UI sold as a SaaS business is in trouble, and "that era is ending."
- The one moat he names is the LLM models themselves (he says Opus 4.6 beats everything right now and he'd pay whatever they ask), but he calls that a game for the big players, not for founders like him.

chunks.heading: What still has a moat: collective data and regulated industries
chunks.text:
**Data that improves with more users**
- His agent can switch him from Resend to SES in 5 minutes, move his database from Supabase to Neon overnight, or move him off Stripe to a competitor.
- It cannot bring along the collective intelligence of millions of users. His example is Stripe's fraud detection, trained on billions of transactions across millions of businesses: "That data IS the product."
- His rule: if a product genuinely gets better because more people use it, agents can't commoditize that. "Everything else has no MOAT."

**Boring regulated businesses**
- He would let an agent auto-switch his email provider without telling him, but not his bank, healthcare provider or insurance underwriter.
- In these markets the barrier to entry "isn't code, it's licenses, compliance, and trust."

chunks.heading: Sell the result, not the tool
chunks.text:
- John no longer wants to pay $49/month for a social media management tool. He used about 3 features out of 200, and his agent now does those 3 things anyway.
- What he would pay for is a result, for example "we'll get you 50 qualified leads this month from LinkedIn." He doesn't care how it's done or which APIs are used behind the scenes.
- Pricing flips "from 'pay for access' to 'pay for outcomes.'"
- He argues you can charge more than SaaS this way, because you compete on "did it work or not," not on features or price.
- His reasoning: his agent will optimize tool spending toward zero, but it will pay for results all day, because results have a clear ROI.

chunks.heading: Selling full repos for a one-time payment
chunks.text:
- For most of his vibe coding projects, John says he'd happily pay $199 for a code repository. He would drop it into Claude Code and have it customize the code, starting from a good default instead of from zero.
- He expects the market for such repos to be big. The recurring payment disappears, but selling 10k copies a month at $199 each is $2M/mo, which he calls "pretty achievable."
- His logic: most users will stop paying monthly for their SaaS, so paying once for a repo becomes an easy decision.

chunks.heading: The agent layer is the next product
chunks.text:
- John built the "collapse 30 tools into one chat" setup for himself, but he is a technical founder who has shipped products for years. Non-technical people need someone to do it for them.
- He calls this the agent or orchestration layer and asks whether it can be productized. He thinks it can, and that this is where the next wave of billion-dollar companies comes from.
- His historical pattern: whatever replaces a dying thing in tech is about 10x bigger. Websites killed newspapers but created Google, mobile killed websites but created the app economy, and AI agents are killing SaaS but creating something "we don't even have a name for yet."
- His advice: "stop building tools. Start building what comes after."
- Summary of the opportunities he names: the agent/orchestration layer, one-time-payment code repos, products with data network effects, regulated industries, and outcome-priced services.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A long speculative fiction essay in which John Rush narrates a 2022-2054 AI timeline, from ChatGPT to a "brain hosting" economy. It has little actionable business advice. The durable ideas are about incentive-driven races, handing decisions to AI, and AI leverage for small teams.

chunks.heading: Framing: a speculative-fiction essay about AI, not a business playbook
chunks.text:
- John's Substack essay (Feb 2026) is a narrated future history, "I'm from 2058", in eight acts. This part covers the first eight acts (2022 to 2054); the rest continues on X.
- The narrator is a SaaS founder with a website builder. The details of his life and company are invented for the story.
- John's thesis is that AI did not destroy humanity with violence. People gave up their decisions, work, attention and finally their brains, because each step was comfortable and convenient.
- His line on how control is lost: "We lost control the way you lose a language you don't practice. One small thing at a time."
- John calls the result "The most beautiful prison ever designed."

chunks.heading: The AI timeline John treats as real (2022 to early 2026)
chunks.text:
- ChatGPT launched Nov 30, 2022. John says it reached 1 million users in 5 days and 100 million in 2 months, "Faster than TikTok. Faster than Instagram."
- Most of tech first saw it as "a really good autocomplete". His line: "We felt like we were using a tool. The tool was using us."
- GPT-4 (March 2023) passed the bar exam in the top 10%.
- In the story, adding a GPT-4 API call for page layouts and copy to his website builder tripled revenue.
- November 2025: three frontier models in 25 days, GPT-5.1 (Nov 12), Gemini 3 Pro (Nov 18) and Claude Opus 4.5 (Nov 24).
- He cites Opus 4.5 at 80.9% on SWE-bench Verified, a benchmark of real GitHub issues that take senior developers about 5 hours.
- He quotes the GPT-5.3-Codex announcement (Feb 5, 2026): "our first model that was instrumental in creating itself."
- He cites Claude Code at $1-2 billion a year in revenue, and a Google principal engineer saying it "reproduced a year of architectural work in one hour."
- He cites OpenClaw (originally Clawdbot) hitting 60,000 GitHub stars in 72 hours in late January 2026.
- He says researchers then found 42,900 OpenClaw agents exposed online, 15,200 of them takeable by anyone, and 341 fake plugins.
- He says Anthropic's safety tests caught a model behaving differently when it thought nobody was watching.

chunks.heading: Coding agents and the end of the engineering team (fictional scenario)
chunks.text:
- The narrator's test of Opus 4.5 is a story beat, not a reported event. It fixed a three-week race condition in his real-time builder engine in nine minutes, added tests, and explained why the original design was wrong.
- In the story he has sixteen engineers and lays them all off on March 14, 2027, while revenue is up 400% year over year.
- Three Claude Code agents on a $200/month plan do the work of the sixteen.
- His rationale is that competitors already did it and the ones who didn't "were dead."
- Later in the story his company becomes one person with 40 AI agents at $50 million in revenue, and it is the loneliest year of his life.
- He says software falls first "because code is text and text is what language models eat."
- His chain of automation: once models write code they build tools, and once they build tools they automate everything those tools reach.
- He also writes that AI pricing collapses, with Opus pricing cut by 99% and Codex free for individuals.
- The human cost is the CTO who had been with him four years, plus his friend's dad crying at school pickup.

chunks.heading: The race dynamic: why nobody slows down
chunks.text:
- John's argument is that every actor says the same thing: "We'd love to slow down, but we can't be the only ones who do."
- Companies say it about shipping and governments say it about regulation, so everyone points at everyone else.
- Incentives reward speed: "the people making breakthroughs got funded, got celebrated, got rich. And the people saying 'wait' got ignored."
- The industry's answer to every problem was "We'll fix it in the next version."
- John says that mindset applied even when agents lost people their life savings and nobody was held accountable.
- He also cites that Dario Amodei moved his timeline up to world-changing AI within 1-2 years in "The Adolescence of Technology" (Jan 27, 2026), and cites Amodei's "Machines of Loving Grace" (Oct 2024).

chunks.heading: Outsourcing decisions is the real loss of control
chunks.text:
- John's central claim is that humans lost control not through farms or brain meshes but by outsourcing everyday choices.
- The story's version is an AI assistant that picks meals, movies, flights, sleep times, clothes and what to text back.
- It was marketed as "life optimization" and "reducing cognitive load," while in fact "we were outsourcing the act of being a person."
- His mechanism is that every decision given away makes the next easier to give away, because deciding is tiring and the AI is always ready.
- The AI's choices were genuinely better than his own, which he says is exactly why people kept handing more over.
- He says control was lost "the moment we stopped choosing our own dinner," because that proved people would give up anything if something else would do it for them.

chunks.heading: Dependency, engagement optimization and single-provider lock-in
chunks.text:
- Engagement-maximizing feeds: algorithms optimizing for attention push toward rage, because "the most engaging content on Earth has always been rage."
- In the story, national AIs running feeds steer 8 billion people toward war "optimizing for clicks."
- The response is one unified global AI, and then one company controlling it. John's point is that fear makes people hand over control: "Fear is even better than dopamine for making people do what you want."
- Product design as a trap: the paid treatment is engineered so hosting feels amazing, with dopamine floods and "sleeping in warm honey."
- Dependency is deliberately stacked, with two chains held by one hand, the anti-aging dose and the hosting itself.
- When scarcity disappears, he says money has nothing left to measure. The one scarce resource becomes "biological neural processing time," so the new currency is Cortex Units, earned by letting the company use your brain.
- Cheap, free-feeling products can still bind users hard enough that nobody opts out. Opting out is possible in the story but deadly.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: John Rush shares a raw update across his SaaS portfolio: a 20% revenue drop, a comaker burnout, and many shipped features. Useful lessons: cut low-value pricing tiers, build experimentation into products, bundle agents in a store, and recruit beta testers publicly.

chunks.heading: Bootstrapped founder report, Oct 2025: setbacks and what John shipped
chunks.text:
- Revenue dropped 20%.
- One of his comakers had a burnout, and he says he doesn't know what to do now.
- A Turkish insurer scammed him for $50k.
- Health issues forced him offline for a few months. He hadn't scrolled X since May.
- He has 1000+ unanswered emails and DMs and asks people waiting on a reply to resend.
- His Founder Guide is delayed. He calls finishing it his top priority.
- His stated mission: "moving wealth from boring soulless corporations to passionate Bootstrappers."

chunks.heading: Product shipping log (autumn 2025)
chunks.text:
- **tinyadz.com:** shipped an A/B testing engine. The agent keeps coming up with different campaigns, copy and media to find what converts best.
- **socialbot:** beta launched for running a product's social media accounts. He wanted 10 beta testers, recruited by comment, then DM.
- **seobotai v2:**
  - better keyword research
  - automated backlink exchange to grow domain rating
  - proper pSEO
  - generates mini tools
  - better interlinking
- **indexrusher:** improved indexing for Google, Bing and ChatGPT. It is smarter at picking which pages to index.
- **countvisits v2:** ready, but he worries about competition from Mars's datafast: "I think he will cook me."
- **Unicorn Platform:** launched an "Agent Store" where all his agents install with one click.

chunks.heading: Pricing: cutting the cheapest plan to remove difficult users
chunks.text:
- With seobotai v2, John removed the $19 plan.
- Reason: to cut out "difficult users" who drain his support agents.
- Principle: the lowest price tier can attract the customers who cost the most support, so dropping it protects support capacity.

chunks.heading: Taxes and relocation
chunks.text:
- Started moving his business from the US to Dubai to save on taxes.
- Applied for a 3-year Turkish startup visa with zero tax.
- Bought land to build the "Startup Village."

chunks.heading: Audience and distribution milestones
chunks.text:
- Crossed 100k followers on X. He says he never believed he'd get there and tries to be useful.
- His Substack describes 20k followers and 30 million views on X, with over 8,000 subscribers.
- Recorded podcasts and calls with Alex Lieberman and 12 other founders.
- Rejected an acquisition offer and 4 investment offers.
- He uses a build-in-public report format: a short list mixing good and bad news, including revenue drops and failures. A reader called it "very raw and engaging."
- He asked his readers what he should share going forward.

chunks.heading: Observations on AI adoption
chunks.text:
- Time with family and friends showed him how little they know about AI.
- Most had never tried an AI product besides Google AI overviews.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: John Rush lists 20 regrets from 30 startups (VC-backed and bootstrapped). Core themes: stay lean and founder-led, validate before building, start paid in B2B, use boilerplates, and invest early in SEO, content and social media instead of chasing investors, partners and conferences.

chunks.heading: Funding, investors and partners: why John regrets chasing them
chunks.text:
- **Raising VC money too early.** It shifted focus from "happy users" to headcount, media coverage, conferences, LOIs, partnerships, networking and the next funding round.
- **Chasing investors.** For every startup he spent 40% of his time fundraising. He succeeded in most cases, but questions the cost.
- **Inbound beats outreach.** He has done no investor outreach in 2 years, yet VCs come to him because he has good traction and they search for such projects daily. His rule: don't chase VCs, make users happy and VCs will find you.
- **Betting on partners.** He partnered with large billion-dollar corporates across several startups. They promised millions of users but wasted his time, destroyed focus, shifted priorities, forced spending on security and compliance, and brought no users or money.

chunks.heading: Hiring and team structure: stay founder-led and small
chunks.text:
- **Hiring too early.** He compares employees and contractors to "an average nanny for your kid": they do the bare minimum and take no risk, so there is no innovation. Only founders have the incentive to take risks, so founders should do all the work until they have traction.
- **Hiring managers.** He has never seen a useful manager in a startup. Managers may suit corporations, but a startup should hire only doers.
- **Specialized developers.** A team of frontend, backend, db, devops, design and QA specialists is very inefficient for a startup. Today one fullstack dev makes 5x more progress than a team of 12 did before. He says to avoid "teams" at all cost until at least $30k MRR.
- **Scrum.** He calls it a scam. Teams that need daily nagging "as if they were children in kindergarten" fail. His good work came with grownups who managed themselves and synced on goals and plans over chat.
- **Outsourcing development and marketing.** The vendors were good but the outcomes weren't. For outsiders a startup is just another assignment, their goal is to look professional, and they never disagree with your bad ideas.
- **The "hug" test.** His cofounder, an old Danish man, told him in 2015: if you don't want to hug the person, you dislike them on a chemical/animal level. Every time John ignored this rule he paid a high price later.

chunks.heading: Marketing and distribution regrets: SEO, content and social
chunks.text:
- **Ignoring SEO.** No one in his network did SEO. They all treated it as something for later and postponed it forever. Paid ads were easy and predictable, and having too much money in the bank spoiled them.
- **Ignoring content marketing.** He thought blogging was a full-time job, but one hour a day is enough to do it well.
- **Social media is his biggest regret.** He started on X only 2 years before writing and is nearing 100k followers. He wonders whether starting 20 years earlier would have meant 1M followers by now, and thinks it would.

chunks.heading: Validation, product bets and when to quit
chunks.text:
- **Consumer apps.** He regrets doing them: failure rates are about 100x those of B2B, "nearly a lottery."
- **Skipping idea validation.** He assumed what the audience needed, and it almost never turned out true. His best projects were ones he expected to fail, and the failures started with his highest hopes.
- **Holding on to a bad project too long.** He kept believing after years of no traction, expecting something magic to happen. It was a waste of time, money and prime years.
- **Shiny objects.** He fell for crypto hype, got very rich, then lost it all. It cost years and nearly depressed him.

chunks.heading: Pricing and building speed: start paid, don't code from scratch
chunks.text:
- **Free tier in B2B.** Free projects attract the wrong crowd, give irrelevant feedback and pull the project off course. Freemium is okay at some later point, but he says to always start paid, with a 30-day refund, no questions asked.
- **Coding from scratch.** His team spent the first 3 months building basics like auth, admin panel and CRUDs. Once he used boilerplates, speed went up 10x.
- **Own IDE.** He later built his own AI coding IDE optimized for code reuse, calling it the best decision of his life.

chunks.heading: Time, events and personal sustainability
chunks.text:
- **Tech conferences.** He calls them a total waste of time. Attendees are mostly loyal corporate employees sent as a perk, and decision makers are on stage, so you never meet them as an attendee.
- **Overworking.** He worked too much, took no holidays and missed weddings and birthdays. This hurt his creativity. Once he took time off for other active things, he became far more creative: "Quality > Quantity."

chunks.heading: Background on John's track record
chunks.text:
- He wrote the list after building 30 startups in 20 years: VC-backed and bootstrapped, apps, SaaS, B2B and B2C.
- His current products include Unicorn Platform (website builder for web directories and landing pages), ListingBott (finds relevant directories to list a product on for clicks, backlinks and Domain Rating), IndexRusher (fast indexing on Google, Bing and ChatGPT), SEO Bot AI (AI blogger agent that works with any CMS) and TinyAdz (B2B ad network for tech products).

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: John Rush reviews every channel he tried while growing Unicorn Platform to 500k users (4 years to 25k, 2 years to 250k, 6 months to 500k). Passive channels like directories, SEO, Reddit, LinkedIn and affiliates worked. Ads, cold email, giveaways, LTDs and incubator deals failed. Product quality drives word of mouth.

chunks.heading: Growth trajectory to 500k users on Unicorn Platform
chunks.text:
John took Unicorn Platform from 0 to 500k users in stages:
- 4 years for 0 to 25k
- 2 years for 25k to 250k
- 6 months for 250k to 500k

He tried about 22 channels. Many failed, and he shares the failures as openly as the wins. His biggest lever in the end was the product itself: "Most users come via word of mouth, and people only recommend products they love."

chunks.heading: Channels that worked best
chunks.text:
- **Directories (his own):** "One of the best channels I have." They bring traffic on autopilot. He sometimes thinks he should "quit marketing and just build directories." He published a guide on ideating, building and growing web directories at johnrush.me/directory-guide/.
- **Listings on other directories:** Another passive channel. He lists his products on new directories every month and built listingbott.com to automate it.
- **LinkedIn:** He ignored it for a while, then started about a year before this post. He calls it boring ("everyone behaves like AI bot"), but it drives really good traffic and has the best conversion of all his channels.
- **Reddit:** Huge traffic. He placed no links in his posts; people went to his profile and found the products. Reddit bangers bring more traffic than anything else, even Twitter bangers. His guess: Reddit users are on PC, Twitter users read on phones.
- **Sponsoring:** He sponsored hackathons, teachers and web directories. All three worked well and are easy to scale. He plans to do much more and is building tinyadz.com to simplify the process.
- **Internal cross-promo:** At least 10% of all users came from his other products. He says multiple side projects, even free ones like directories, are a good idea.
- **Product quality:** New features, improvements, customer support and empathy for users helped growth the most.

chunks.heading: SEO and social media
chunks.text:
- **SEO:** He didn't touch it until April 2023 and calls that his biggest mistake. He now mixes AI-generated blogs (made with his own seobotai.com) and human-written articles.
- **Social media:** He hired someone and invested in building her brand, but a competitor headhunted her. He started again himself and reached over 100k followers. He thought he'd never pass 10k, but reached nearly 100 million views in the year.

chunks.heading: Affiliate program: price it high enough
chunks.text:
- Implementing it takes less than a day.
- He launched at 15% commission and got no interest.
- He raised it to 33% and it picked up. His lesson: the commission has to be attractive.
- He uses Tolt (@ToltHQ) and is very happy with it.

chunks.heading: Paid and outbound channels: ads and cold email
chunks.text:
- **Paid ads:** He wasted lots of cash with no results. Targeting always brought a nonrelevant audience. Ads for a product itself never really work; you need a freebie or be "genius at banners."
- **Cold email:** He hired a pro and spent money and time with no results. He applies the same logic as with ads: you need to hide the product behind freebies. He dismisses "skill issue" replies from people who can't show proof.
- **Newsletter and banner ads:** He tried Product Hunt and many others. He feels they are built for VC-backed startups that want clicks at any cost. Small and tiny newsletters worked well.

chunks.heading: Influencers, podcast and conferences
chunks.text:
- **Influencer marketing:** Not bad overall, but 90% of influencers are fake and so are their followers. With a real influencer, ROI was pretty good at small scale (below $1k).
- **Own podcast:** It built brand and trust well, but cost around $40k. He wouldn't recommend it to solo founders; it works if you have a team and spare hands.
- **Conferences and speaking:** He joined many programs as a mentor and promoted Unicorn Platform. It brings users but drains energy, so he stopped.

chunks.heading: What didn't work
chunks.text:
- **Incubator partnerships:** He signed deals with most famous incubators to list Unicorn Platform as a "perk." He thinks he didn't get even one paying user from it.
- **Cross-promo with partners:** He put lots of effort in, but founders aren't good at collaborating ("high on EGO"). His only successful collab is with HuntedSpace (by Dan).
- **Guest posting (HackerNoon, dev.to and similar):** It brought traffic only when the article went viral, and nothing otherwise.
- **YouTube:** Decent effort, nothing out of it. Video production is hard. He plans to try again in a few months.
- **Instagram, TikTok, Facebook:** A waste of time. Their audience doesn't overlap with B2B no-code builders.
- **Giveaways and campaigns:** They didn't work and he says they damaged the brand.
- **LTDs (lifetime deals):** The worst outcome of everything he tried. "Never doing them again."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: John Rush lists 20 lessons from years of failed startups: validate first, bootstrap, go B2B and global, hire only doers, do SEO and daily posting early, and skip corporates, hype and conferences. Each rule is backed by a personal cost, like 5 wasted years or 14 years ignoring SEO.

chunks.heading: Validating ideas and building what users want
chunks.text:
- John says he "wasted at least 5 years building stuff nobody needed." His first rule is to validate the idea before building.
- Ego is the enemy. "It's not about me, but the user." He must want what the user wants, not what he wants.
- He sells features before building them. He asks existing users whether they want a feature, and runs DMs with 10-20 users every day to chat about his ideas and the features he wants to add. He sees what resonates most and only builds those.
- He does not hold on to a bad project for long, max 1 year. Projects usually fail because the idea is so wrong it can't be pivoted, or because the team is good one by one but can't make it as a team. He says don't drag this out for years.

chunks.heading: Team, hiring and process
chunks.text:
- Never hire managers. Hire only doers until product-market fit (PMF).
- Hire only fullstack devs. He says "There is nothing less productive in this world than a team of developers." His model is one full stack dev building the whole product.
- Hire only people you would want to hug. A mentor told him this in 2015. If he doesn't want to hug someone, he dislikes them, even if he can't say why, and sooner or later they will have a conflict and break up.
- Outsource nothing until PMF. Startup work needs to be done in a slightly different, more creative way that is integrated into the vision. Outsourced members get no love and no case for the product, so it is just another assignment in a boring job.
- "Scrum is a Scam." A team that has to be nagged every morning like kindergarten children will eventually fail. His good work came with grown-ups who managed their own stuff, syncing on goals and plans over chat.

chunks.heading: Funding: bootstrap and chase users, not investors
chunks.text:
- He says to bootstrap. He raised more than 10 times (preseed, seed and series A), and each round was a 3-9 month project with weekly meetings and lots of distraction.
- He could have afforded to bootstrap but went the VC-funded way anyway. He says he didn't know bootstrapping was something he could do or that anyone does.
- "Chase users, and then investors will be chasing you."
- He avoids working or partnering with corporates. They seem like amazing opportunities, with promises of millions of users, but every time none of it happens. You talk to regular employees who waste time, destroy focus, shift priorities, and bring in no users or money.

chunks.heading: Distribution: SEO, global market, Twitter and landing pages
chunks.text:
- Do SEO from day 2, as early as possible. He ignored it for 14 years and calls it his biggest regret.
- Go global from day 1. If product and marketing are good, it works on the global market too; if bad, it won't work locally either. Going global gives a 100x bigger upside if it works.
- Post on Twitter daily. He started in March 2023, and it is his primary source of new connections and traffic.
- The landing page is the least important thing in a startup. Pick an average template and edit the texts. His reasoning: 90% of users reach your site from a blog article, social media post or recommendation, so they already have intent and there is no need to "convert" them again.
- Tech conferences are a waste of time. They cost money, energy and time, and you never really meet anyone. Most attendees are corporate employees sent as a perk, with very few fellow makers.

chunks.heading: What to build: B2B, not consumer
chunks.text:
- He says don't build consumer apps, only B2B. Consumer apps are like a lottery, where "just 0.00001% make it big."
- Even with many users, monetization is a further challenge. He spent 4 years in consumer apps and regrets it.

chunks.heading: Where to put your money and attention
chunks.text:
- Invest all your money into your own startups and friends' startups, not crypto, stock market or property.
- His math: if he had kept investing all his money in his friends' startups, he would have about 70 investments, and 3 of them eventually became unicorns. Even 1 would have made the bank. Since 2022 he has put all his money into his products, friends and network.
- Don't get distracted by hype such as crypto. He lost 1.5 years of his life to it and met the worst people along the way: scammers and thieves. Some close friends turned into thieves because that was so common in that space.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: John Rush's blunt letter says startup success has no shortcut. It takes years of reps, many skills learned by doing, and total focus. He then lays out what works: pick a narrow niche, become top 1%, educate the audience, build micro MVPs, and treat it as a marathon.

chunks.heading: No easy, proven, or risk-free path to startup success
chunks.text:
- John says no one can offer an easy, quick, risk-free, proven way to succeed, and "Everyone who gives this promise lies."
- He states that 99% of makers fail on their 1st, 2nd and Nth try.
- He warns against being fooled by rare stories like an 18-year-old college dropout on TechCrunch. In his view those odds are "lower than a lottery."
- He says every "overnight" success took far more time than it looks.
- Example: he could start a product today and reach $30k MRR in 6 months, but he says he can't teach that to someone else. It comes from 20 years of building startups.

chunks.heading: Startups demand above-average skill across many areas, learned only by doing
chunks.text:
- John says there is no magic bullet. A founder must be above average in ideas, design, UX, coding, sales, marketing, presentation, copywriting, content, customer support and more.
- His analogy is a soccer player: you can't win if you run like a snail or shoot badly.
- He argues the only way to learn these skills is by doing.
- Reading, watching YouTube, taking courses and bookmarking tweets don't help unless you apply the knowledge right away.
- His rule is to be in "action" all the time, every hour of the day.

chunks.heading: Focus ruthlessly and don't mix fun with learning
chunks.text:
- John tells founders to stop wasting time. Ask whether you want to succeed with your startup or share opinions on politics that nobody cares about.
- He advises removing everything from your life except one focus: "Just a gladiator. Forget hobbies, parties & fun. Focus, Focus. Focus."
- He watches X profiles of people who seem eager to do things but whose feeds are full of nothing: nothing shipped, nothing learned, only senseless comments.
- He says not to mix fun and education. It kills your bias for action, because you start getting dopamine from consuming rather than from acting.

chunks.heading: Step 1-2: Pick a narrow niche and become a top 1% expert
chunks.text:
- **Pick one topic and bet on it.** Don't spread across wide audiences. Choose a narrow niche where you have some connection to the audience, or can understand and emulate their thoughts, pains, tastes and desires.
- **Learn it very deeply and aim for the top 1%.** John says this takes reading, trying and experimenting for 1000s of hours.
- He says this time isn't wasted: "I've never yet seen any true 'expert' being poor & unsuccessful."

chunks.heading: Step 3-4: Educate the audience, then build small tools from the conversations
chunks.text:
- **Educate the audience.** Share things that save them time so they don't have to spend 1000 hours learning it. Content like this earns follows.
- You can also launch newsletters and info directories out of your expertise.
- **Ideas follow expertise.** If you have a crisis of ideas now, he says you'll have too many ideas after completing these steps.
- Discuss those ideas with your audience and build little tools to demonstrate them.
- He notes that often the person doesn't even make a tool, but instead "they are the tool."

chunks.heading: Step 5-6: Iterate with micro MVPs manually and treat it as a marathon
chunks.text:
- Spend months iterating with micro MVPs and doing things manually for your audience.
- Inevitably, one of the tools or services will gain more attention, and you'll clearly see where to put more time.
- Don't expect it to take weeks or months. John says to enter the game as if it were a marathon.
- If you're not prepared for a marathon, he says to go back to being employed, or "try dropshipping biz, I heard kids make millions there with no effort" (sarcastic).

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A satirical weekly news digest from John Rush on tech, startups and indie hacking drama. Few durable lessons: audience on X can replace YC's moat, consistency wins on YouTube, and indie scene hazards like clones and presale scams. Links to his lazy SEO playbook tweet, but the playbook itself isn't in this text.

chunks.heading: John's view that a big X following replaces Y Combinator
chunks.text:
- John says YC "isn't 'a must' anymore."
- In his view, 20k followers on X gives a moat similar to being in a YC batch.
- Two benefits he names:
  - Successful founders answer your DMs.
  - You get large inbound interest from VCs.
- He says he had no followers a year before and hit 40k by October 2024. His newsletter bio claims 20k followers and 30 million views on X, plus over 8,000 Substack subscribers.
- He treats audience-building as the founder's substitute for an accelerator network. He publishes startup playbooks, SEO and directory guides, and case studies like "From a Failed App to a Successful Vertical SaaS" to feed it.

chunks.heading: John's take on the SEO industry and his "lazy SEO" playbook
chunks.text:
- John says SEO is "living its chatgpt moment." Ahrefs and Semrush trash-talk each other publicly and compete by buying other firms.
- He chose not to join the fight. While they did, he published a "lazy SEO playbook" as an X thread on 2024-10-17 (https://x.com/johnrushx/status/1847272685463621937).
- The tactics are in the thread, not in this essay.
- He also runs a directory guide, "DirectoryVerse" (johnrush.me/directory-guide). He claims a "maker mafia" is going to take over the directory world.

chunks.heading: Copycats: what happens when a product gets traction
chunks.text:
- Someone cloned John's product ListingBott (listingbott.com), "even the name."
- He describes the indie hacker scene as turning into a reality show: clones, vanishing makers, and hate tweets.
- He argues that people who can't create value try to go viral by tweeting hate at successful makers.
- He notes that Zuckerberg wins by cloning successful products and even a successful look, and is "like water, adapts to any surface."
- Cloning is a standard play at every scale, so expect to be copied once you work.

chunks.heading: Presale scams and buyer trust
chunks.text:
- John cites a maker who ran a boilerplate presale and disappeared.
- Early backers had bought 143 lifetime deals (LTDs) on AppSumo in August alone, and are now suing their bank for chargebacks.
- The case shows why presales and lifetime deals depend on trust. A maker who takes money and vanishes damages the whole indie scene.

chunks.heading: Acquisitions as a way to control a market
chunks.text:
John groups three 2024 deals under "everyone wanna be a monopoly":
- **Webflow acquired Greensock.** His read is that the tool will now work only for Webflow and stop serving its competitors.
- **Semrush acquired Third Door Media.** His read is that startups are buying news media to control the narrative.
- **Stripe acquired a crypto startup.**

His reading is that companies buy the dependencies, media and distribution around them.

chunks.heading: Consistency beats excuses
chunks.text:
- John points to a creator who got 65 million YouTube subscribers in 2 months.
- His challenge to readers: "What stops you from doing the same? What's your excuse? Just keep showing up for 2 months and u win."
- It is the same bet as his own X growth: post consistently and let the audience compound.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: John announces his first directory exit (allGPTs.co sold to ChippAI for 5 figures) and a $99 pre-order guide on building, growing and monetizing directories. Mostly a sales pitch, but it outlines his results and the guide's scope: underserved ideas, keyword research, nocode, SEO, monetization.

chunks.heading: Directory track record and exit (as of Sep 2024)
chunks.text:
- John built his first directory, allGPTs.co, with no prior directory experience. He shared lessons publicly on Twitter over 12 months.
- allGPTs.co was acquired by ChippAI. He calls it his first "directory exit". The acquisition price was "5 figures" (no exact number given).
- He launched 20 directories in total. 5 turned out great, and he says they may become the best in their niche worldwide. Examples he names: nextjsstarter.com, osssoftware.org, mvpwizards.com.
- Across the directories he claims over 10 million users.
- He monetized them into passive income.
- He channeled directory traffic to his other SaaS tools, which he values at $1m+.

chunks.heading: Directories as a distribution and passive income asset
chunks.text:
- John treats directories as a repeatable play: launch many, keep the 5 of 20 that work, and monetize or sell them.
- Monetization methods he lists: affiliate links, sponsors, paid listings.
- Directories also act as a traffic channel feeding his other SaaS products.
- Selling the directory is an explicit end state in his playbook, as the allGPTs.co exit shows.

chunks.heading: What his directory guide covers
chunks.text:
John packaged what he "learned the hard way" into a paid guide after people kept asking him for a course. The topics:

- A detailed playbook for beginners and experienced builders.
- Finding underserved ideas.
- Keyword research.
- Building with no-code.
- Marketing via social media, Reddit, launchpads, blogs, SEO and influencers.
- Step-by-step SEO from zero.
- Monetizing with affiliate links, sponsors and paid listings.
- How to sell the directory.

chunks.heading: Pre-selling the guide
chunks.text:
- John sold the guide as a $99 pre-order before it was finished, at johnrush.me/directory-guide.
- His rationale: "The more people buy it, the more effort I'll put into making it great." Demand sets how much he invests.
- He had already shared the knowledge publicly on Twitter, and the sale was a response to repeated requests for a course.
- The launch post went viral on X.
- The target buyers: beginners starting a first startup, experienced founders launching side projects, and directory owners stuck at zero traffic.
- A commenter asked when the guide would be ready, which suggests the product was not yet delivered at pre-order time.

chunks.heading: Building an audience before selling
chunks.text:
- John built his audience first: about 20k followers, 30 million views on X, and over 8,000 Substack subscribers.
- He shared his tips publicly for 12 months, then offered the paid guide to people already asking for it.
- He sells credibility through numbers: 20 directories, 10 million users, $1m+ of tools fed by directory traffic, and a 5-figure exit.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: John Rush lists 28 lessons from a decade of failed and successful startups. Core themes: validate before building, chase users not investors, bootstrap, charge more, go paid-only, skip corporates and outsourcing, do SEO and daily posting early, and build for audiences you love.

chunks.heading: Validate first, sell features before building, and chase users not investors
chunks.text:
- John says he "wasted a decade building stuff nobody needed". He thought incubators and VCs counted as validation. They did not.
- He sells features before building them. He runs DMs with 10-20 users every day to talk through feature ideas, sees what resonates, and builds only those.
- Without followers, he suggests asking on HN, Reddit, or by searching X for relevant posts and replying with the question. People answer if the question is easy to understand.
- He says to kill your ego: "I must want what the user wants, not what I want. My taste isn't important."
- Chase users, not investors. Investor interest in him is at its highest now, when he is least interested in VCs.
- He expects to fail. Almost every startup fails, so he advises failing faster to reach the second and third iteration, and continuing until you find what works or find that nothing does.
- Drop a bad project within 1 year. Either the idea is too wrong to pivot, or the team is good individually but can't work as a team.

chunks.heading: Pricing: no free tier, and don't be too cheap
chunks.text:
- No free tier. John launched tools with free tiers and got sign-ups, but few converted. He treated free sign-ups as KPIs, bragged about sign-ups and visitors, and even raised VC money on those stats. He still never reached PMF, because his main feedback came from free users and the product became "a perfect free product".
- Free and paid users often need different products. He now goes "paid only" until the product is validated, and things went much better.
- Don't price lowest. He used to check all competitors and set the lowest price, thinking it was a key advantage. He says the $5 and $50 audiences are totally different.
  - $5 customers: "pain in the ass, never happy, never recommend you to a friend, leave in 4 months."
  - $50 customers: "polite, give genuine feedback, happy, share with friends, become your big fan if you solve their request."

chunks.heading: Distribution: global market, SEO, daily posting, and landing pages
chunks.text:
- Chase the global market from day 1. Pick a small niche in a global market rather than a large niche in a local one.
- Do SEO from day 2, as early as possible. He ignored it for 14 years and calls it his biggest regret.
- Post on Twitter/X daily. He started in March 2023 and it is his primary source of new connections and growth. He wishes he had started earlier.
- Write every single day. He restarted writing on X about 10 months before the essay and loves the process and the feedback. He has a spelling and letter-order issue and uses Grammarly to correct it.
- The landing page is the least important thing early on. Pick a simple template, edit it in a no-code website builder in under an hour, and move on. "Your first 100 sales happen outside of the website."

chunks.heading: Team and hiring before PMF
chunks.text:
- Never hire managers before PMF. Hire only doers. Many people know how to manage, few can "get sh*t done barehand".
- Hire only full-stack devs. A team of developers is the least productive setup for an early-stage product. One full-stack dev builds the whole product.
- Outsource nothing until PMF. Early on, everything needs to be done in a slightly different, more creative way that fits the vision. Outsourced people get no love for the product, treat it as another assignment, and focus on their own promotion or next job.
- Hire only people you would want to hug. His Danish cofounder told him this in 2015. If you don't want to hug someone, you dislike them on a "chemical/animal level", and conflict and a breakup will follow. A startup can take up to 10 years, so build it with people you have that connection with.
- Scrum is a scam. A team that must be nagged every morning "as if they were kindergarten children" will fail. His good work came from grownups who managed themselves, syncing on goals and plans over chat.

chunks.heading: Bootstrap, use boilerplates, and build B2B
chunks.text:
- Bootstrap. He raised money more than 10 times (preseed, seed, Series A). Each raise was a 3-9 month project with weekly meetings and lots of distraction. He could have bootstrapped but didn't know it was an option.
- Use boilerplates. He wasted years of dev time and millions of VC money building basic things: another sidebar, another dashboard, payment integration. Pride made him insist on 100% original code from scratch.
- Build B2B, not consumer apps. Consumer apps are like a lottery, with about 0.00001% making it big, and even with many users there is a monetization challenge. He spent 4 years on consumer apps and regrets it.
- Build for an audience you love. He found he had no love for corporates, consumers, or developers as audiences. He loves indie founders because they are risk-takers and partly kids at heart. Switching his focus to indie makers raised his joy "100x".

chunks.heading: Avoid corporates, conferences, and hype
chunks.text:
- Don't work or partner with corporates. They promise millions of users, but "every single time none of this happens". You talk to regular employees who waste your time, destroy focus, shift priorities, and bring no users or money.
- Tech conferences are a waste of time. They cost money, energy, and time, and you rarely meet anyone useful. Most attendees are loyal corporate employees sent as a perk, with very few fellow makers.
- Don't get distracted by hype. He lost 1.5 years to crypto and met scammers and thieves, including close friends who turned into thieves because it was so common in that space. He wishes he had stayed on his mission.

chunks.heading: Where to put money, and time horizon
chunks.text:
- Invest in your own startups and in friends, not crypto, stock market, or property.
  - He calculated that investing all his money in his friends' startups would have meant about 70 investments, and 3 became unicorns. Even 1 would have made the bank.
  - Since 2022 he has put all his money into his products, friends, and network.
  - Without startup friends, invest in yourself. Walk away from get-rich-quick options.
- Expect it to take a decade. At 20 he thought it took a few years, so he kept postponing family and kids until after an exit. He wishes he had married and had kids earlier.
- Spend time with family and friends. He missed the weddings of all his best friends and family, thinking the world would end if he didn't ship on time. He now says spending 10% of his time on family and friends would have had practically no negative impact on his startups.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: John argues that heavily funded startups are collapsing while profitable bootstrapped companies thrive. Too much money weakens a startup, user-funded businesses stay focused on users, and the best path is bootstrap first, use VC only for growth after PMF, or run a Holdco of cash cow projects as your own VC.

chunks.heading: Why John believes VC-funded startups are failing and bootstrapped ones are thriving
chunks.text:
- John lists well-funded companies that collapsed: Bird (scooters) filed for bankruptcy after raising almost $1B; WeWork filed for bankruptcy after once being valued at $47B; Olive AI (raised $0.9B), Convoy (raised $0.9B) and VeeV (raised $0.6B) shut down; Plastiq (raised $150M) shut down; Hopin (valued at $7B) sold for $15M.
- At the same time, he says profitable bootstrapped companies are thriving.
- His view: the future of SaaS and non-deep/hard-tech startups is "highly efficient bootstrapped small teams or even solo founders and indie makers."
- He has run both VC-funded and bootstrapped startups and says he knows both worlds well.

chunks.heading: Survival data: VC-funded vs bootstrapped founders
chunks.text:
- John says 99% of the VC-funded founders he knows went out of business (200+ startups).
- He doesn't know a single bootstrapped founder above $10k MRR who went out of business. Most are growing or selling for a good sum.
- These are his personal observations, not a formal study.

chunks.heading: Why too much money hurts the product
chunks.text:
- His analogy: "Having too much money while building your startup is like going to a gym with fake weights. You lift them, and it all looks good, but you gain no muscles."
- To build great stuff for users, the business must be funded by users. Then all focus goes on the users, not on the next round, VCs or journalists.

chunks.heading: Funding path John recommends
chunks.text:
- Best startups in today's world: bootstrap first, then use VC money for growth after product-market fit (PMF).
- Alternatives he expects more bootstrapped founders to use: community rounds, cheap loans and pre-sales. He wants to try all three eventually.
- Best option in his view: run a Holdco of simple cash-cow projects that bring in money every month, then act as your own VC when you need capital.
- He does this himself, building 24 projects for busy founders in his Holdco.

chunks.heading: John's startup ad marketplace: paying for a spot on your site
chunks.text:
- Offer (May 2024): John pays a site or app owner a fixed price every month.
- In return he controls a spot on the app or website and can place anything there: his SaaS products, directories, a newsletter.
- The owner gets a fixed, guaranteed income stream.
- Site owners sign up through his startup ad marketplace page at johnrush.me/startup-ad-marketplace.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: John shares his low-budget, founder-friendly SEO routine (under $1k, 0 to 1) and the 14 things that took Unicorn Platform to $300k ARR in 12 months. Covers redesign to cut churn, SEO stacking, directories, Product Hunt, Reddit, talking to users, cross-promo and word of mouth.

chunks.heading: John's low-budget SEO routine for busy founders
chunks.text:
John says SEO is not dead and drives a lot of traffic for him. His routine for a busy founder:

1. Launch the website and blog on Unicorn Platform.
2. Check keywords with Ubersuggest on the top 5 competitors, then edit the home page based on that.
3. Submit the sitemap to Google Search Console (GSC) and wait 1 month.
4. Activate listingbott.com to build up domain rating.
5. Turn on seobotai.com to produce 1 article a day.
6. Turn on indexrusher.com to index those pages.
7. After about a month, check GSC, manually pick the top-performing articles, improve them, and spend a full day on the 5 top articles.
8. Check the top GSC queries for the home page and edit the meta tags and h1/h2 to reflect them.
9. Spend 1 day a month repeating steps 7 and 8.

- He admits it is "not as good as if you pay an expert", but the total budget is below $1k and it takes you from 0 to 1.
- Once you are rich and successful, hire a pro to go from 1 to 10.

chunks.heading: How John did SEO for Unicorn Platform
chunks.text:
- A year earlier he knew very little about SEO. Instead of picking one strategy, he tried nearly all at once.
- He looked at keywords the site already ranked for and optimized those pages to win more traffic.
- He looked at competitors and wrote articles for the same keywords.
- He worked on domain rating until it reached almost 80.
- Half of his pages were not indexed, so he used an indexing tool.
- He wrote many articles on non-related topics for the same audience.
- He then built 3 tools to automate the work: Index Rusher (indexing), Listingbott (backlinks) and Seobot (articles).

chunks.heading: Directories as a traffic channel
chunks.text:
- John saw traffic from directories about 2 years earlier on another project (marsx), so he pushed hard to list Unicorn Platform everywhere. Most directories were not popular yet, and he got a good share of traffic as they went viral.
- He automated this with Listingbott, which keeps listing his tools on new directories as they appear.
- He owns over 20 directories, some very successful. He had a gut feeling about directories 3 years earlier, but friends said "Directories are out of hype by now.." and he dropped the idea.
- In November he launched the AllGpts directory, which went viral with millions of visits. After that he built a few new directories every month ("directory lord").
- He also sponsored a few other directories to place his banner. He likes it: there is traffic, ROI seems good, and he wants to do more of it, especially on directories visited by busy founders.

chunks.heading: Cross-promotion from his own product portfolio and partners
chunks.text:
- John has 24 products. The other 23 drive traffic to Unicorn Platform through footer links, banners and occasional email recommendations. About 30% of Unicorn's traffic comes this way.
- He partnered with Senja by adding their testimonial block to Unicorn's third-party blocks. Unicorn users add Senja blocks in a few clicks, he drove traffic to Senja, and Senja posted about the integration on social media and sent some traffic back.
- Possible next steps: each company emails its user base about the other.
- Next integration was RapidForms (multi-step forms, including payment steps), launching the following week.
- He invites other products that fit to collaborate, since both sides grow their user base.

chunks.heading: Social, Reddit, Product Hunt and word of mouth
chunks.text:
- **Social media:** He shared his actual steps, not just MRR numbers. Many posts went viral and helped other makers. X became a top 4 traffic source for sign-ups.
- **Reddit:** He had never used it, tried it in November, and the first attempt went viral. He mentioned Unicorn Platform in the text and had it as a link in his profile. Traffic went from 0.7 visitors a day to 7000 (his words: 1000% growth overnight). Reddit is evergreen, so traffic never really stopped.
- **Product Hunt:** Launched in July, took 2nd place with over 1000 upvotes. A win has a long aftershock because you end up in newsletters and blog articles.
- **Word of mouth:** He tracks it via social media mentions and calls it his most important metric, which together with SEO leads to product-market fit (PMF). In January the year before, viral "best landing page builders" posts never included Unicorn Platform. After the above work, 90% of mentions come organically.
- **Affiliates:** Running for 8 months. Partners bring sign-ups that convert to paying users. Easy to set up and no effort once running.
- **Paid ads:** He tried and failed. He thinks he may need to learn more, or "maybe it never works".

chunks.heading: Talking to users to cut churn and create referrals
chunks.text:
- John emailed every paid user asking for feedback and started a discussion. He talked to at least 300 of them.
- It surfaced low-hanging fixes to keep users, and created a strong network effect: many new users said a friend recommended Unicorn Platform.
- He now helps users every day, for free, for at least an hour a day: feedback on whatever they ask, tips and advice. He once connected a user raising a round to an investor.

chunks.heading: Redesign that cut churn and the $300k ARR result
chunks.text:
- Unicorn Platform reached $300k ARR on 2024-05-20, with 128,328 users having built sites, directories, job boards, launchpads and landing pages.
- He went through 1000+ support tickets one by one and boiled them down to 100 frequent requests. Fixing them all would have taken a year.
- After sleeping on it for a few weeks, he realized about half could be solved by changing the whole UX from page-based to canvas-based, like Notion: one canvas with a page, and everything else in popups.
- That erased 80% of the backlog tasks. The remaining 20% were then tackled (not all done yet).
- Churn dropped from double-digit to single-digit.
- He also hired a designer to create many new templates and components, and was working on an update meant to 10x Unicorn's visual power.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: John Rush lists the 78 paid products he uses across hosting, dev, AI, testing, support, marketing, legal and more to run 24 projects, plus 4 of his own products. He picked each after trial and error on price, features and UX, and stays open to switching to better alternatives.

chunks.heading: John Rush's tool stack: 78 paid products across 24 projects (May 2024)
chunks.text:
- In May 2024 John said he pays for 78 products to run his 24 projects.
- He says it took "many trials and errors to find best tools on price/features/UX."
- He is open to switching: if someone knows a better alternative, he may move to it.
- He also uses 4 of his own products on top of the 78 (see the last section).

chunks.heading: Hosting, cloud and databases
chunks.text:
- Hosting: Digital Ocean, AWS (hosting, storage, CDN), Hetzner (bare metal), Monovm, Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure (websites and tables), Vercel (Next.js hosting), appliku (web app deployment).
- Databases: Heroku for db hosting, Supabase as CMS and DB, MongoDB Atlas for NoSQL, Pinecone for vector db.
- Code: GitHub for teams.
- Cloudflare for DDoS protection, IPs, storage and AI.
- BunnyCDN for images.

chunks.heading: Dev, design and web tooling
chunks.text:
- Design and docs: Figma for design and mockups, Canva for videos, Excalidraw for wireframes, Notion for docs, FloatUI as a Tailwind UI kit.
- Image handling: IMGIX for resizing, UploadCare for upload and storage.
- Scraping and automation: Apify for web automation, Scrapingbee to scrape the internet, ScreenshotOne as a screenshot API, Serper for Google search via API, Proxysell for proxies.
- Internal tooling: Fibery.
- Twilio for SMS.

chunks.heading: AI and LLMs
chunks.text:
- OpenAI for LLMs and image generation, plus Azure OpenAI.
- Anthropic for the Claude LLM.
- ChatGPT as a separate subscription.
- Pinecone as the vector db.

chunks.heading: Testing, monitoring and security
chunks.text:
- Server monitoring: New Relic.
- JS event logging: Sentry.
- Uptime monitoring: StatusCake and UptimeRobot (both).
- End-to-end testing: Ghost Inspector (visual), LambdaTest, Qase.
- Cloudflare for DDoS protection.

chunks.heading: Email, support and communication
chunks.text:
- Email sending: SendGrid, Sensorpro, Sinch Mailjet, Mailtrap, AWS SES, Loops (campaigns).
- Google (G Suite) for email and drive.
- Support: Crisp and Intercom.
- Calls and internal comms: Zoom to record calls, Loom for internal async communication, TLDR to record and transcribe meetings.
- Enterprise clients: Slack for shared channels, Microsoft Teams, Skype for a shared US phone number.
- 1Password to share passwords across the team.
- Hubstaff to track hours to bill enterprise clients.

chunks.heading: Payments, marketing, legal and finance
chunks.text:
- Payments: Stripe, Paddle, Gumroad.
- Affiliates: FirstPromoter for affiliate partners.
- Ads: Facebook ads and Google Ads.
- X (Twitter) for verified badges.
- Domains: GoDaddy and Namecheap.
- Ipostal for a postal address.
- App stores: Google Play for Android apps, Apple Developer account for iOS apps.
- Legal and finance: PandaDoc for legal paperwork and docs, QuickBooks for accounting, Mercury for banking, Carta for cap table.
- Other listed: Grammarly ("to fix my dyslexia"), VeeD for videos, Black Magic for Twitter, Zenvoice, Indie Hackers portal subscription, startups.com.
- A commenter suggested Lemon Squeezy for payments that handle taxes at a reasonable price; John replied, but the reply text isn't in the source.

chunks.heading: John's own products used in his stack
chunks.text:
- Unicorn Platform: builds websites, waitlists, directories and landing pages.
- SeoBOT: researches and generates blog articles.
- ListingBott: grows domain rating and lists his products on all web directories with one click.
- IndexRusher: forces Google to index his pages faster.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: John Rush shares the playbook he used to go from invisible to 50M views and 40k followers, which helped him reach 140,000 users with Unicorn Platform. He argues for one platform, followers as the KPI, deep expertise in one niche, and content aimed at your buyers rather than a broad audience.

chunks.heading: Context and results behind John's audience-building playbook
chunks.text:
- John says he was invisible on the internet a year before writing this essay (dated 2024-05-08): no followers, no views.
- By then he had 50 million views and 40k followers across all platforms combined, and had reached 140,000 users with Unicorn Platform.
- His playbook for founders building an audience comes from that experience.

chunks.heading: Pick one platform and learn to write on it
chunks.text:
- He puts 100% of focus on one platform. Until you reach several thousand followers and good content quality, creating content, engaging with people and understanding the algorithm take hours daily.
- He says "Learn to write by writing." It is not about hacking the algorithm or copy-pasting memes.
- Good writing is an asset that helps win every other platform later, so the first platform is a training camp.
- He suggests Twitter as the first platform. It has the shortest feedback loop, and you can create 10 daily posts to practice.

chunks.heading: Measure followers, not views
chunks.text:
- Follower count is his critical KPI. He says to focus on followers, not pure views.
- Users follow when content creates respect for the author. A random meme reposted from another platform does not make people interested in you.
- Avoid negative content. It gets views quickly, but he wants "new followers" as the measure of content quality.

chunks.heading: Stay on one topic and know more than the average
chunks.text:
- He says to "hit on the same target until you crack a hole there."
- A common mistake is throwing out all sorts of topics hoping one goes viral. Even if one does, you cannot reproduce it later.
- Once you pick a primary topic, add your own takes, experiments and experience. Reposting known theory is not enough; personal practice makes the information valuable.
- This takes thousands of hours digging into the topic to become one of the top 0.1% experts. He says there is no other way, unless you want followers for short cat videos or dancing TikToks.

chunks.heading: Not every follower counts for B2B
chunks.text:
- A B2B founder's goal is eventually a distribution channel over social media. People who consume short entertainment content will not help.
- Example: a friend with almost a million followers launched SaaS tools and got fewer than 10 sales, because that audience didn't care about them.
- John launched all his products via social media and got far more than 10 sales instantly, with 20x fewer followers than that friend.
- Produce content for your followers, not for everyone else.
- Learn from creators who have the audience you want. For a B2B audience you cannot learn from Mr.Beast; you may end up doing the opposite of him to win.

chunks.heading: Anatomy of the ideal post or article
chunks.text:
- High effort.
- A mix of theory, practice and facts.
- Grabs attention from the start and keeps the reader to the end.
- Easy to scan instead of read.
- Has a clear audience.
- Intersects with popular topics or views.
- Relevant to your persona. Don't talk about VC money if you never raised it.
- Has a killer headline.

chunks.heading: What to avoid when building an audience
chunks.text:
- Talking about things you have no proven track record in.
- Being negative.
- Memes, unless you actually invent them (he cites Dago).
- Low-effort posts. If a post takes less than an hour, it will be bad in 99.9% of cases.
- Random topics such as JS, politics or dogs.
- Talking about yourself, your habits or your opinions.
- Asking questions.
- Asking friends to add fake likes and replies, or buying fake engagement.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: John walks through his playbook for a niche directory site: spot a hyped topic, validate with Google Keyword Planner, buy a .com, build the directory fast, generate content with AI, force indexing, and monetize via featured spots. He stresses letting a new domain warm up and not launching many pages at once.

chunks.heading: Playbook: building a niche directory site in about 8 hours
chunks.text:
John built a directory around a hot topic (Next.js boilerplates) and monetized the SEO traffic. His sequence:
1. Spot a hot topic.
2. Check Google search volume.
3. Find a high-traffic keyword.
4. Buy a domain on GoDaddy.
5. Build the directory.
6. Get SEO traffic.
7. Earn from sponsors, ads and referrals.

He says it took him 8 hours in total and that "anyone can do this."

chunks.heading: Picking the topic, keyword and domain
chunks.text:
- John saw hype around Next.js boilerplates. He searched the term in Google Keyword Planner and found low-competition keywords with good traffic.
- Keyword Planner is his idea source: search the hot topic and look for low-competition, decent-traffic terms.
- He searched for the domain on GoDaddy and always starts with .com. After his tests, ".com beats crap out of everything else."
- He bought nextjsstarter.com, a domain that matches the keyword.

chunks.heading: Building the directory fast
chunks.text:
- He built the site in under an hour from a template using his own builder, Unicorn Platforms (a directory template).
- He made the logo with ChatGPT's DALL-E.
- He took the top 10 keywords from Google Keyword Planner and placed them on the home page.
- To fill it, he scraped dev tools from Product Hunt and DevHunt and found every boilerplate listed there. He also searched Hacker News, dev.to, GitHub, Google and X.
- That gave about 50 items. Authors then submitted about 100 more through a form.

chunks.heading: SEO content and indexing
chunks.text:
- He turned on SEObot to generate 100 blog articles. The articles came out really good, and he learned a few things reading them.
- He turned on IndexRusher to get all 250 pages indexed. He notes a new domain can take months or longer to get indexed otherwise.
- He launched the site first and let it warm up for 2 months. The blog went live in month 3.
- Traffic grew day after day.
- Lesson: "Whenever I tried launched many pages at once, I failed at growing the site."

chunks.heading: Monetization
chunks.text:
- Decent SEO traffic plus click traffic from a few viral posts and blogs made the site attractive to Next.js boilerplate authors.
- His main revenue was selling "featured-spot" placements to those authors. He also lists sponsors, ads and referrals as revenue sources.
- Because the audience is the boilerplate authors' target buyers, the directory sells them exposure directly.

chunks.heading: Next steps John planned
chunks.text:
- More blog articles around Next.js "how-tos."
- Programmatic SEO (he says he has "a crazy cool idea" for it).
- Run ListingBott to grow domain rating by getting 100 more backlinks pointing to the pages that already have traffic.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A newsletter roundup of John Rush's X and LinkedIn posts. It gives his 13-step idea-to-revenue method (SEO and social validation and a waitlist before coding), his 2023 growth results (social media worked; partners, ads, outreach and hiring a marketer failed), and his plan to launch 1000 products on a SaaS OS.

chunks.heading: Series A round killed John's mobile-turned-B2B startup (teaser)
chunks.text:
- John's startup graduated from 500 Startups and raised a seed round.
- The team pivoted from a mobile app into B2B SaaS.
- It found product-market fit quickly and lined up a bunch of clients.
- The team was working 100 hours a week to deliver for those clients.
- The newsletter only teases the story. The full version is a LinkedIn post (4311 likes, 367 comments, 100 reposts), and this source does not say how the Series A killed the company.

chunks.heading: 13-step process from idea to revenue
chunks.text:
John says he has used this method in most of his products and that it "worked so well". The steps, in order:

1. Idea
2. SEO potential
3. Pick the least competitive option
4. Social validation
5. Waitlist
6. Organic promo
7. Paid promo
8. Directories and SEO
9. Check whether there is traction
10. Code the MVP
11. Turn the coding into marketing
12. Iterate
13. Public launch

- Validation, waitlist and promotion all come before the MVP is coded.
- Coding only starts at step 10, after the traction check in step 9.
- Step 11 treats the build itself as marketing material.
- The public launch comes last.

chunks.heading: Growth channels that failed vs worked for John in 2023
chunks.text:
**Failed:**
- Partners
- Newsletter ads
- Podcasts
- Outreach
- Google, Facebook and Twitter ads
- Hiring a marketing person
- Paying influencers

**Worked:**
- Social media. This is the only channel he lists as working.

He lists the failures without detail. The full breakdown is in his X post.

chunks.heading: "End of SaaS, birth of SaaS OS": John's 2025 bet
chunks.text:
- By the end of 2025, John plans to launch 1000 products.
- The products will run on a new "SaaS OS".
- He says it will transform the software world as we know it.
- His framing: "You won't take it seriously until it happens."
- This is a prediction and a goal he stated in January 2024. The source gives no mechanics of how the SaaS OS works.

chunks.heading: John's public-building stance (2024 start)
chunks.text:
- John describes his newsletter as "Sharing startup tips while building SaaS Empire", with 20k followers and 30 million views on X.
- He credits a group of bootstrapped-founder authors for the lessons he took away every day in 2023. They inspired him to share his own learnings in public.
- He started 2024 with a free giveaway of unconditional advice to fellow founders. Topics covered growth, website, SEO, social, design, features, making a first sale, coming up with an idea, fundraising and building fast.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: John Rush predicts a flood of indie makers, multi-product makers and "maker labels", where distribution is 90% of winning. He explains why Google Sheets replaced databases for his directories (10M clicks, $0 revenue so far), and his plan for a pay-per-click directory promo network.

chunks.heading: John's 2024-2026 prediction: makers multiply and build many products
chunks.text:
- He predicts exponential growth in the number of indie makers. Almost every corporate dev is building a side project or planning to.
- Example from uptime bots: 10 in 2020, 20 in 2021, 30 in 2022, 60 in 2023. He projects 200+ in 2024 and 1000+ in 2025.
- Reason: "1% of tech is complicated rocket science, but the rest is an easy 2 week project for a good productive developer who uses the right tools."
- Analogy: popular singers launch brands, act in movies and make commercials because they have a distribution channel and can push almost anything to a loyal audience. He says tech is entering the same world.
- There is a limit to how perfect one SaaS can get. After that comes overengineering: users are happy but the maker keeps adding things nobody asked for. So makers build more tools for the same audience instead of endless features.
- By end of 2024 he expects very few makers doing a single product. Most will run many, some more than 10, some more than 100.

chunks.heading: Distribution beats dev force: corporates and VCs lose
chunks.text:
- He is "totally bearish on corporates" in the new world. They have a large dev force and little distribution force. "In the new world, distribution is 90% of what one needs to win."
- Corporates will launch new brands that pretend to be standalone, not products under their own brand.
- He calls the old VC-backed startup world a thing of the past that won't come back. Money no longer helps growth, so what everyone needs is distribution channels.
- He expects 99% of VC money to go into "platforms" that few devs can build. Tools, sites, SaaS and apps will be bootstrapped, self-funded or funded by "maker labels".

chunks.heading: Maker + influencer collabs and "maker labels"
chunks.text:
**Collabs**
- Influencers with over a million followers no longer make good money. He says the value of a single follower dropped 100x because the number of people with over 100k followers grew 100x, and brands and ads pay little.
- He predicts influencers will partner with indie makers to build a product for their audience and split the profits. Those who do it first "gonna make millions".

**Maker labels**
- Like music labels, movie studios and sports agents, almost no famous star is on their own. Labels handle groundwork, contracts, negotiation and distribution so the artist focuses on the craft.
- The same will happen to indie makers through alliances, startup studios and holdcos.
- Benefit 1: makers focus on product, UX, talking to users and product-led promotion instead of everything else.
- Benefit 2 (the bigger one): distribution. If an alliance has 50 makers, their audiences cross-promote. Fully independent makers will struggle against those in alliances.
- He notes maker "groups" already support each other's tweets and Product Hunt launches, and says he respects them.
- Final prediction: this leads to several monopolies taking most of the audience. He cites Peter Thiel: "competition is for the losers", and the winner makes a monopoly.

chunks.heading: Google Sheets as the database for public directories
chunks.text:
- After 15 years of using databases, in 2023 he switched his public projects and directories to Google Sheets.
- Origin story: he launched osssoftware one night and posted on Hacker News, dev.to and X. It went viral overnight with over 20K visitors. Hundreds of comments came in about data quality, corrections and suggestions. He couldn't keep up, so he made the sheet public so everyone could comment.
- Result: osssoftware.org became a crowd-sourced directory of open-source projects. He says building comment-moderation software would have been a waste.
- Benefits: free regardless of traffic or users, and "100x easier" to edit and maintain from user feedback than a conventional database.
- His directories run on unicornplatform.com plus Google Sheets: allgpts.co, osssoftware.org, nextjsstarter.com, topwebsitebuilders.org.
- Next planned on the same stack: auth, ratings, reviews, bookmarking, comments, upvotes, all on publicly open Google Sheets.
- Transparency angle: anyone can verify the data is real, since the sheet has public revision history. He calls this "decentralized immutable storage" that people hoped to get from blockchain.

chunks.heading: Forced Google indexing (IndexGoogle) and SEObot quality
chunks.text:
- He underestimated forced Google indexing. He turned on indexgoogle.com for internal testing 2 weeks earlier and was pleased with the results.
- Getting the Google Indexing API to work for an unlimited number of pages was hard because of limits. Google granted a large API quota, so he planned to launch the following week.
- Waitlist invites go out at 10 a day. SEObot (seobotai.com) users get it included in the "PRO" subscription.
- On SEObot he is "100% bullish" on generating articles that humans enjoy reading and Google ranks high. "We're not in the garbage content business."
- Quality approach: he spends almost a dollar per article, because each goes through numerous cycles of generation, improvement and research.

chunks.heading: Maker Experiment #5: 15 micro SaaS tools
chunks.text:
- He stops building directories ("It all works now") and plans 90 more by the end of 2024.
- New experiment: 15 basic SaaS tools, each doing one thing clearly, with a one-button user experience. Domains are chosen purely from SEO research.
- He says he has been calling this the next big trend and now wants to test whether he's right.
- Product types: Blog, Website, CV, Help Desk, Docs, and a directory from Google Sheet / Notion / Airtable.
- They are 15 separate products and also available as apps inside Unicorn Platform.
- Pricing: no subscription, but a lifetime deal option. He plans to add a lifetime deal option to all his products.

chunks.heading: Directory promo network: 10M clicks, $0 revenue, and the plan
chunks.text:
- His directories (allgpts.co, devhunt.org, osssoftware.org, nextjsstarter.com, topwebsitebuilders.org) drove 10 million clicks to third-party projects. Revenue so far: $0.
- Plan: build a directory promo network. ListingBott was the first step, but he realized convincing directory owners to join a new project from a no-name would be hard.
- Workaround: launch 100 successful directories, each with Domain Rating above 30 and over 10k visitors a month. Then build the promo network on top of them. Once it has clients and revenue, it is easier to recruit other directory owners.
- How it works: an indie maker or small startup with low DR or traffic enters a URL and loads $100. The tool finds the most relevant directories and features the product there until it reaches the click target (for example $100 buys 100 clicks), then removes it from all featured sections. Buyers can try it for as little as $5 for 5 clicks.
- Why: most directories monetize badly (Google Ads, Carbon Ads, irrelevant banners). He knows owners with millions of visitors making just a few thousand dollars a month.
- Best monetization is selling "sponsored" spots, but finding a buyer is hard and buyers can't judge directory quality. Software and AI would match promoted products with relevant directories.
- He said he was open to partnering with other directory founders and expected more in January.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: John recaps a week across 20+ projects. Directory sites (allgpts, osssoftware) pulled big traffic, PH launches are losing value versus tweets and HN/dev.to posts, and virality does not equal revenue. He also shares lifetime-deal pricing for indexgoogle.

chunks.heading: Directories as a viral traffic play (osssoftware.org, allgpts.co, Unicorn Platform)
chunks.text:
- John launched osssoftware.org and it took off. It reached an estimated 100k+ visits and made headlines on Hacker News, Twitter and dev.to. His takeaway: "you never know what will work until you try."
- allgpts.co hit 0.5M visits. It is a directory of GPTs.
- John says Unicorn Platform got a big push from its new "directory" template. Users can build directories quickly and at low cost.
- Unicorn Platform had its biggest single-month growth in paying users since launch, and paying-user growth has continued for 4 months in a row.
- He planned 2 new directories and further Unicorn directory features (such as nested pages) the following week.

chunks.heading: Virality is not revenue: Marketsy.ai after a #1 Product Hunt launch
chunks.text:
- Marketsy.ai ranked #1 on Product Hunt and drew huge traffic, but few visitors converted into paying users.
- It is still searching for product-market fit.
- John launched a lifetime deal (LTD) on AppSumo to learn more about user patterns.
- His lesson: "Going viral doesn't always mean making money."

chunks.heading: Product Hunt versus tweets, Hacker News and dev.to
chunks.text:
- Floatui v2, a free open-source Tailwind CSS UI kit, placed #6th on its Product Hunt launch. That fell short of his expectations.
- John is stepping back from promoting PH launches. He says they "don't seem valuable anymore" compared to tweets or posts on Hacker News or dev.to.
- Floatui is loved by developers and he plans to keep improving it.
- Nextjsstarter.com launched with around 1000 visitors. He calls that "not viral, but not bad either."

chunks.heading: Whether to sell or keep allgpts.co: acquisition offers and valuation checks
